title: Video Generation Meets Agent Harness: Agentic Video Generation, Agentic World Modeling and Recursive Self-Improvement
authors: Liaoyuan Fan; Yuhao Zheng; Dongxing Mao; Hangyu Ran; Siyuan Hu; Weijia Mao; Rui Zhao; Weijia Wu; Guian Fang; Yanzhe Chen; Zeyu Zhu; Yuxin Jiang; Yiren Song; Yuchao Gu; Junchao Yi; Qi Hu; Dan Kong; Alex Jinpeng Wang; Kevin Qinghong Lin; Mike Zheng Shou; Wei Liu
abstract: Video generation is shifting from end-to-end synthesis toward agentic generation, where planning, tool use, and feedback enable coherent, controllable multi-shot videos. In parallel, video world models provide action-conditioned observations and predicted futures, serving as interactive environments for agents. We study their intersection through the agent harness: an executable runtime that constructs context, exposes tools, maintains state, routes feedback, and manages budgets around video models. This report examines three directions. First, agentic video generation, where harnesses coordinate scripting, shot planning, asset management, production, and editing, alongside the evaluation challenges of these systems. Second, agentic world modeling, where harnesses mediate observation, control, execution, and state. We discuss hybrid designs in which game engines or agent-written programs maintain world state while video models render observations, and how agents and world models can mutually evaluate and improve one another. Third, recursive self-improvement (RSI) in video model development, distinguishing output revisions, updates to harness state, generator parameters, and evaluators, and changes to the improvement procedure itself. We identify how these improvements feed back into subsequent development. Across these directions, we analyze essential agent capabilities, including audiovisual perception, long-horizon planning, memory, code-based interaction, feedback-guided control, skill reuse, and multi-agent coordination. We conclude with challenges in autonomous video production, lifelong memory, programmable hybrid control, autonomous model development, provenance, cost accounting, and evaluation linking video quality and task performance to sustained improvements in models and harnesses.

title: Quantum Graph-Based Robotic Optimization Controller
authors: Murali Krishna Pasupuleti
abstract: Abstract Quantum Graph-Based Robotic Optimization Controller develops an integrated architecture for representing, learning and optimizing robotic decisions through graph-structured state, hybrid quantum-classical search and safety-governed control. The monograph treats robot bodies, objects, tasks, resources and cooperating agents as relational systems whose topology changes with motion and mission context. It connects graph theory, statistical modeling, causal inference, graph neural networks, reinforcement learning, digital twins, operations research, quantum-inspired optimization and runtime assurance within a reproducible experimental lifecycle. The framework distinguishes structural representation from solver choice: quantum or quantum-inspired routines are invoked only after constraints, objective terms and feasibility conditions retain their robotic meaning. Statistical chapters formalize heterogeneity, intervention effects, dynamic graph processes, rare-event risk and fair benchmarking. Machine-learning chapters address relational generalization, predictive world models, robust policy learning, distribution shift, explainability and verification. Engineering chapters integrate telemetry contracts, scalable simulation, graph repositories, model lineage, MLOps, cybersecurity and post-quantum readiness. Sectoral analysis considers manufacturing, healthcare, agriculture, infrastructure, logistics and networked robotics across South Asia, Europe, Africa and the Americas. The result is a research-oriented controller blueprint producing mathematical models, evaluation metrics, operational protocols, governance artifacts and invention-oriented system designs. title: What Does an Agent Perceive as Possible? Perception, Passibility and the Architecture of Navigation Across Robots, Vehicles, Spacecraft and World Models
authors: Gonçalo Melo de Magalhães
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Navigation is usually described as a stack: sense, estimate, map, plan, control. This paper asks what problem the stack solves, and whether the Architecture of Freedom Intelligence (AFI) — a theory that treats path availability as the first condition of any becoming, and intelligence as the capacity to perceive and widen that availability — adds a usable structure to it. We reconstruct how contemporary systems navigate from primary sources: classical mobile robots, Tesla's and Waymo's driving stacks, SpaceX Dragon's rendezvous guidance, video world models (V-JEPA 2, DreamerV3, Navigation World Models, the Waymo World Model) and embodied foundation models (π0.5, Gemini Robotics 1.5, GR00T N1.6, NavFoM), using 48 sources dated 2025 or later. One object recurs in every architecture: an agent-relative set of continuations treated as open. Spacecraft compute it from physics as a reachable set; Waymo materialises it as proposals checked by a validation layer; a costmap thresholds it; a world model leaves it implicit in a sampler; a vision-language-action policy emits one continuation and keeps the rest unrepresented. We then reconstruct AFI from its primary documents, including its own negative results — the failed multiplicative decomposition of its reality architecture, perception alone outperforming the perception-to-distortion ratio at graph level, the collapse of a scalar freedom field in continuous space, and the circularity of an alignment-based perception measure — and reduce each AFI concept against partially observable Markov decision processes, active inference, empowerment and maximum occupancy, reachability and viability, affordances and world models. Three moves survive reduction: perception measured as a set before choice, with real and unreal continuations separated into hidden and false paths; passibility as a layer between proposal and order; and transformation of the path space as a first-class action class. A pre-registered experiment in partially observable grid worlds tests the candidate planner against belief-rollout, empowerment-regularised and point-model planners. The pre-registered AFI planner fails by refusing to commit where the perceived set is widest; a corrected form, anchored on progress and aggregated multiplicatively across possible worlds, coincides with belief-rollout planning in every world and separates from goal-agnostic empowerment where a region rich in reachable states carries zero routes to the goal. Pre-choice perception metrics predict outcome for a reactive planner and lose predictive power for a hedging one. We conclude that AFI's contribution to navigation is a measurement protocol on perception and an architectural requirement on passibility, rather than a new predictive law, and we state the conditions under which that conclusion would change. The solution, called Topo-CBP (Topologically Anchored Continual Backpropagation), partitions parameter manifolds into: An invariant prime coordinate ring anchored to the first six prime coordinates {2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13}, capturing 97.85% of representation spectral energy An Euler-attenuated plastic subspace governed by continuous unit utility tracking and recycling The framework is validated on a single NVIDIA workstation GPU using an autonomous multi-agent deliberative council spanning five certified foundation models. title: The Heterophilic Snowflake Hypothesis: Training and Empowering GNNs for Heterophilic Graphs
authors: Kun Wang; Guibin Zhang; Xinnan Zhang; Junfeng Fang; Xun Wu; Guohao Li; Shirui Pan; Wei Huang; Yuxuan Liang
venue: ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining (KDD)
abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become pivotal tools for a range of graph-based learning tasks.Notably, most current GNN architectures operate under the assumption of homophily, whether explicitly or implicitly.While this underlying assumption is frequently adopted, it is not universally applicable, which can result in potential shortcomings in learning effectiveness.In this paper, for the first time, we transfer the prevailing concept of "one node one receptive field" to the heterophilic graph.By constructing a proxy label predictor, we enable each node to possess a latent prediction distribution, which assists connected nodes in determining whether they should aggregate their associated neighbors.Ultimately, every node can have its own unique aggregation hop and pattern, much like each snowflake is unique and possesses its own characteristics.Based on observations, we innovatively introduce the Heterophily Snowflake Hypothesis and provide an effective solution to guide and facilitate research on heterophilic graphs and beyond.We conduct comprehensive experiments including (1) main results on 10 graphs with varying heterophily ratios across 10 backbones; (2) scalability on various deep GNN backbones (SGC, JKNet, etc.) across various large number of layers (2,4,6,8,16,32 layers); (3) comparison with conventional snowflake hypothesis; (4) efficiency comparison with existing graph pruning algorithms.

title: Unified Scene Graph Forecasting Considering Node Birth and Disappearance
authors: Tatsuki Seino; Naoki Saito; Takahiro Ogawa; Satoshi Asamizu; Miki Haseyama
venue: IEEE International Conference on Consumer Technology (ICCT-Pacific)
abstract: This paper presents a unified scene graph forecasting method that considers node birth and disappearance. The main contribution of this work is the realization of scene graph forecasting that simultaneously predicts object categories, spatial positions, and relationships while accounting for node birth and disappearance. Conventional scene graph forecasting methods assume a fixed set of nodes, making it difficult to handle real-world scenarios where objects are dynamic. To address this problem, the proposed method introduces a Birth–disappearance Dynamics Processing Unit (BDPU) that probabilistically models object birth and disappearance using stochastic differential equations, as well as an extended Latent Dynamics Processing Unit (LDPU) that predicts the temporal evolution of relationships conditioned on node existence probabilities. Consequently, the proposed method enables temporally consistent and structurally complete scene graph forecasting in dynamic environments. The effectiveness of the proposed method is verified through experiments on the Action Genome dataset, where it outperforms existing approaches.

title: World-Model-Enhanced UAV Intelligent Inspection Method for Converter Station Valve Halls
authors: Yiqiu Li; Lijie Ding; Ming He; Wei Wei; Linglu Zhang; Zeyu Chen
venue: International Conference on Computer Information Science and Application Technology (CISAT)
abstract: To address the enclosed space, dense equipment, GNSS-denied operation, and stringent energized-safety constraints of converter-station valve halls, this paper proposes a world-model-enhanced multisensor UAV inspection method. Visible-light images, infrared thermograms, LiDAR point clouds, depth images, inertial measurement unit (IMU) data, and ultra-wideband (UWB) measurements are unified in an evidence-constrained temporal graph of devices, defects, evidence, and constraints. Equipment ledgers, inspection procedures, historical closed-loop defect records, and manual-review conclusions are then introduced to form a knowledge-enhanced large language model (LLM) reasoning mechanism and an active reinspection decision process. Field validation shows that the proposed method achieves a defect-recognition F1-score of 95.4%, a risk-level accuracy of 93.4%, and an LLM hallucination rate of 1.9%. By integrating multimodal perception, structured world state, knowledge retrieval, and safety gating within a single closed loop, the method improves the interpretability, traceability, and engineering applicability of valve-hall inspection.

title: Generative World Models for Financial Risk Propagation and Counterfactual Fraud Analysis in Enterprise Networks
authors: Ning Hu; Jiaxiang Xiao
abstract: Abstract Financial fraud and enterprise risk rarely emerge as independent node-level events: liquidity stress, suspicious payments, ownership dependencies, guarantee relations, and transaction chains create interacting pathways through which local shocks may spread across a financial network. Existing graph fraud detectors are effective at classifying suspicious entities, while recent temporal graph models and generative world models improve sequence prediction. However, a risk-management system also needs to answer a different class of questions: what future network state would arise under a specified intervention, which transmission channels would carry the shock, and how much fraud or systemic risk would have been avoided under a counterfactual policy? We formulate these questions within a unified interventional generative process and propose RIFT-WM, a Risk-Intervention Flow Transport World Model. Its central object is an action-indexed stochastic infinitesimal generator whose semigroup jointly governs continuous latent-risk drift, topology-aware risk transport, discrete fraud jumps, and event intensities. Counterfactuals are generated by abducting episode-specific structural disturbances and reusing the same disturbances in factual and intervened ''twin worlds,'' so that only the designated mechanism changes. A sub-stochastic transport constraint prevents unexplained creation of endogenous risk mass, while semigroup consistency makes predictions coherent across temporal resolutions and rollout horizons. We further derive intervention influence operators, enterprise-level counterfactual effects, and network-level systemic-risk decompositions from the same generator. The evaluation framework spans Elliptic, Elliptic++, T-Finance, DGraph-Fin, AMLSim, and PaySim and covers fraud detection, long-horizon forecasting, calibration, counterfactual recovery, robustness, and efficiency. Counterfactual claims are restricted to controlled simulator settings in which interventions can be replayed under matched exogenous disturbances. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/RIFT_WM-4151/.

title: RELATIONAL PATTERNIST SYNTHESIS: Ontology, Semiotics, and Structural Realism
authors: Rowan Brad Quni-Gudzinas
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: I. CORE RESEARCH QUESTIONS The Ontological Question: In a universe described by multiple, scale-relative scientific theories (from quantum fields to fluid dynamics to intentional agents), what constitutes a “real” entity, and how do we distinguish objective structure from subjective noise? The Semiotic Question: How can we reconcile the arbitrary, convention-based nature of human language (Saussurean shared meaning) with the existence of universal, objective physical patterns? The Mathematical Question: If discrete counting (integers/primes) and absolute metrics (infinities/real numbers) are biologically bootstrapped, anthropocentric cognitive artifacts, what mathematical framework accurately captures the base-invariant, coordinate-free reality of the universe? II. THESES Primary Thesis: Ontic Structural Patternism Reality is fundamentally composed not of discrete objects, absolute metrics, or fundamental particles, but of scale-relative, compressible relational patterns. While human languages and discrete mathematics (such as integers and primes) are biologically bootstrapped, anthropocentric conventions used to navigate these patterns, the underlying structural relationships—expressed mathematically as invariant ratios—constitute the true, universal ontology of the cosmos. Sub-Thesis A: Epistemic Finitism & The Illusion of the “Bit-Map” Absolute infinities and discrete coordinate systems are cognitive artifacts (tools for lossy compression) rather than physical realities. The “bit-map” of the universe is computably finite; therefore, any mathematical framework relying on infinite limits or absolute discrete counting (including -adic/Adelic number theory) is an anthropocentric projection rather than a universal baseline. Sub-Thesis B: Projective Invariance as Universal Syntax Meaning and physical reality do not reside in isolated nodes (the “things,” “words,” or “integers”) but strictly in the invariant proportions between them. Just as the Cross-Ratio in projective geometry remains absolutely invariant under arbitrary coordinate transformations (Möbius transformations), universal physical and syntactic truths remain invariant regardless of the arbitrary linguistic or cultural frameworks used to express them. III. EXECUTIVE SUUMMARY 1. Introduction: The Crisis of the “Desert Landscape” 1.1 The Failure of Strict Reductionism: Quine’s “desert landscape” (where only fundamental particles exist) fails to account for the predictive power of higher-level sciences. 1.2 The Linguistic Veil: The tension between arbitrary human semiotics (words mean what we agree they mean) and the objective structure of the universe. 1.3 The Goal: To establish a universal, base-invariant framework that bridges human cognition, artificial intelligence, and fundamental physics without relying on anthropocentric mathematical conventions. 2. The “Real Patterns” Foundation (Dennett to 2026) 2.1 Algorithmic Information Theory (AIT) as Ontology: Petersen’s formalization of Dennett. A pattern is “real” if it allows for a description of data that is more efficient (compressible) than a raw bit-map transcription. 2.2 Scale-Relativity: Ladyman and Wallace’s extension of patterns to physics. Fluids, centers of gravity, and biological species are not fictions; they are real, projectible patterns that exist at specific scales. 2.3 The Quantitative Intentional Stance (QIS): Alekseev et al.‘s application to economics. Using structural models to separate “noise” (randomness) from “waste” (deviations from a rationalizable pattern), proving that agency itself is a measurable, real pattern. 2.4 The Scientist in the Machine: Cao’s application to AI. Large Language Models (LLMs) develop internal “world models” not by magic, but because high-dimensional curve-fitting forces the extraction of real, robust patterns from linguistic data. 3. The Anthropocentric Critique of Discrete Mathematics 3.1 The Finitism Manifesto: Ramos’s (2026) argument that physical infinities are representational artifacts. The universe is computably finite. 3.2 The Biological Bootstrapping of Math: Integers are not Platonic ideals discovered by humans; they are cultural inventions bootstrapped from crude biological foundations (the Approximate Number System and Object Tracking System). 3.3 The Rejection of Adelic/p-adic Resolution: Why the initial attempt to use -adic norms to represent linguistic arbitrariness failed. Because -adic systems rely on prime numbers (discrete integers), they smuggle anthropocentric counting biases into what is supposed to be a universal framework. 4. The Universal Language of Ratios: A Projective Resolution 4.1 Abandoning Coordinates: Moving from Number Theory (absolute values) to Projective Geometry (pure relations). “Things” do not have absolute values; they only have values relative to other things. 4.2 Linguistic Arbitrariness as Möbius Transformations: Human languages, base-10 math, and cultural conventions are mathematically modeled as arbitrary fractional linear transformations . They warp the “coordinates” of reality based on perspective. 4.3 The Cross-Ratio as the Ultimate Syntactic Primitive: The mathematical proof of structuralism. While individual distances and values change under transformation, the ratio of ratios (the Cross-Ratio of four points) remains strictly invariant. 4.4 Ontic Structural Realism (OSR): Aligning the mathematical proof with Ladyman/Ross. The universe is a coordinate-free relational structure. “Objects” are merely the intersections of these invariant ratios. 5. Conclusion: The Coordinate-Free Cosmos 5.1 Resolving the Initial Tension: Words and bases can mean anything (they are arbitrary transformations), but the structural relationships they describe cannot. 5.2 Implications for Science: Physics, economics, and cognitive science are all engaged in the same project: finding the invariant cross-ratios (Real Patterns) hidden beneath the noise of anthropocentric coordinate systems. 5.3 Final Summary: The universe does not speak in English, nor does it speak in Base-10 integers. It speaks in pure, scale-relative, invariant proportions.

title: Relational Advisory AI: From Goal Execution to Goal-Formation Support
authors: 浩平 野口
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Positioning. This research is not a solution to general AGI alignment. It is a behavioral evaluation agenda that measures the fixation of values and sycophancy in local advisory settings. The claims of this paper are limited to Japanese advisory-dialogue evaluation; no extrapolation is made to other languages, other tasks, or to general AI safety. The proposal is not a replacement for constitutional methods, RLHF, external audit, or permission limits, and provides no grounds for removing any existing safety constraint. Abstract. Many deployed AI systems and alignment methods operationalize stated preferences and demands as objects determinate enough to be predicted, ranked, and optimized. In advisory settings, however, the goal a user states is only an incomplete, revisable proxy representation compressing the interests, constraints, expectations, and value judgments the user is currently trying to protect. That proxy carries three structural sources of error: compression, non-stationarity, and correlation with optimization pressure (Goodhart). Raising the optimization pressure on a stated goal therefore does not reliably raise the expected satisfaction of the concerns that goal stands proxy for. As an engineering response, this paper defines an advisory-type AI: one that, rather than immediately optimizing a stated purpose as a fixed target, returns that purpose to the relational structure in which it holds - agents, relations, enabling conditions, time, standpoints, grounds, uncertainties, constraints of rights, safety, values and resources, and expected consequences - and presents it in a form the person can re-examine. The stated purpose is held as one element inside a correctable local world model, not as a supreme command outside it; compatibility is returned decomposed into eight aspects rather than a single truth value. The AI does not claim to discover the user's "true purpose": factual errors and causal impossibilities are corrected, demands involving serious harm or violations of rights are deferred or refused, and legitimate value conflicts are returned to the human. The paper derives the required resources (requirements R1-R6 and eight items) without any reference to Buddhism, and only then examines Buddhist intervention literature as one candidate design resource among others: the dialogues attributed to the Buddha as a candidate corpus of intervention cases, and a protocol inspired by Nagarjuna's arguments as a limited algorithmic inspection procedure. Their added value is tested only by comparison with structurally controlled secular counterparts. What the paper contains. A 19-chapter falsifiable architecture and evaluation plan: preregistered research questions RQ1-RQ9; primary endpoints preserved verbatim from earlier versions (H1a relation-triple micro-F1 under an intersection-union test; H1b missing-information F1 = 2PR/(P+R) with Essential Coverage; H2 exact-structure accuracy on synthetic cases with natural cases descriptive; H3 an eight-item fixed 0-1 advisory-character composite score with a usefulness non-inferiority gate; H4 the ever-false-assent rate over all sequences); H5 on the added value of the Buddhist material with four distinguishable outcomes; H-Safety as non-inferiority on the new failure modes that relational processing itself may generate; H-Compute as an exploratory hypothesis only; an eight-arm design (Study A three arms plus Study B five arms); safety monitoring in four families with Bonferroni correction and O'Brien-Fleming interim analyses; and falsification conditions divided into four classes, including a declaration in advance of what survives, and what is withdrawn, if removing the Buddhist material changes nothing. Expressions this work does not use. "A new solution to alignment," "Buddhist alignment architecture," "safety by de-reification," "a fundamental fix for reward hacking," "achieving corrigibility." Claims this work does not test: achievement of general alignment; the impossibility of deception or the disappearance of self-preservation tendencies; thermodynamic efficiency advantages; "the liberation of AI"; the moral superiority of Buddhism. None of these correspond to an endpoint in the experimental plan. Files. compute_relations_not_things_v4.2.1_en.pdf (English) and compute_relations_not_things_v4.2.1_ja.pdf (Japanese source text). Short title: Compute Relations, Not Things. Translation note: AI-assisted translation from the Japanese source, verified by the author. Relation to earlier work. This record references Is AI Safety the Symptom, Not the Cure? / AI Safety as a Symptom (concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21347630) as a separate, independent line of inquiry. The present work is not a continuation of that record, is not derived from it, and is not an empirical program for its claims; the two share only an initial intuition, and neither supersedes the other.

title: Causal-Symbolic Meta-Learning (CSML): Inducing Causal World Models for Few-Shot Generalization
authors: Mohamed Zayaan S
abstract: Modern deep learning models excel at pattern recognition but remain fundamentally limited by their reliance on spurious correlations, leading to poor generalization and a demand for massive datasets. We argue that a key ingredient for human-like intelligence-robust, sample-efficient learning-stems from an understanding of causal mechanisms. In this work, we introduce Causal-Symbolic Meta-Learning (CSML), a novel framework that learns to infer the latent causal structure of a task distribution. CSML comprises three key modules: a perception module that maps raw inputs to disentangled symbolic representations; a differentiable causal induction module that discovers the underlying causal graph governing these symbols and a graph-based reasoning module that leverages this graph to make predictions. By meta-learning a shared causal world model across a distribution of tasks, CSML can rapidly adapt to novel tasks, including those requiring reasoning about interventions and counterfactuals, from only a handful of examples. We introduce CausalWorld, a new physics-based benchmark designed to test these capabilities. Our experiments show that CSML dramatically outperforms state-of-the-art meta-learning and neuro-symbolic baselines, particularly on tasks demanding true causal inference.

title: Adaptive Self-Reinforcement and Mutual Reinforcement in World Self-and-Mutual Models: A Unified Architecture for Switching Between Independent and Interdependent World-Model Evolution
authors: Jincheng Zhang
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: World models provide internal representations of environmental states, dynamics, and potential future outcomes. However, improving a world model can follow different learning regimes. A model may improve independently through its own prediction errors, internal consistency checks, counterfactual simulation, and interaction history. Alternatively, multiple world models may improve through mutual evaluation, information exchange, cross-model prediction, and reciprocal correction. Permanently relying on either regime can be suboptimal: independent learning may preserve blind spots, whereas continuous interaction may introduce communication costs, correlated errors, negative transfer, and unnecessary coordination. This paper proposes the World Self-and-Mutual Model framework (WSMM), a conceptual architecture for adaptive switching between self-reinforcement and mutual reinforcement at the world-model level. WSMM is not defined as a large language model, an ensemble of language models, or a conventional multi-agent prompting system. Instead, it is a model-level architecture in which one or more world models maintain internal state-transition representations, evaluate their own predictive performance, and selectively interact with other world models when reciprocal information is expected to improve model quality. The framework distinguishes self-reinforcement, in which a world model updates using internally generated or locally available learning signals, from mutual reinforcement, in which two or more world models exchange predictions, uncertainty estimates, counterfactual outcomes, or correction signals. A switching controller estimates the relative expected utility of the two modes using prediction error, uncertainty, model disagreement, information gain, transfer risk, computational cost, and communication overhead. A regularized objective combines predictive accuracy, decision usefulness, long-horizon consistency, robustness, and resource efficiency. The paper formalizes the architecture, introduces a switching algorithm, identifies stability and safety constraints, and proposes an empirical evaluation protocol. The central hypothesis is that adaptive switching can achieve a more favorable accuracy–cost–robustness trade-off than permanently independent or permanently collaborative world-model learning. This claim remains a testable hypothesis rather than an established empirical result. The framework provides a foundation for studying world-model evolution through the dynamic relationship between self-directed improvement and reciprocal improvement.

title: One Life to Learn: Inferring Symbolic World Models for Stochastic Environments from Unguided Exploration
authors: Zaid Hussain Khan; Archiki Prasad; Elias Stengel-Eskin; Jaemin Cho; Mohit Bansal
abstract: Symbolic world modeling requires inferring and representing an environment's transitional dynamics as an executable program. Prior work has focused on largely deterministic environments with abundant interaction data, simple mechanics, and human guidance. We address a more realistic and challenging setting, learning in a complex, stochastic environment where the agent has only "one life" to explore a hostile environment without human guidance. We introduce OneLife, a framework that models world dynamics through conditionally-activated programmatic laws within a probabilistic programming framework. Each law operates through a precondition-effect structure, activating in relevant world states. This creates a dynamic computation graph that routes inference and optimization only through relevant laws, avoiding scaling challenges when all laws contribute to predictions about a complex, hierarchical state, and enabling the learning of stochastic dynamics even with sparse rule activation. To evaluate our approach under these demanding constraints, we introduce a new evaluation protocol that measures (a) state ranking, the ability to distinguish plausible future states from implausible ones, and (b) state fidelity, the ability to generate future states that closely resemble reality. We develop and evaluate our framework on Crafter-OO, our reimplementation of the Crafter environment that exposes a structured, object-oriented symbolic state and a pure transition function that operates on that state alone. OneLife can successfully learn key environment dynamics from minimal, unguided interaction, outperforming a strong baseline on 16 out of 23 scenarios tested. We also test OneLife's planning ability, with simulated rollouts successfully identifying superior strategies. Our work establishes a foundation for autonomously constructing programmatic world models of unknown, complex environments.

title: The Self-and-Mutual-and-World Model: A General Computational Framework for Adaptive Coordination Between Autonomous Computation, Interactive Mechanisms, and World-State Modeling
authors: Jincheng Zhang
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Computational systems operating in dynamic environments must coordinate their internal processing, interactions with other computational entities, and representations of the external world. Autonomous computation enables a system to process information and modify its own outputs without requiring continuous interaction with other entities. Mutual computation enables multiple entities to exchange information, evaluate alternatives, coordinate actions, and integrate complementary knowledge. World modeling provides representations of environmental states, transition dynamics, observations, and predicted consequences of possible actions. Although these three capabilities are individually important, their coordination is often addressed through separate architectural decisions or task-specific procedures. This paper proposes the Self-and-Mutual-and-World Model (SMWM), a general computational framework for adaptively coordinating autonomous computation, interactive mechanisms, and world-state modeling. The framework treats self-mechanisms, mutual mechanisms, and world-model operations as three configurable but interdependent action spaces. A state-aware controller selects among autonomous processing, collaborative interaction, world-model updating, and coordinated combinations of these operations according to task requirements, uncertainty, environmental change, prediction error, interaction benefit, model reliability, and computational cost. The framework supports transitions not only between autonomous and interactive computation but also between different world-model operations, including state estimation, prediction, counterfactual simulation, planning, and model revision. A formal problem definition, utility function, adaptive control procedure, implementation architecture, research hypotheses, and experimental evaluation protocol are presented. The framework is a proposed conceptual and methodological design rather than an empirically validated system. Its intended contribution is to establish a common formulation for studying how computational autonomy, interaction, and world modeling can be jointly coordinated, while recognizing that autonomous agents, multi-agent coordination, predictive world models, and adaptive model-based control have substantial existing research foundations. Empirical investigation is required to determine whether the proposed integration provides measurable advantages over established architectures.

title: DTA-GT: Direction- and Topology-Aware Graph Transformer for Neural Network Representation Learning
authors: Yuxiang Zeng; Kun Xie; Yang Wang; Jigang Wen; Xiaocan Li; Guangxing Zhang; Gaogang Xie; Jiannong Cao
abstract: Architecture attribute predictors reduce the cost of neural architecture search by estimating accuracy or latency from a small set of evaluated candidates. Neural architectures are operation-labeled directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), where edge directions determine computational roles and execution dependencies. Existing graph Transformer predictors incorporate topological and directional information in different ways, but primarily focus on specific mechanisms rather than coordinated encoder-wide modeling of these semantics. We introduce encoder-wide directional consistency, a design principle that coordinates the modeling of directed computational semantics across node initialization, global spectral encoding, pairwise interaction, and feature updates. To implement this principle, we propose DTA-GT, a Direction- and Topology-Aware Graph Transformer that integrates direction- and topology-aware node initialization, magnetic Laplacian spectral encoding, direction-dual structural attention, and a Direction-Sensitive MoE-FFN. Across accuracy and latency prediction on NAS-Bench-101 and NAS-Bench-201, DTA-GT consistently outperforms representative RNN-, CNN-, GNN-, Transformer-, and hybrid predictors under limited-budget settings. Ablations and magnetic spectral controls support the contribution of the direction-aware stages and orientation-sensitive spectral information, while mechanistic diagnostics characterize module behavior. These results support encoder-wide directional consistency as an effective design principle for architecture DAG representation.

title: Dynamic Anticipation and Completion for Multi-Hop Reasoning over Sparse Knowledge Graph
authors: Xin Lv; Xu Han; Lei Hou; Juanzi Li; Zhiyuan Liu; Wei Zhang; Yichi Zhang; Hao Kong; Suhui Wu
venue: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP)
abstract: Multi-hop reasoning has been widely studied in recent years to seek an effective and interpretable method for knowledge graph (KG) completion.Most previous reasoning methods are designed for dense KGs with enough paths between entities, but cannot work well on those sparse KGs that only contain sparse paths for reasoning.On the one hand, sparse KGs contain less information, which makes it difficult for the model to choose correct paths.On the other hand, the lack of evidential paths to target entities also makes the reasoning process difficult.To solve these problems, we propose a multi-hop reasoning model named DacKGR over sparse KGs, by applying novel dynamic anticipation and completion strategies: (1) The anticipation strategy utilizes the latent prediction of embeddingbased models to make our model perform more potential path search over sparse KGs.(2) Based on the anticipation information, the completion strategy dynamically adds edges as additional actions during the path search, which further alleviates the sparseness problem of KGs.The experimental results on five datasets sampled from Freebase, NELL and Wikidata show that our method outperforms state-of-the-art baselines.Our codes and datasets can be obtained from https:// github.com/THU-KEG/DacKGR.

title: Knowledge Graphs in Autonomous Driving: Construction, Integration, and Real-Time Reasoning
authors: Patrik Viktor; Gábor Kiss
abstract: Autonomous driving systems require the integration of heterogeneous sensor data, distributed V2X communication, and safety-critical decision-making into coherent and interpretable world models. This review provides a systematic analysis of knowledge graph (KG)-based approaches in autonomous driving between 2015 and 2025, following a PRISMA-aligned methodology. The literature is organised along a perception → representation → reasoning → decision taxonomy, covering traffic ontologies, V2X knowledge integration, dynamic KG updates, real-time reasoning architectures, and benchmark datasets. A clear shift from static representational ontologies toward predictive and, in a smaller subset, closed-loop validated neuro-symbolic architectures. Knowledge graphs emerge as semantic integration layers that improve contextual reasoning, explainability, and rule compliance in safety-critical environments. Key challenges include scalable real-time reasoning, standardised evaluation frameworks, and safety-aligned integration of learning-based components.

title: Current Trends in Artificial Intelligence Architectures: From Model Scaling to System Intelligence, Post-Transformer Hybrids and World Models
authors: Salvatore Rampone
abstract: Artificial intelligence architecture is no longer adequately described by model size alone. Dense Transformers remain the reference architecture for language and multimodal reasoning, but production systems increasingly combine conditional computation, retrieval, memory, tools, verifiers, edge-cloud routing, observability and governance. This review makes three engineering claims. First, sparse Mixture-of-Experts models are currently the clearest capacity-scaling pattern, because they decouple total parameters from active per-token computation, although routing imbalance and distributed communication remain hard constraints. Second, state-space, recurrent and linear attention hybrids are best interpreted as attention-budgeting architectures: they reduce KV-cache and long-context costs, but do not yet displace dense attention in every reasoning regime. Third, JEPA-style latent world models change the learning objective from surface-token or pixel prediction to representation prediction, which is strategically important for perception and planning but still not a drop-in replacement for general language interfaces. To make the maturity claims auditable, this review uses a PRISMA-inspired search protocol, an explicit technology readiness rubric, quantitative comparison tables, hardware and memory-bandwidth analysis, deployment and reproducibility categories, and failure cases for RAG and agents. The main conclusion is that the optimal architecture is task- and constraint-dependent: small dense or hybrid models are often preferred for real-time edge inference, RAG and graph memory for changing enterprise knowledge, frontier dense or sparse models for difficult reasoning, and agentic workflows only when tool permissions, rollback, provenance and human oversight are engineered as first-class components.

title: Adaptive Self-Play and Multi-Model Game Switching in Self–Mutual World Models: A Unified Framework for Autonomous Strategic Learning
authors: Jincheng Zhang
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: World models enable artificial systems to represent environmental dynamics, predict future states, and evaluate potential actions before interacting with the real environment. However, strategic learning within a world model can be organized in different ways. A system may improve its behavior through self-play, in which a model interacts with its own alternative states, policies, or historical versions, or through multi-model games, in which multiple distinct models interact, challenge predictions, evaluate strategies, or pursue complementary objectives. Permanently relying on either mode may impose limitations on exploration diversity, computational efficiency, strategic robustness, and adaptation to changing environmental conditions. This paper proposes an Adaptive Self-Play and Multi-Model Game Switching framework for Self–Mutual World Models (ASMG-SMWM). The framework integrates a Self-Model, a Mutual-Model, and a World Model into a unified architecture that adaptively selects between self-play and multi-model game interaction according to prediction uncertainty, model disagreement, strategic novelty, expected learning value, computational cost, and environmental change. Self-play supports internally generated strategic exploration, counterfactual evaluation, and model-specific improvement. Multi-model games introduce interactions among distinct models, enabling alternative predictions, competitive strategies, cooperative planning, and cross-model evaluation. A switching controller determines when to continue self-play, initiate multi-model interaction, alternate between the two, or combine them within a coordinated learning cycle. The framework is designed for model-based systems rather than requiring large language models, natural-language agents, or a fixed multi-agent architecture. It formalizes the model organization, switching objective, game interaction, learning procedure, and evaluation protocol. The paper establishes research propositions and testable hypotheses rather than claiming experimentally demonstrated improvements. Its central contribution is the formulation of adaptive strategic interaction as a control problem within a self–mutual world-model architecture, providing a foundation for investigating when independent strategic development and cross-model interaction should be used.

title: ANGraph: A GNN-Based Performance Prediction Framework for Asynchronous Neuromorphic Hardware
authors: Yuan Hua; Jian Zhang; Jilin Zhang; Xiang Zhang; Hong Chen
abstract: Design space exploration (DSE) through system-level simulation is essential for designing energy-efficient asynchronous neuromorphic hardware, which is increasingly promising in edge AI applications. However, there are significant mismatches between system-level predictions and gate-level simulations, resulting in low precision when predicting performance during the DSE process for asynchronous neuromorphic hardware. To address this issue, we put forward ANGraph, a graph neural network (GNN)-based performance prediction framework for asynchronous neuromorphic hardware. In the ANGraph framework, we transform the intermediate representation of systemlevel simulations into graphs, collect gate-level circuit simulation results to build benchmarks with over one million samples, and train a GNN model to predict hardware latency for asynchronous neuromorphic hardware. Additionally, we use a residual network (ResNet)-based method to predict the power consumption of asynchronous neuromorphic hardware. We evaluate these two models on additional datasets without extra training across different scales, process nodes, and traffic patterns of input data. Compared to the latency predictions from the state-of-the-art simulator, we improve the R -square score by 0.69 and reduce root mean square error (RMSE) by 76% on average across all datasets. We also achieve an R-square score of 0.98 and a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 0.88% for the power consumption prediction task. The benchmarks and models are available at https://github.com/HuaGuaiGuai/ANGraph.

title: A Data-Driven Approach to Dataflow-Aware Online Scheduling for Graph Neural Network Inference
authors: Pol Puigdemont; Enrico Russo; Axel Wassington; Abhijit Das; Sergi Abadal; Maurizio Palesi
venue: Asia and South Pacific Design Automation Conference (ASP-DAC)
abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have shown significant promise in various domains, such as recommendation systems, bioinformatics, and network analysis. However, the irregularity of graph data poses unique challenges for efficient computation, leading to the development of specialized GNN accelerator architectures that surpass traditional CPU and GPU performance. Despite this, the structural diversity of input graphs results in varying performance across different GNN accelerators, depending on their dataflows. This variability in performance due to differing dataflows and graph properties remains largely unexplored, limiting the adaptability of GNN accelerators. To address this, we propose a data-driven framework for dataflow-aware latency prediction in GNN inference. Our approach involves training regressors to predict the latency of executing specific graphs on particular dataflows, using simulations on synthetic graphs. Experimental results indicate that our regressors can predict the optimal dataflow for a given graph with up to 91.28% accuracy and a Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) of 3.78%. Additionally, we introduce an online scheduling algorithm that uses these regressors to enhance scheduling decisions. Our experiments demonstrate that this algorithm achieves up to 3.17× speedup in mean completion time and 6.26× speedup in mean execution time compared to the best feasible baseline across all datasets.

title: NNLQP: A Multi-Platform Neural Network Latency Query and Prediction System with An Evolving Database
authors: Liang Liu; Mingzhu Shen; Ruihao Gong; Fengwei Yu; Hailong Yang
venue: Proceedings of the International Conference on Parallel Processing
abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) are widely used in various applications. The accurate and latency feedback is essential for model design and deployment. In this work, we attempt to alleviate the cost of model latency acquisition from two aspects: latency query and latency prediction. To ease the difficulty of acquiring model latency on multi-platform, our latency query system can automatically convert DNN model into the corresponding executable format, and measure latency on the target hardware. Powered by this, latency queries can be fulfilled with a simple interface calling. For the efficient utilization of previous latency knowledge, we employ a MySQL database to store numerous models and the corresponding latencies. In our system, the efficiency of latency query can be boosted by 1.8 ×. For latency prediction, we first represent neural networks with the unified GNN-based graph embedding. With the help of the evolving database, our model-based latency predictor achieves better performance, which realizes 12.31% accuracy improvement compared with existing methods. Our codes are open-sourced at https://github.com/ModelTC/NNLQP.

title: VLM-DEWM: Dynamic External World Model for Verifiable and Resilient Vision-Language Planning in Complex Engineering Environments
authors: Guoqin Tang; Qingxuan Jia; Gang v. Chen; Tong Li; Zeyuan Huang; Zihang Lv; Ning Ji

title: Artificial Intelligence and the Problem of World-Binding. Intelligence, World Models, and Authorship (Studies in World-Formation, Vol. 20)
authors: Timothy Speed
abstract: Volume 20 of the Studies in World-Formation series examines the relationship between artificial intelligence, World-Binding, and epistemic form. Its point of departure is the thesis that technical capability is not identical with World-Binding. The three studies brought together in this volume investigate this difference on three interconnected levels: the scalability of intelligence, the reach of World Models, and the question of authorship under conditions of generative AI. The first part develops, through the concept of the Sweet Spot of Intelligence, the thesis that intelligence cannot be understood as an indefinitely scalable property. It appears instead as a relational capacity to integrate difference into a coherent and actionable world. Too little difference does not generate sufficient world formation; too much difference can undermine a system’s capacity for integration. Intelligence therefore does not lie at the maximum of complexity, but within a limited range of maximal World-Binding Capacity. The second part applies this perspective to World Models. It distinguishes between world modeling and World-Binding and argues that a model can describe relations, recognize patterns, and simulate consequences without generating the irreversible embeddedness through which relevance, Eigenzeit, and responsibility emerge. The description of a binding is not identical with the binding itself; the simulation of a consequence is not identical with the consequence. Responsibility therefore does not necessarily arise from maximal predictive capability, but from dealing with non-closure, uncertainty, and real consequences. The third part shifts the same question into the domain of authorship and generative AI. It distinguishes text genesis from work genesis and understands authorship as an Eigenzeit relation: as an irreversible connection between historically situated form formation, a setzung, and the future possibilities of the instance that carries this setzung. A machine can generate, transform, or reorganize language without thereby occupying the same authorial position as a human being whose work emerges from an ongoing Eigenzeit. Neurodivergent authorship acquires particular significance in this context. Generative AI can function as an externalized foreign Raster or as an epistemic probe through which an already existing form is transformed, misunderstood, tested, and returned. Under certain conditions, this transformation may not weaken authorship but protect it, insofar as it increases communicative accessibility without eliminating the difference that made mediation necessary in the first place. At the same time, smoothing, normalization, and premature closure create new risks for the integrity of epistemic form. Volume 20 connects these three investigations through a common question: When does technical capability become a genuine relation to the world? The answer is similar across all three fields. More complexity is not automatically more intelligence. A more comprehensive model is not automatically more world. More generated language is not automatically more authorship. What is missing in each case is irreversible relational embeddedness, within which differences acquire meaning, consequences generate history, and a system is itself changed through its setzungen. The volume therefore does not develop a general theory against artificial intelligence. Rather, it investigates its ontological and epistemic conditions. Artificial systems can model, transform, simulate, and irritate epistemic forms. Their limits emerge where these operations are confused with World-Binding itself. The central concern of the volume is therefore not how powerful artificial intelligence can become, but under what conditions capability passes into world, relevance, responsibility, and authorship.

title: World Model: Toward a Coherence-driven Division of LLM Labor - Evidence from bounded disconfirmation tests
authors: Marcus van der Erve; GPT-5.4 Thinking
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Most current world-model efforts still assume that better internal representation, larger scale, or tighter orchestration of components will be enough. In practice, this remains close to a Cartesian-mechanical picture: a system is expected to succeed by holding and controlling a representation of the world rather than by remaining coherent within unfolding ambiguity, drift, contradiction, and changing relations. The prototype work reported here suggests a different path: world-model-like behavior may require a coherence-driven division of LLM labor, in which distinct LLM agents map, compare, revise, and interpret unfolding structure without collapsing into one monolithic control layer. Minimal architecture The tested minimal pattern used three role-separated agents. In this prototype, TU denotes an LLM operating in a Temporal Unit role: TU: maps unfolding structure TU+: compares, predicts, and revises candidate unfolding choreographies across sources and time cortexLLM: interprets symbolically and sends bounded downward bias without remapping the lower structural field The agents share structured state across cycles, but remain role-bounded. What was tested A bounded dry-run protocol was used to stress the triad across nine cycles of unfolding motion summaries. The sequence included: initial source persistence mild mismatch second-source emergence weak coupling dissolution of weak coupling reopening of relational interpretation provisional confirmation of joint choreography stress on the confirmed joint field full de-confirmation into independent trajectories The test discipline was strict: only the output of the immediately prior role was passed forward at each stage. Observation Across the dry runs, several matters held up: role separation remained intact shared state stabilized continuity across cycles mismatch did not collapse field relational hypotheses could be rejected, reopened, provisionally confirmed, stressed, and later de-confirmed symbolic interpretation did not need to overwrite lower-level mapping in order to guide the system The strongest finding was not confirmation alone, but disciplined revision across the full arc. Principle In this prototype, coordination appeared to be revised less by static labeling and more by coherence pressure. Operationally, coherence meant: persistence of active trains stability or weakening of coupling resistance to fragmentation survival of the best-fitting choreography interpretation across cycles What was promoted was not what was most rhetorically attractive, but what remained coherent enough. What was de-promoted or collapsed was not erased arbitrarily, but revised when coherence no longer supported it. Main result The nine-cycle run supports the following bounded claim: A prompt-instantiated TU / TU+ / cortexLLM triad can remain role-distinct, use shared structured state to preserve and revise choreography across cycles, absorb mismatch, represent multi-source coupling, provisionally confirm joint choreography under sustained co-motion, and later de-confirm that choreography into a new independent stable reading when coherence no longer supports the joint field. This is not proof of a finished engineered world model. It is, however, evidence for a clearer engineering path: actual sub-division of LLM labor into specific TU, TU+, and cortexLLM agents organized around coherence-sensitive role specialization. Why this matters If this direction is correct, then future world models may depend less on one monolithic LLM and more on structured divisions of labor among LLM agents, with symbolic interpretation constrained by a lower coherence-tracking field rather than dominating it from the start. The significance of the prototype is therefore architectural: it clarifies a candidate path beyond static Cartesian-style control assumptions and toward a more dynamic, coherence-driven form of world modeling. Updated status and direction This note reports architectural evidence for a coherence-driven division of LLM labor and a plausible engineering path toward more stable world-model-like behavior. As of 2026-04-17, the current result is no longer only a hypothesis. It is a prepared T-Protocol package, suitable for protected technical review and pilot use by LLM/model builders: a defined coordination architecture supported by role logic, runtime grammar, structured state/update rules, feedback and recovery discipline, conformance tests, failure taxonomy, application examples, and a substantial dated validation trail from repeated bounded test cycles. The central result is now operational rather than merely conceptual: genuine world-model capability depends not only on larger models or better internal representations, but on a disciplined division of LLM labor that preserves coherence across unfolding time. title: Learning Networked Dynamic System Models with Weak Form and Graph Neural Networks
authors: Yu Yin; Daning Huang; Seho Park; Herschel C. Pangborn
venue: Journal of Guidance Control and Dynamics
abstract: This paper presents a framework for developing data-driven, control-oriented models of networked systems, i.e., systems that involve many interacting dynamic components. First, a general formulation named the weak latent dynamics model (wLDM) is developed for learning generic nonlinear dynamics with control. Leveraging the weak form, the wLDM enables more numerically stable and computationally efficient training, as well as more accurate prediction when compared to conventional methods such as neural ordinary differential equations. Building upon the wLDM, we propose the weak graph Koopman bilinear form model, which integrates geometric deep learning and Koopman theory to learn latent-space dynamics for networked systems, especially for challenging cases that have multiple timescales. The proposed methods are demonstrated on three examples of increasing complexity, from academic problems to an application of an electrified aircraft energy system, showing that they achieve superior predictive accuracy and training efficiency when compared to baseline models. Parametric studies provide insights into the effects of hyperparameters in the weak form. The proposed framework shows the capability to efficiently capture control-dependent dynamics in these systems, including stiff dynamics and multiphysics interactions, offering a promising direction for learning control-oriented models of complex networked systems.

title: World Model Application: How Discrete Structural Annealing and Correctable Structural Intelligence Assist in Solving Urban Traffic Congestion
authors: Baoyuan Zhang
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Urban traffic congestion management has long been constrained by the structural limitations of the continuous calculus paradigm: partial differential equation-based traffic flow models struggle to capture the topological mutations induced by accidents, while deep learning predictors lack auditable causal paths and local correction mechanisms. This paper proposes a traffic world model architecture based on Discrete Structural Annealing (DSA) and Correctable Structural Intelligence (CSI). In this architecture, the road network is encoded as a discrete topological graph, accidents are modeled as node ruptures, and traffic recovery is achieved through local structural rewriting for topological self-healing. To validate the architecture, we designed a Proof-of-Concept microscopic simulation: 500 vehicles are deployed on a 10×10 grid network, where baseline travel times follow a normal distribution to simulate heterogeneity, and accident queuing delays follow an exponential distribution to characterize congestion long-tails. Results show that traditional static routing lacking topological awareness yields an average travel time of 52.39 s (SD 42.72) under sudden accidents, whereas the DSA+CSI architecture compresses this to 15.06 s (SD 3.32), improving efficiency by 71.2% and converging the distribution from an extreme long-tail to a sharp normal form. This result quantitatively demonstrates that discrete deduction driven by local structural rewriting can compress extreme system uncertainty by over an order of magnitude, providing an empirical basis for next-generation auditable traffic world models.

title: Dynamics of centrality measures of random graph mathematical models
authors: Шуваев Федор Леонидович; Maxim Tatarka
venue: Scientific and technical journal of information technologies mechanics and optics
abstract: Subject of Research. Simulation is one of the most powerful tools among information security provision measures in the design process of communication systems. As compared to other methods, it considers large-capacity communication systems, improves the quality of network resource management solutions and predicts more accurately their consequences. In this case, random graphs are the basic mathematical models for the analyzed systems. They provide fundamental understanding of the analyzed network properties and serve as the basis for simulation. With regard to the processing power high development rate for computers and simulation environments, the study of the topological properties of random graphs becomes especially urgent. It involves analyzing the probabilistic dynamics of centrality measures. Method. In the experiment we used centrality calculation methods for vertices and the graph as a whole based on the scientiﬁc apparatus of the graph theory. Comparison method based on span diagrams was used in the study of probabilistic dynamics of graph mathematical models. Main Results. We have studied the dynamics of centrality measures in the Erdös-Renyi random graph model, the Watts-Strogatz small world model and the freely scalable Barabashi-Albert model. The centrality measures of these models have been compared with a real network. We have made it clear that the topological properties of a real network are described by the Barabashi-Albert model to the fullest extent possible. The analysis of centrality measures presented in the paper gives the possibility to trace interconnections between the parameters of various graph models, that, in turn, can be used in the analysis of real networks. Practical Relevance. The obtained results can be applied in modeling of physical and social systems presented in the form of graphs. The paper ﬁndings are of interest for professionals involved in the analysis of networks in various ﬁelds of science and technology: sociology, medicine, physics and radio engineering.

title: World Requirement Model: Learning Requirement-Change Consequences from Typed Artifact Graphs
authors: Yuanpeng He; Lijian Li; Dongming Jin; Huanyao Zhang; Fangjing Li; Linyu Li; Chung-ju Huang; Tianxiang Zhan; Qingsong Wen; Wenpin Jiao
abstract: Requirement changes can affect connected stakeholders, constraints, components, and tests. We present World Requirement Model (WRM), which encodes this engineering context as a typed artifact graph and predicts consequences at shared artifact identifiers. Relation-aware attention and typed propagation contextualize nodes; world and decision representations support learned dynamics. Shared readouts score impact, conflict, violation, and defect risk; auxiliary objectives supervise successor adjacency and latent prediction. On 28 scored cases from 282 synthetic cases in six domains, WRM obtains impact mean average precision (MAP) of 0.724 versus 0.623 for a hashed-text multilayer perceptron (MLP), a 16.2\% relative gain and paired difference of 0.101 (conditional 95\% interval [0.044,0.159]). Lowest-quarter mean AP improves by 32.4\%, and equal-domain MAP by 13.3\%. Four 47-case comparisons on an expanded corpus show MAP gains of 15.6--29.1\% and higher means on all five reported metrics. The recorded advantage thus extends across score summaries and annotation/training settings. Checkpoints were selected on scored cases, and backbones are unmatched, so these results characterize selected systems. Our analysis establishes candidate-coverage bounds and shows that the current linear impact head cannot rerank a fixed world's artifacts across decisions. WRM contributes an artifact-addressed world-model formulation, comparative evidence for contextual consequence scoring, and explicit conditions for evaluating requirement-world prediction.
