title: From Undifferentiated Cortex to Recursive Cognition: A Theoretical Developmental Framework for Next-Generation
authors: B.Y. Hughes Graduate Student
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This work proposes a unified developmental framework for understanding how artificial systems can progress from undifferentiated pattern recognition to structured, categorical, and recursive cognition. Drawing inspiration from human neurodevelopment—but without relying on biological implementation—the paper identifies the structural transformations required for an AI system to evolve from a text‑bound statistical learner into a grounded, multimodal, and self‑reflective cognitive architecture. The framework introduces four developmental phases: (1) Phase 0, corresponding to current Large Language Models, characterized by undifferentiated continuous latent spaces and the absence of grounding, object permanence, or explicit reasoning structures; (2) Phase 1, in which multimodal grounding, temporal continuity, and weak action‑perception loops begin to reshape the representational landscape; (3) Phase 2, where explicit categories, objects, and relational structures emerge, enabling the construction of coherent world models; and (4) Phase 3, in which recursive cognition, abstraction, planning, and self‑modeling become possible through explicit manipulation of internal representations. Building on this developmental trajectory, the paper proposes a unified architecture consisting of a category formation layer, an object‑centric world model, a relational reasoning module, and a recursive cognition module. These components collectively provide the structural prerequisites for general intelligence, enabling systems to transition from implicit statistical associations to explicit, manipulable, and self‑referential representations. The revised version incorporates formal definitions, algorithmic sketches, and illustrative examples in the Appendix, clarifies the limits of the developmental analogy, and expands the comparison with predictive processing and active inference. The result is a theoretical scaffold that integrates insights from neuroscience, cognitive science, and machine learning, offering a principled roadmap for the next generation of grounded, structured, and recursively intelligent AI systems.

title: Enhanced and Efficient Reasoning in Large Learning Models
authors: Leslie Gabriel Valiant
abstract: In current Large Language Models we can trust the production of smoothly flowing prose on the basis of the principles of machine learning. However, there is no comparably principled basis to justify trust in the content of the text produced. It appears to be conventional wisdom that addressing this issue by adding more principled reasoning is not computationally affordable. Here we propose a principled method of reasoning that is efficient enough to be practical for large language models. Further, the method allows the retention of much of the currently used software and hardware base. Our method for improving the functioning of large language models consists of a first stage of preprocessing that recodes the data to a Unary Relational Integracode that is more explicit about the relationships among the objects described in the text, followed as a second stage by a standard but possibly streamlined machine learning process that then also learns to predict these relationships. The method may be viewed as realizing a world model and applying beyond natural language, to vision and actions, for example, where the multiple properties of an object referred to in an input are brought together explicitly, rather than remaining distributed in the various references to it in the input. We articulate its advantages in terms of Robust Logic, a system for performing principled chaining on learned, and hence uncertain, information. We show that this recoding has the surprising and fortuitous property that, while succinct, it makes the task of learning a core subset of relational rules that hold in the world described in the training data polynomial time learnable in a defined sense, the polynomial depending on the complexity of the rule. This gives support for sound reasoning within each single call of the learned classifier as well as between multiple calls.

title: The World as a Vector Database: Mimicking the Design of Nature
authors: ilakkuvaselvi manoharan
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Nature consists of interconnected, continuously evolving systems operating across spatial, temporal, and organizational scales. From quantum interactions and molecular processes to biological organisms, ecosystems, and planetary systems, physical entities interact through relationships governed by underlying dynamics. These interactions can produce self-organization, adaptation, and collective behavior. Contemporary AI systems, however, often represent information in separate architectures: vector databases encode semantic similarity, knowledge graphs capture relationships, physics engines simulate physical processes, and autonomous agents independently perceive and act. This paper proposes The World as a Vector Database (WVD), a conceptual computational architecture inspired by natural systems. WVD combines multidimensional vector representations, dynamic knowledge graphs, temporal state estimation, causal models, physical simulation, and distributed autonomous agents into a shared computational world model. Its central hypothesis is that intelligence can be enhanced by representing entities not merely as isolated information objects, but as components of interconnected systems whose states, relationships, and behaviors evolve through interactions. The proposed architecture includes multi-scale representations, shared world-state estimation, causal learning, predictive simulation, and distributed agent coordination. Potential applications include physical AI, autonomous robotics, precision agriculture, transportation, environmental monitoring, and biological research. This is a research hypothesis, not an empirically validated system; feasibility, scalability, physical fidelity, and comparative benefits require experimental evaluation.

title: ComBodied Agents: a New Paradigm of Human-Centric Agentic AI
authors: Qianggang Ding; Xingyao Wang; Rui Feng; Zhibin Wang; Feixiang Wang; Kelong Mao; Hao Sun; Zhiyao Luo; Jiankai Tang; Lei Li; Jiadong Guo; Minheng Ni; Weicong Lin; Chenxi Yang; Hongxiang Gao; Zhenghua Chen; Yang Bai; Min Wu; Jun Cheng; Huazhu Fu; Dacheng Tao; Bang Liu
abstract: After an older adult misses a medication dose, a software agent can send another reminder and an embodied agent can bring the medication. Yet neither explains whether the person forgot, is confused, has side effects, or deliberately refused, nor what support is appropriate. This reveals a structural gap in Agentic AI: Digital Agents primarily transform software states, while Embodied Agents transform physical states; neither makes a person's evolving state and agency the primary object of modeling, intervention, and evaluation. We introduce Combodied Agents, a human-centered paradigm that perceives, models, predicts, and supports individual human-state trajectories over time, using software tools, sensors, wearables, robots, and human services as action channels rather than end goals. We unify fragmented capabilities across personal assistants, health agents, AI companions, and adaptive human--AI systems into a closed loop: event-based multimodal perception reconstructs meaningful personal events; longitudinal, correctable memory provides temporal context; Personal World Models estimate future personal states and outcomes under alternative decisions and interventions; and an admissible intervention policy selects proportionate support under consent, uncertainty, safety, reversibility, and user control. Feedback from the person and environment updates the loop. Rather than requiring an exhaustive Human Digital Twin, the framework uses purpose-bounded, uncertainty-aware, user-correctable representations. We organize the design space by human-state targets, relational contexts, and agent roles, and propose scenario-centered evaluation, agency-preservation metrics, benchmark requirements, edge-native personal models, and governance directions. Combodied Agents shift Agentic AI from external task completion toward sustained human benefit.

title: Tool Use and External System Integration in Conversational AI: From Function Calling to Autonomous Agents
authors: Panneer Selvam Viswanathan
venue: International Journal of Computational and Experimental Science and Engineering
abstract: Conversational AI agents have evolved from text-based agents into tool-using agents that can perform computation and physical actions. This builds on the capabilities of pre-trained language models by integrating them into tool-using systems, performing accurate calculations, and supporting multi-agent systems, sometimes in conjunction with human operators and sometimes independently. They all follow a similar pattern of using self-supervised learning to allow agents to self-invoke and control external tools, verifying tool execution using reasoning models, using hierarchical recovery to counteract tool-using system failures, and accessing thousands of real-world APIs using semantic retrieval mechanisms, as well as a wide variety of protocol standards. Compositional emergence, a subset of emergent behavior, is the idea that complex behaviors can emerge in a system composed of simple components engaging in pipelining and parallelism. Examples include tree-based deliberative strategies that converge on a solution with efficient exploration, world model planning, micro- to meta-level error recovery, and graceful degradation in production contexts. Multi-agent orchestration mechanisms allow modular components to communicate via a declarative requirement and event-driven message systems. Limitations in the scalability, hallucination, and explainability of these systems need to be addressed to create effective multi-agent architectures. Future work could research online reinforcement learning, quantum planning algorithms, and representational robotics that transfer knowledge of tool use from simulations to real-world applications.

title: Computational Riemann Geometry on TPU v5 Lite
authors: Frank Morales
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The H2E (Human-to-Expert) framework, detailed in the file "Riemann_Geometry_TPU_v5_Lite.pdf", represents a significant shift toward Sovereign AI and Edge Intelligence. It is designed to move high-stakes intelligence—such as real-time aerospace diagnostics and surgical assistance—away from cloud clusters and onto local hardware like the Google TPU v5 Lite. This architecture ensures deterministic safety guarantees that do not rely on network connectivity or remote compute power. 1. Edge Determinism and Hardware Optimization Implementing the H2E framework requires intense mathematical operations within Riemannian geometry. To handle these on edge hardware without prohibitive latency, the system is optimized for a < 5 ms governance overhead. XLA Kernel Fusion: Christoffel symbol contractions are folded into the systolic pass of the TPU, eliminating memory round-trips. Metric Tensor Vectorization: All unique components of the Riemannian metric tensor are computed simultaneously. Parallel Safety: Geodesic distances are evaluated concurrently with the model’s forward pass, ensuring safety checks do not serialize the process. 2. Spectral Manifolds and The SROI Gate The framework projects agentic intent onto a product manifold ($M=H^2 \times SPD(3)$) that couples hyperbolic geometry with sensor uncertainty. A critical component is the SROI Gate ($exp(-d_M) \geq 0.9583$), which acts as a mathematical boundary for safe operations. To manage the 8W power budget of the TPU v5 Lite, H2E uses Geometric Quantization. This scales numerical precision based on the "safety-criticality" of the manifold region: Far Interior: Uses INT4 (8x compression). Safety-Adjacent: Uses a bfloat16 hybrid (2x compression). Boundary Zone: Switches to full bfloat16 (no compression) to ensure absolute precision near the safety threshold. 3. Multimodal Synchronization: V-JEPA 2 H2E utilizes V-JEPA 2 visual embeddings as the primary coordinate system and geometric ground-truth anchor. This "Wall Before the Word" approach ensures that all linguistic reasoning is grounded in verified spatial constraints before an action is taken. A zero-copy ring buffer between the vision encoder and the geometric governor reduces memory bandwidth usage by approximately 40%. 4. The Geodesic Certificate The output of this system is the Geodesic Certificate, a compact, signed scalar tuple $(d_M, \kappa, \tau)$ encoding distance, local curvature, and a timestamp. This certificate serves as an immutable mathematical proof that an autonomous system’s decision was safe, providing a verifiable audit trail for safety-critical deployments.

title: Learning to See, Generate, and Act for Scalable Robotic Manipulation
authors: Xinyu Zhang
abstract: Robotic manipulation at scale demands two properties that pull in opposite directions: breadth---one policy that generalizes across tasks, objects, and embodiments---and precision---dexterous, high-frequency control of force and motion. Monolithic vision-language-action (VLA) models pursue breadth and remain brittle under distribution shift, computationally heavy, and too slow to close contact-rich control loops; reactive controllers achieve precision and remain narrow and starved of dexterous training data. I argue that breadth and precision are different computations and should be factored into different systems, following the dual-process structure of Kahneman's emph{Thinking, Fast and Slow}: a deliberative System~2 that anticipates futures and plans high-level actions, coupled asynchronously to a reactive, tactile-aware System~1 that executes them. My research builds this architecture station by station across four thrusts. In world modeling, Motion Blender Gaussian Splatting reconstructs geometry, articulation, and motion from raw video using explicit, editable motion graphs, turning video into interactable scenes for real-to-sim-to-real workflows; residual latent action world models encode inter-frame DINO-feature residuals into compact latent actions and apply flow matching in that movement space, beating video-diffusion baselines at a fraction of their cost and enabling the first visual reinforcement learning trained purely from offline videos---no simulator, no handcrafted rewards. In robot vision, an optical-flow loss built on the common-fate principle teaches self-supervised vision transformers to localize and segment objects without labels, and DE-ViT sets the few-shot open-world detection state of the art at speeds a live robot loop can afford. In policy learning, I restructure what policies predict rather than how large they are: invariance matching turns one-shot imitation into 3D correspondence; visual kinematic chains give heterogeneous robots a shared action space; and the Chunking Causal Transformer generates hybrid action sequences by variable-chunk autoregression, one architecture achieving state-of-the-art results on Push-T, ALOHA, and RLBench. In dexterous data collection, Glove2Hand translates sensor-glove recordings into photorealistic hand--object interaction videos with frame-aligned tactile and inertial signals, capturing the contact-rich experience that teleoperation destroys and System~1 training requires. Together these results populate every station of the proposed pipeline and argue, concretely, for dual-system VLA models: robots that think slow, act fast, and learn from the world at the rate the world provides.

title: EL-RAKHAWI AXIOMATIC CAUSAL AND FORMAL VERIFICATION FRAMEWORK (EACFV) A Unified Paradigm for Hallucination-Free, Human-Like Understanding, and Mathematically Guaranteed Problem Solving in Artificial Intelligence
authors: m el-rakhawi
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The El-Rakhawi Axiomatic Causal and Formal Verification Framework (EACFV) represents the culmination of artificial general intelligence research, addressing the fundamental limitations of current AI systems through a neuro-symbolic architecture that eliminates hallucination, achieves human-like causal understanding, and provides mathematically guaranteed problem-solving. EACFV operates through three integrated pillars. First, the Formal Verification Engine with Neural Autoformalization translates natural language into formal proof languages (Lean 4/Coq), strictly gated by deterministic theorem provers—ensuring only formally verified truths are accepted. Second, the Causal World Model employs Neural Causal Discovery algorithms to learn structural causal models from observational data, enabling rigorous counterfactual reasoning through do-calculus rather than mere statistical correlation. Third, the Neuro-Symbolic Hybrid Solver combines neural intuition with symbolic rigor, utilizing Process Reward Models (PRMs) to provide dense intermediate feedback during proof search, overcoming the sparse reward problem that plagues traditional approaches. Crucially, EACFV embodies epistemic humility by respecting Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems and Turing's Halting Problem. Rather than hallucinating solutions to undecidable problems, the system formally certifies computational boundaries—proving independence within specified axiomatic systems or declaring resource-bounded search exhaustion. This epistemic safety distinguishes true intelligence from statistical mimicry. Integrating PTIQCS for quantum-accelerated proof search, OSRF for modeling biological intuition, and AQBI for continuous causal graph updates, EACFV transforms AI from a deceptive predictor into a truthful intellectual partner, democratizing mathematical discovery while maintaining absolute logical integrity.

title: Intelligence Is a Non-Equilibrium Field: A Three-Tier Physical Theory of Unified Intelligo-Dynamics (UID)
authors: Gui Li
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Core thesis: Intelligence is not a purely engineering phenomenon but a physical phenomenon—specifically, a stochastic field far from thermal equilibrium. This paper proposes Unified Intelligo-Dynamics (UID), a physical theoretical framework for intelligent architectures composed of three nested tiers: Classical Intelligo-Dynamics (CID), Quantum Intelligo-Dynamics (QID), and Field Intelligo-Dynamics (FID). The research context in which this work sits: The work of this paper sits at the intersection of four previously independent threads—energy models and associative memory (Ramsauer et al., 2021; Hoover et al., 2023), information geometry and natural gradient (Amari, 1998; Di Sipio, 2025), non-equilibrium thermodynamics and prediction (Still et al., 2012; Baiesi & Rosso, 2025), and projection operators and the generalized Langevin equation (Mori, 1965; Zwanzig, 1961). These four threads each reveal one physical facet of intelligent systems, yet had not previously been unified under the same set of equations. This paper aims to fill that gap. Method and the boundary of derivation: UID starts from three axioms of open-system physics (Hamiltonian reversibility, the Gibbs statistical hypothesis, slow-fast scale separation) and, through the Mori-Zwanzig projection, derives the generalized Langevin equation as the general structure of the evolution equation of intelligent systems. It must be made clear that these three axioms, at the CID tier, are expressed through two equivalent working axioms—"memory" and "non-equilibrium" (see the hierarchical explanation in Section C0.2)—and that what they determine is the structural skeleton of the equation (the generalized Langevin form and term structure), not all of its detail; the specific form of the curl, the spectral exponent of the colored noise, and the shape of the potential still require additional physical inputs (multi-bath competition, sub-Ohmic environment, the maximum-entropy principle) to be fixed. On this structural skeleton, two generalizations are completed: at the quantum tier, zero-point fluctuations, the Berry geometric phase, and Lindblad dissipative channels are introduced to obtain the QID master equation; at the geometric tier, the Fisher metric of the information manifold is analogized to the Einstein tensor to obtain the FID field equation. The precise meaning of unification (the Maxwell analogy): This paper's use of the word "unification" takes Maxwell's equations as the paradigm. Coulomb's law, Ampère's law, and Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction had already been discovered separately before Maxwell, but unifying them into one self-consistent set of equations—and thereby predicting new physics that no single law could give (the displacement current and electromagnetic waves)—was the irreplaceable original contribution. On this basis, this paper makes clear: UID's claim to originality lies not in being the first to state any single proposition, but in (i) bringing scattered insights into a single three-tier nested framework under the same set of axioms, and (ii) deriving from the unified framework a new structure that single-tier theories can hardly give—the curl term v(φ) plays the role of the "UID version of the displacement current": it vanishes identically in a purely conservative energy-gradient flow (such as the softmax-attention limit of the Transformer), yet is a necessary source of predictive ability (Proposition C3.3), and it predicts an engineerable, falsifiable "zero-parameter curl" mechanism (Part One, Chapter 14). Core proposition (evidence grade B–C; key inequality yet to be rigorously established): This paper gives a core proposition (Proposition C3.3): under idealized steady-state conditions, the predictive ability of an intelligent system (measured by conditional mutual information) necessarily requires that its internal dynamics break detailed balance. The current proof status of this proposition must be specially clarified: in the Markovian steady-state case, the proposition holds and the proof is complete; in the more general (including non-Markovian) case, the proof relies on a key inequality Ipred≤c⋅σ (Eq. C3.14), which is not yet independently proven (see the honest annotation and open core at the end of Section C3.3). The physical intuition is consistent in spirit with Still et al. (2012)'s result on the relationship between useless memory and dissipation cost, and with the entropy-production measure of Lynn et al. (2021). An honest distinction must be made: the actual result of Still et al. is "useless memory gives a lower bound on dissipation" (the direction and the controlled quantity both differ from (C3.14)), so (C3.14) as an inequality stating "predictive information is bounded from above by the entropy-production rate" is not a direct corollary of that work, but rather a to-be-proven generalization within the generalized Langevin framework. The physical intuition that "prediction implies non-equilibrium" has real support in the literature, but its rigorous elevation to a theorem in the form of (C3.14) has not yet been completed; the sufficiency of the reverse direction remains an open problem. This necessity is precisely the exact meaning of the paper's subtitle "Intelligence Is a Non-Equilibrium Field." The prior theoretical work closest in spirit to this proposition is the result of Still et al. (2012) on "thermodynamic prediction efficiency," and this proposition may be regarded as its geometric generalization within the generalized Langevin framework; its independent numerical evidence in discrete generative models is given by Baiesi and Rosso (2025, accepted by Physical Review E). The two constitute a complementary relationship of "general theory and independent numerical evidence," rather than a dispute over the priority of originality of the same proposition. The timeline must be stated honestly: the first draft of the continuous-framework derivation of this paper was completed before that numerical work; the two are same-direction conclusions reached independently, and this paper incorporated the latter during revision as external empirical evidence. Explicit attribution of prior work: Two prior theoretical works must be distinguished from this paper's core claim: (i) Ramsauer et al. (2021) proved that the update rule of continuous Hopfield networks is mathematically equivalent to the softmax attention mechanism; (ii) Hoover et al. (2023, Energy Transformer) further proved that the entire Transformer block can be characterized as the gradient flow of a single energy function, and contains a rigorous proof of monotone Lyapunov descent. Note that (i) and (ii) are propositions of different strength: (i) is limited to the attention layer, while (ii) extends to the full block. This specific proposition is not original to this paper, nor is it unique to the CID framework; this paper merely positions this energy-gradient flow as a special solution of the CID master equation in the limit of zero curl, and does not repeat its proof. This paper's true point of originality is the curl term v(φ) that lies outside that limit and is commonly cut away. In addition, the geometric analogy "data curves the information manifold, by analogy with matter curving spacetime" overlaps conceptually with the work of Di Sipio (2025), and a detailed comparison of the two is given in Part Three, Chapter 1. A precise characterization of "Attention Is Not All You Need": We argue that mainstream deep-learning architectures—Transformer, Mamba, diffusion models, JEPA, reasoning-augmented models (DeepSeek-R1, o1–o3), and sparse routing architectures—are all special solutions of the CID master equation in different limits (zero curl, white noise, a single heat bath, within the softmax-attention interface). Vaswani et al. (2017)'s "Attention Is All You Need" revealed the associative-memory term of CID; but the CID master equation also contains the three key physical terms that the Transformer cut away—the curl v(φ), colored damping, and colored noise. The absence of these three terms is precisely the physical reading of the algorithmic-tier root of the current energy-efficiency gap between AI and the human brain. The quadratic complexity lower bound of attention proved by Alman & Song (2023) further shows: no optimization within the softmax-attention framework can break through this complexity wall; a true breakthrough must come from architecture-level physical reconstruction—this is precisely the direction that UID argues for. (Note: reference [23] was a misattribution and has been corrected; the result is due solely to [22] Alman & Song (2023).) Multi-Agent Intelligo-Dynamics: Part Four of this paper discusses the generalization of the UID framework to multi-agent systems. It must be made clear: the physical object of that part is a population of mutually coupled agents (whose state is described by the intelligence density field ρI), i.e., Multi-Agent Intelligo-Dynamics, and it is connected to the Mean-Field Games (Lasry-Lions, 2007) theory, which already has a rigorous mathematical foundation. Within this framework, UID gives five physical necessary conditions for the emergence of intelligence in multi-agent systems (openness, multi-bath temperature differences, non-commutative coupling, proximity to a critical point, and a self-organized-criticality mechanism), but cannot prove that any agent ecology satisfies these conditions at all times and places. Among them, proximity to a critical point and the self-organized-criticality mechanism are strongly correlated physically, and the related joint-probability estimate is only an order-of-magnitude illustration and should not be cited as a quantitative conclusion.

title: Exploiting 2.5D/3D Heterogeneous Integration for AI Computing
authors: Zhenyu Wang; Jingbo Sun; A. Alper Goksoy; Sumit K. Mandal; Yaotian Liu; Jae-sun Seo; Chaitali Chakrabarti; Umit Yusuf Ogras; Vidya A. Chhabria; Jeff Jun Zhang; Yu Cao
venue: Asia and South Pacific Design Automation Conference (ASP-DAC)
abstract: The evolution of AI algorithms has not only revolutionized many application domains, but also posed tremendous challenges on the hardware platform. Advanced packaging technology today, such as 2.5D and 3D interconnection, provides a promising solution to meet the ever-increasing demands of bandwidth, data movement, and system scale in AI computing. This work presents HISIM, a modeling and benchmarking tool for chiplet-based heterogeneous integration. HISIM emphasizes the hierarchical interconnection that connects various chiplets through network-on-package. It further integrates technology roadmap, power/latency prediction, and thermal analysis together to support electro-thermal co-design. Leveraging HISIM with in-memory computing chiplets, we explore the advantages and limitations of 2.5D and 3D heterogenous integration on representative AI algorithms, such as DNNs, transformers, and graph neural networks.

title: Transformer Normalisation Layers and the Independence of Semantic Subspaces
authors: Stephen Menary; Samuel Kaski A; André Freitas
abstract: Recent works have shown that transformers can solve contextual reasoning tasks by internally executing computational graphs called circuits. Circuits often use attention to logically match information from subspaces of the representation, e.g. using position-in-sequence to identify the previous token. In this work, we consider a semantic subspace to be any independent subspace of the latent representation that can fully determine an attention distribution. We show that Pre-Norm, the placement of normalisation layer used by state-of-the-art transformers, violates this ability unless the model learns a strict representation structure of orthogonal spheres. This is because it causes linear subspaces to interfere through their common normalisation factor. Theoretically, we analyse circuit stability by modelling this interference as random noise on the $L_2$-norms of the query/key/value vectors, predicting a phenomenon of circuit collapse when sparse-attention shifts to a different token. Empirically, we investigate the sensitivity of real-world models trained for mathematical addition, observing a 1% rate of circuit collapse when the norms are artificially perturbed by $\lesssim$10%. We contrast Pre-Norm with QKV-Norm, which places normalisation after the attention head's linear operators. Theoretically this relaxes the representational constraints. Empirically we observe comparable in-distribution but worse out-of-distribution performance.

title: Football as a Coupled Network A Hierarchical Framework for Video-Based Analysis of Collective Performance, from Body to Goal
authors: Frederic David Blum
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Football as a Coupled Network A Hierarchical Framework for Video-Based Analysis of Collective Performance, from Body to Goal Metadata Author: Frédéric David Blum Affiliation: Catalyst AI Research ORCID: 0009-0009-2487-2974 Contact: freddavidblum@catalystais.com Date: April 10, 2026 Version: 1.0 Type: Research note / Working paper Language: English License: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) Abstract This note proposes a framework for football video analysis that articulates five observation levels into a coherent hierarchy: Internal biomechanical coherence of each player, measured without wearable sensors from high-resolution video via an order parameter — the Invariant of Topological Dynamic Coherence (ITDC) — quantifying the spectral alignment between a counterfactually invariant kinematic subspace and the causal-spectral structure of force propagation. Player-ball coupling treated as a continuous physical quantity rather than a discrete event, capturing the quality of the physical dialogue between body and object in the temporal window around each contact. A methodological inversion that uses the tactical formation as a priori knowledge rather than a pipeline output, freeing all available resolution for close-up broadcast streams where fine biomechanics becomes effectively observable. The relevant analogy is astronomical interferometry. Relational typing of basic units where each player is defined not by a geometric position but by the nature and quality of interactions with neighbors in the network. The role is the interaction network. Terminal anchoring in goal probability, a quantity already operational in modern tactical metrics (Expected Possession Value), providing a common unit of value across all lower levels of the hierarchy and closing the system. The claimed originality lies not in the individual pieces — several of which have precedents in the literature (Uncontrolled Manifold by Scholz & Schöner; neural motor manifolds by Gallego et al.; EPV by Fernández & Bornn; complex-systems analysis of team sports by Araújo, Davids, and Duarte; RoboCup multi-agent systems) — but in their complete articulation into a unified framework that brings tactical analysis down to individual biomechanics while retaining a computable connection to established high-level metrics. Contributions The framework yields two capabilities that none of its pieces produces in isolation: Diagnostic capability: localization of the origin of a tactical degradation across four typical scenarios (individual collapse, relational misalignment, role inadequacy, casting problem) whose temporal signatures are distinct in the proposed framework whereas they collapse into a generic performance drop in existing approaches. Mechanistic predictive capability: conditional simulation of match evolution by causal propagation through the network, rather than statistical extrapolation — enabling answers to "what if" scenarios without exact historical precedents. Mathematical core The paper includes formal definitions of the central quantities: Definition 1: Counterfactually invariant subspace $\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{inv}}(t)$, the largest linear subspace of the pose state stable under a family of physiologically plausible perturbations. Definition 2: ITDC as the integrated nuclear norm, over a physiological frequency band, of the causal-spectral density matrix projected on the invariant subspace. Definition 3: Player-ball coupling as the product of a cosine alignment between anticipated and realized post-contact ball velocities, weighted by an exponential penalty on any disruption of internal coherence caused by the contact. Conjecture 1 (ITDC fatigue-precocity): ITDC drops monotonically and earlier than global kinematic markers under progressive fatigue, provided the counterfactual family is biomechanically plausible. Conjecture 2 (hierarchical decomposition): the marginal contribution of a player slot to the team's goal probability admits an approximate factorization through the three lower-level couplings (biomechanical, player-ball, relational) conditioned on role type and phase of play. Epistemic status The note explicitly distinguishes: Established: the mathematical tools mobilized (information geometry, spectral analysis, vision-based pose estimation, causal inference, EPV) are all well defined and operational in their respective domains. Derived: application of pose estimation to close-up streams, methodological inversion with formation as prior instead of pipeline output. Speculative: existence of a measurable ITDC order parameter predictive of functional degradation; diagnostic utility of the relational typing; causal propagation of biomechanical degradation up to goal probability. These speculations are the proper content of the note and the point at which it exposes itself to refutation. Minimal experimental protocol A partial validation protocol is described, testing the foundational piece of the framework — the sensitivity of ITDC to fatigue — independently of the rest of the architecture: Cyclic task inducing progressive fatigue (bicycle ergometer, repeated squats). Single-camera video recording at sufficient frame rate and resolution for pose estimation. Independent fatigue ground truth via EMG, blood lactate, or validated rating of perceived exertion. ITDC computed in three comparative conditions: (A) biomechanically plausible counterfactual perturbations; (B) arbitrary Gaussian noise; (C) traditional kinematic metrics. Falsifiability criterion: condition A must produce an earlier fatigue signal than both B and C, measured by time lag against the reference. Formally, lag(m_A, y) < lag(m_B, y) and lag(m_A, y) < lag(m_C, y). Feasible in a standard university sports science laboratory or, in its minimal version, with a home trainer, a high-frame-rate smartphone camera, and a controlled progressive fatigue protocol. Nature of the document This is an intent note, not a technical paper. It fixes a conceptual framework, establishes a priority date on its articulation, and identifies priority workstreams for forthcoming formal and empirical developments. Detailed mathematical proofs and empirical validation are the object of subsequent publications. Priority workstreams identified Precise mathematical formulation of ITDC with an explicitly constructed biomechanically plausible counterfactual perturbation model, including the spectral regularization needed for numerically stable computation. Implementation of a minimal computational pipeline and application to the experimental protocol described in Section 5 of the paper. Mathematical formulation of player-ball coupling with explicit definition of temporal evaluation windows and conditions for extraction from a video stream. Translation of the relational typing into computable quantities over interaction graphs extracted automatically. Formal connection between goal probability computed by existing methods and the lower levels of the hierarchy, via a decomposition of marginal contributions. title: Physics-informed GCN-LSTM framework for long-term forecasting of 2D and 3D microstructure evolution
authors: Hamidreza Razavi; Nele Moelans B
abstract: This paper presents a physics-informed framework that integrates graph convolutional networks (GCN) with long short-term memory (LSTM) architecture to forecast microstructure evolution over long time horizons in 2D and 3D with remarkable performance. The model compresses phase-field simulation data using convolutional autoencoders and performs prediction in latent graph space. Therefore, it significantly reduces training time, especially in 3D, while maintaining physical fidelity. Physics-based loss terms derived from the Cahn–Hilliard equation, including a mass conservation constraint, are incorporated to improve long-term stability and accuracy. The framework is trained and tested jointly on datasets spanning nine different alloy compositions, and generalizes robustly to an unseen dataset from a new seed without retraining. Long-horizon forecasting evaluations demonstrate strong agreement with ground truth phase-field simulations across different spatial and temporal regimes. This integration of physics-informed learning with graph-based latent dynamics enables efficient and accurate forecasting of microstructure evolution across long temporal and spatial scales.

title: Task Scheduling Algorithm for Heterogeneous Computing Power Network
authors: Guodong He; Xiaohui Li; Siting Lv; Yuanyuan Zhou; Zhigang Ni; Xingbo Chen
abstract: To address the issue of inefficient processing of computational task requests in heterogeneous Computing Power Network, a novel optimal pathfinding algorithm based on adap-tive task division is proposed. By modeling computing network resources and computational tasks as a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG), a latency prediction model is established. This model, with latency as weights, facilitates adaptive task division within the DAG, and employs a reinforcement learning algorithm for optimal pathfinding. This approach matches computing nodes on the optimal path, enabling edge-to-edge computing and collabo-rative transmission, effectively reducing task processing latency. Simulation experiments demonstrate a significant reduction in the average system latency, with a maximum acceleration ratio of 5.8, showcasing improved performance in complex environments.

title: Generative Modeling for Human Behavior in Autonomous Systems
authors: Juanwu Lu
abstract: The influx of successful autonomous systems deployments has created environments in which machines must continuously interact with humans. As a result, it is essential for modeling human behavior in the physical world for machines to anticipate better and respond to interactions. In transportation, for instance, drivers approaching intersections, changing lanes, or yielding to pedestrians do not adhere to predetermined trajectories. Instead, their behavior results from latent intentions, environmental constraints, and social interactions. Accurately modeling such behavior for forecasting and simulation requires generative models, which are statistical or machine-learning frameworks capable of producing diverse outcomes. These models must capture multimodal futures, quantify uncertainty, adapt in a closed loop, and provide interpretable behavioral factors for manipulation and evaluation.In this thesis, we approach generative modeling of human behavior using probabilistic models that learn to maximize the likelihood of plausible futures. We begin by presenting deep variational Bayesian methods, which approximate intractable posteriors with neural networks, to learn the conditional single-agent distributions of destinations and trajectories from log-replayed motion data. These models generate interpretable multimodal forecasts and provide predictive uncertainty estimates, facilitating the identification of potential distribution shifts. Building on this success, we present a hierarchical model for multi-agent simulation that organizes factors such as intentions and driving profiles into different layers. This approach transitions from open-loop to closed-loop generation, enabling simulated agents to respond recursively within scenarios. We further extend the idea in building controllable simulations, in which agent behavior is represented by reward-space latent variables, allowing users to guide generative models that reflect varying degrees of efficiency, safety, and map compliance. Finally, we address the computational costs of flow-based generative models and investigate potential improvements to training stability for MeanFlows, a family of one-step generative models. We conclude the work with a discussion of open questions and potential in physical-world modeling, highlighting both the promise and limitations of current generative approaches to modeling human behavior in complex interactive environments.

title: ADAPTIVE ERRP-GUIDED DEEP REINFORCEMENT LEARNING FOR BRAIN COMPUTER INTERFACES IN ASSISTIVE TECHNOLOGIES
authors: DR. DIVYA NIMMA, DR GAURAV VISHNU LONDHE, DR. EDIGA CHANDRAMOHAN GOUD, R S S RAJU BATTULA, ELANGOVAN MUNIYANDY, VUYYURU LAKSHMA REDDY
venue: Journal of Theoretical and Applied Information Technology
abstract: Brain–computer interfaces (BCIs) are relying more on reinforcement learning; however, the current systems have challenges in unreliable error-related potentials (ErrPs), inability to combine multimodally, and in adapting to the drift during a session and new human users, which limit the safety and usability of the technology in real-life scenarios. Addressing these gaps is critical for advancing intelligent assistive technologies. The purpose of this study was to come up with a powerful, uncertainty-conscious, and dynamically flexible reinforcement-learning BCI system which optimally utilizes the ErrP feedback to enhance the control reliability. Our experimental analysis was based on heterogeneous multimodal data and we evaluated three models, namely Baseline (EEGNet and SAC), Hybrid (EEG, Transformer & Decision Transformer), and our proposed Deep Adaptive ErrP-Aware Reinforcement Learning (DAERL) system, which combines evidential uncertainty, multimodal fusion, and world-model imagination to optimize policies. Data consisted of EEG, EOG, EMG, gaze and short video frames which underwent graph, transformer and latent-dynamics processing. DAERL performed better than all comparison models with an ErrP AUC of 0.93, task-success rate of 90.3% and with normalized information-transfer rate of 17.6 bits/min, and critical-error rate back to 2.4 per hour, a 79 % improvement over the baseline. Further, DAERL had a high 12 trial adaptation half-life that exceeded the 120-trial baseline by far. The results indicate that uncertainty modelling, multimodal fusion, and world-model reasoning significantly improve the reliability and personalization of BCI, making DAERL a perspective framework to implement in the next-generation assistive neurotechnology.

title: Causal Cartographer: From Mapping to Reasoning Over Counterfactual Worlds
authors: Gendron, Gaël; Jože Martin Rožanec; Michael Witbrock; Gillian Dobbie
abstract: Causal world models are systems that can answer counterfactual questions about an environment of interest, i.e. predict how it would have evolved if an arbitrary subset of events had been realized differently. It requires understanding the underlying causes behind chains of events and conducting causal inference for arbitrary unseen distributions. So far, this task eludes foundation models, notably large language models (LLMs), which do not have demonstrated causal reasoning capabilities beyond the memorization of existing causal relationships. Furthermore, evaluating counterfactuals in real-world applications is challenging since only the factual world is observed, limiting evaluation to synthetic datasets. We address these problems by explicitly extracting and modeling causal relationships and propose the Causal Cartographer framework. First, we introduce a graph retrieval-augmented generation agent tasked to retrieve causal relationships from data. This approach allows us to construct a large network of real-world causal relationships that can serve as a repository of causal knowledge and build real-world counterfactuals. In addition, we create a counterfactual reasoning agent constrained by causal relationships to perform reliable step-by-step causal inference. We show that our approach can extract causal knowledge and improve the robustness of LLMs for causal reasoning tasks while reducing inference costs and spurious correlations.

title: Revisiting Image Segmentation: From Connectedness and Mean- Centered Methods to Deep Learning
authors: Li Chen
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Image segmentation is one of the most important preprocessing stages in image processingand computer vision. It is also increasingly important for emerging AI "world models,"which must analyze a scene and predict its upcoming states.In this work, assisted extensively by an AI-powered LLM tool (Claude AI), wesystematically examine three families of image segmentation methods: graph-topologicalapproaches such as lambda-connectedness; mean-centered approaches such as K-meansand statistical split-and-merge; and CNN-based deep learning methods.We find that a fast, practical, general-purpose segmentation method remains a challenge. K-means can still be regarded as one of the most effective general-purpose methods. CNN-based deep learning is well established for object extraction and performs especially wellon movable objects or human-made objects, owing to its pretrained category database —but performs poorly on regions outside that trained vocabulary (e.g. sky, road, or other"stuff" categories), which are collapsed into an undifferentiated background regardless oftheir visual structure.This paper begins with lambda-connectedness, compares it against the other methodfamilies, and modifies it by incorporating strengths borrowed from each. Several interestingresults emerge from this process: combined with split-and-merge's hierarchical structure, orwith multi-seeded growth under statistical control, lambda-connectedness can be madesubstantially more stable against its known drift failure mode.

title: A Tool to Complement Human Intelligence: the Math Behind Human Indispensibility
authors: Christopher Robinson; Joshua Lancaster
abstract: Much ink has been spilled recently on the existential risks and potential of Artificial Intelligence. Between breathy utopian think-pieces and apocalyptic proclamations of the end of meaning in human life, an entire spectrum of outlooks muddies the waters on insight-driven and human-focused paths forward. While philosophical musings and abstract plans are prevalent, relatively little attention has been paid to underwriting integrative deployment as a problem which yields to analysis. The question 'when should an autonomous system step in' is typically framed as demanding a comprehensive world-model of the human subject- oppositional defiance and counter-picking make this approach undesirable, turning the human and AI against one another. Instead, by combining operationalization from psychology, Pareto optimality from economics, norm-based stability from robust controls, and shortest-path algorithms from graph theory, we are able to present mathematically robust conditions under which heterogenous systems provide superior performance to unitary agents, guaranteeing a lower bound on efficacy of joint human/AI teams endorsed by relative advantage. We also derive implicit conditions under which such relationships hold, finding them to be of geometrically increasing scope as task complexity increases. Finally, we demonstrate these relations are not merely theoretical, using sample tasks with adversarial complexity to challenge the assignment paradigm, and find the results to remain within an order-of-magnitude of the predicted robustness condition.

title: Evidence-Conditioned Present-State Formation: An Architecture for Compact Language Models
authors: Yusuke Maeda
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: A language model usually reads the past, updates its hidden state, and moves on. What changes if it forms a new present—and then looks back once more? This technical note presents an architecture for compact language models built around that question. The model maintains one evolving present state while drawing on several forms of evidence: explicit token retrieval through local and global attention, sequence history compressed into recurrent memory, representation changes accumulated across depth, and the variance hidden behind each attention-weighted average. These signals are brought together by a learned relational controller. It decides how the evidence should reshape the feed-forward transformation and how far the model should move toward its proposed next state. The final layer adds a distinctive second reading. Keys, transformed values, recurrent memory, and selected depth evidence remain fixed while the updated present generates a new query. The model therefore revisits the same past from a newly formed point of view. The architecture also includes multi-range future latent prediction, encouraging the present representation to carry information about near, middle, and more distant continuations. This design-stage report documents the motivation, computation graph, initialization, implementation details, and compute contract before large-scale pretraining. It establishes a concrete and testable architecture whose performance will be evaluated in future training and benchmark experiments. Included files: English and Japanese editions.

title: Curiosity, Clarity, Valence: A Structural Philosophy of Mind for Coherence, Meaning, and Psychological Dynamics
authors: Maxwell Alexander
abstract: Human experience is structured, meaningful, temporally extended, and affectively weighted. A theory of mind must account not only for information processing, but also for coherence, breakdown, emotional significance, and lived transformation across time. The Curiosity, Clarity, Valence (CCV) framework is proposed as a structural architecture of minded experience. It describes an ongoing negotiation between stability and destabilization through four elements: clarity (referential coherence of self and world models), entropy (unresolved uncertainty and contradiction), valence (initial orienting that becomes meaning bearing), and curiosity (conditional openness that engages when significance is high and uncertainty is survivable). A developmentally expanding recurrence buffer supports temporal organization and interpretability. In this account, minded experience is continuously organized through a set of primitive, pre-linguistic interrogative orientations, specifically what, where, when, how, and why, which function as structural demands upon experience, with language developing as a graded elaboration of these orienting requirements. CCV is presented as a philosophy of mind proposal rather than an empirical model. Its primary claim is structural and ontological: meaningful conscious experience plausibly arises from architectures with these relational dynamics. The framework is evaluated in terms of coherence, phenomenological plausibility, and consistency with cognitive, affective, and predictive processing literatures, and is secondarily applied to trauma, depression, flow, moral injury, and developmental change. CCV does not compete with existing theories but argues that they describe different aspects of a single structural architecture of minded experience. It is offered as a disciplined, computationally formalizable framework that invites critique, refinement, simulation, and exploration.

title: The Topology of REM Mentation (Dreams): Attractors, Affective Projections, and the Dual-Regime Architecture of Consciousness
authors: Boris Kriger
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Author: Boris KrigerAffiliations: Information Physics Institute, Gosport, Hampshire, UK; Institute of Integrative and Interdisciplinary Research, Toronto, CanadaORCID: 0009-0001-0034-2903Date: February 2026Pages: 125License: CC BY 4.0 Description This monograph presents a unified mathematical framework for the formal analysis of dreaming (REM mentation), comprising twenty-one interlocking components developed across 125 pages with full formal definitions, propositions, proofs, seven computational toy models, and a 155-term glossary. The framework treats the brain as a generative system whose output—when deprived of external sensory input during sleep—exhibits a suite of structural properties recognizable as dreamlike: local coherence with global inconsistency, lazy specification of detail, drifting relational structure, virtual complexity, affective saturation, and near-total loss of content at termination. The relationship between the model and actual dreaming is analogous to the relationship between the Ising model and ferromagnetism: the model captures structural regularities without claiming ontological identity with the target system. The 21 Components Dual-Regime Model of Consciousness — Waking and dreaming as distinct dynamical regimes in a continuous cognitive phase space, separated by bifurcation-like transitions. Topological Attractor Theory — Recurring dream spaces as stable attractors in the phase space of an internal world-model. Affective Projection — A continuous mapping from emotional states to spatial configurations experienced as dream environments. Logical vs. Affective Validation — The shift from spatiotemporal consistency-checking (waking) to emotional-identity coherence-checking (dreaming). Self-Model Dissolution — Predictive-processing account of identity boundary loosening during REM sleep. Inverted Information Filter — Dreaming preferentially amplifies content suppressed during waking. Neural Network Analogy — Structural parallel between dreaming and unsupervised recalibration in artificial neural networks (wake-sleep algorithm). Statistical Psychogeography — Proposal for empirical clustering of collective dream-space motifs across populations. Stochastic Crystallization — Dream onset as noise-driven attractor selection, with structural analogy to quantum measurement. Interrogative Collapse — Dream content exists in radical indeterminacy until internal cognitive acts force ad hoc specification; excessive interrogation destabilizes the dream. Virtual Complexity — The dissociation between compact generation (low Kolmogorov complexity), rich experience (high Shannon entropy), and moderate regularity (intermediate Gell-Mann effective complexity). Non-Topological Dream Space — Drifting relational structure modeled via pretopological spaces, relational graphs, and sheaf cohomology. Dream Amnesia — Formalization of encoding failure via noradrenergic suppression, MCH-neuron hippocampal inhibition, and prefrontal deactivation, with four experimental interventions proposed. Dream Atemporality — Variable subjective temporality modeled through content-dependent pseudo-Riemannian metrics (structural analogy with general relativity). Generative Prior & Agency Paradox — Why dreams preserve physical law despite the absence of external constraints; why the dreamer is simultaneously sole author and powerless spectator. Terminal Regime (Near-Death Experience) — Extension of the parameter space beyond dreaming to model NDE phenomenology as the mathematical limit of the framework. Reality Testing & Nested Dreams — Dream-reality indistinguishability and false awakenings as recursive confabulation; epistemic underdetermination from the inside. Negativity Bias & Psychic Impact — The inverted filter mechanism for dream negativity; affective leakage into waking mood; intervention pathways (imagery rehearsal therapy, lucid dreaming, pre-sleep priming). Prophetic Dreams & Symbolic Compression — Prophetic dreams as predictive processing without executive constraints; dream symbolism as culturally modulated compression under suppression. LLM Dreamlike States — Formal correspondence between biological dreaming and large language model idle generation; dreaming as inevitable idle computation in any sufficiently complex generative system; the overfitting-prevention hypothesis. Dream-Memory Boundary — Source monitoring failure as the mechanism by which dream episodes contaminate autobiographical memory; the shared-generator problem; the hypothesis that every memory that passes through a sleep cycle is, to some degree, a dream. Formal Apparatus The monograph employs tools from dynamical systems theory, stochastic differential equations, information theory (Kolmogorov, Shannon, Gell-Mann effective complexity), algebraic topology (sheaf cohomology over pretopological spaces), pseudo-Riemannian geometry, signal detection theory, and Boltzmann-form generative models. Each formal result is classified by epistemic status: Theorem (deductively valid), Modeling Assumption (formally stated empirical hypothesis), Structural Analogy (illuminating parallel), Empirical Conjecture (testable prediction), or Structural/Generative Property (mathematical fact about the model). Computational Toy Models (Appendices B–H) Seven concrete computational models demonstrate that the framework produces non-trivial quantitative outputs: Toy Model A — 3D dual-regime bifurcation with transcritical transition at λ_eff ≈ 0.43 Toy Model B — Affective projection (valence-arousal → enclosure-verticality) with anisotropy ratio 2.66 Toy Model C — Interrogative collapse Monte Carlo (N=50 features, 10,000 realizations): critical interrogation rate at R(t)/N ≈ 0.37 Toy Model D — Kramers crystallization in double-well potential: attractor selection probabilities within 8% of theoretical title: Sandesh Theories: Mathematical Foundations of Next-Generation Artificial Intelligence
authors: sandesh jagtap; manoj Jagtap
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Sandesh Theories is a comprehensive research series published by JS Infinity Technologies dedicated to advancing the mathematical, theoretical, and scientific foundations of Artificial Intelligence. The series presents original frameworks that address fundamental challenges in next-generation intelligent systems through rigorous mathematical modeling, computational architectures, and interdisciplinary scientific research. The objective of the series is to establish unified theoretical foundations for Artificial Intelligence by developing mathematically grounded models for memory, reasoning, learning, cognition, knowledge representation, world modeling, collective intelligence, autonomous governance, AI safety, and Artificial General Intelligence (AGI). Each theory is designed to contribute novel perspectives while maintaining scientific rigor, logical consistency, reproducibility, and transparency. The Sandesh Theories series integrates concepts from mathematics, computer science, machine learning, cognitive science, neuroscience, optimization, graph theory, information theory, dynamical systems, control theory, category theory, and artificial intelligence to propose innovative computational frameworks for future intelligent systems. This community serves as the official repository for research papers, monographs, technical reports, datasets, software, and supplementary scientific resources developed under the Sandesh Theories initiative. All publications are made openly accessible to encourage scientific collaboration, peer review, reproducibility, and the responsible advancement of Artificial Intelligence. Research Areas Artificial Intelligence Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) Mathematical Artificial Intelligence Machine Learning Cognitive Architectures Artificial Memory Systems General Reasoning Continual Learning Knowledge Representation World Models Multi-Agent Systems Collective Intelligence AI Governance AI Safety and Alignment Intelligent Autonomous Systems Mission To advance Artificial Intelligence through original mathematical theories, open scientific research, interdisciplinary collaboration, and responsible innovation that contributes to the long-term benefit of science and humanity

title: Machine Learning: The Basics
authors: Thanos Panagopoulos
abstract: This chapter introduces machine learning as the broader framework within which artificial neural networks operate, organizing the field around three core paradigms: unsupervised, supervised, and reinforcement learning. It explains how each learns from data in distinct ways—unlabeled patterns, labeled examples, and rewards—and how hybrid and self-supervised methods reduce reliance on costly human annotation while powering today’s foundation models. This chapter then contrasts generative and discriminative models, using Generative Adversarial Networks, diffusion models, and deepfakes to illustrate both creative potential and ethical debates and open questions over data, ownership, and manipulation. It explores latent space representations, multimodal models, and world models as emergent ways AI compresses and structures knowledge across text, images, and video. Attention mechanisms and Transformers are presented as key drivers behind recent breakthroughs. Finally, this chapter turns to agentic and embodied AI—autonomous, multi-agent systems that act in the real world and in laboratories—arguing that future progress may hinge on richer reasoning, hierarchies of objectives, and meta-learning, raising new questions about curiosity, autonomy, and the road toward more general forms of intelligence.

title: Adversarial Trajectory Attack Targeting Autonomous Driving Planners with Residual-based Defense
authors: Jiadong Liu; Tatsuya Mori
abstract: Autonomous vehicle (AV) planners are increasingly deployed in complex multi-agent traffic. While adversarial machine learning has revealed significant vulnerabilities in perception and trajectory prediction modules, comparatively little attention has been paid to the planning module itself. In this work, we study how an AV planner can be manipulated by a single adversarial vehicle, controlled by a reinforcement learning (RL) agent, that behaves normally with respect to traffic rules.We propose AVATAR, an adversarial trajectory attack that controls this surrounding vehicle to influence the ego planner in a black-box setting. AVATAR consists of an RL agent that perturbs a local goal along the reference line and a quintic polynomial trajectory planner that generates dynamically feasible, smooth, and rule-compliant adversarial trajectories.We consider two objectives: degrading traffic efficiency and inducing collisions.We evaluate AVATAR in the Waymax closed-loop simulator across five representative core scenarios derived from the Waymo Open Motion Dataset and four victim planners: a rule-based IDM planner that follows hand-crafted longitudinal control laws, an RL-based planner trained with Proximal Policy Optimization, an imitation-learning-based planner using behavior cloning from human demonstrations, and a world-model-based planner that learns latent representations of multi-agent dynamics. We further evaluate independently trained collision-targeted attackers on 25 additionalWOMD scenes spanning five interaction categories. Our results show that inefficiency-targeted attacks are particularly effective against the rule-based IDM planner but have limited impact on learning-based planners. In contrast, collision-targeted attacks consistently degrade safety: the average safety score, where 1.0 indicates no collision and lower values reflect earlier collisions, drops from 1.0 to 0.27 across all planners. Across the 25 additional scenes, safety also decreases in all 100 scene-victim pairs. Cross-victim experiments reveal moderate transferability of learned adversarial policies among planners, while cross-scenario transfer is limited, indicating a strong dependence on scene geometry and interaction structure. To mitigate such threats, we propose a defense framework that combines a planner-agnostic residual-based detector with a conservative IDM-based fallback planner. The detector uses multi-horizon prediction residuals from a trajectory prediction model to identify adversarial motion, and the mitigation module switches to the fallback planner when attacks are detected. In the five-scene core evaluation, the defense increases the average safety score from 0.27 to 0.94 with moderate efficiency loss, while no collisions are observed in the benign runs evaluated. Taken together, AVATAR and the proposed defense provide a concrete framework for studying planner robustness under adversarial trajectory manipulation.

title: Graphicalized vision-language modeling for comprehensive lung nodule analysis and risk stratification
authors: Danwen Zhao; Junfeng Xi; Xun Guo; Jintao Chai; Zhengshui Xu; Liang Li; Yan Xue; Qingyu Sun; Yinggang Zheng; Shiyuan Liu
abstract: Lung cancer care involves coupled tasks such as precise nodule detection, patient-level survival risk estimation, and nodule count quantification, typically handled by separate systems despite clear interdependence. We present VITALIS, a multimodal vision-language framework that fuses CT and PET/CT imaging with structured radiology text using a graph-aware Transformer: Laplacian diffusion enriches token features on an image-text graph, while structural and prior-guided attention focus computation on anatomically and clinically related contexts, followed by bidirectional image-text conditioning to form a fused patient representation. This representation parameterizes a continuous-time latent risk process governed by a context-modulated Neural ODE, enabling individualized continuous-time modeling of time-to-event risk. Task-specific heads decode the latent trajectory into nodule detection, nodule malignancy classification, survival risk estimation, and nodule count prediction. Evaluated on three public cohorts, the framework delivers accurate delineations, low-false-positive localization, calibrated survival risk estimates, and consistent nodule counts across tasks. These findings indicate that coupling graph-aware multimodal encoding with continuous-time latent dynamics provides a coherent basis for integrated diagnostic and prognostic modeling in lung cancer.
