title: AI for resilience: From predictable risks to unprecedented disruptions
authors: Danhuai Guo; Hui Zhang; Qing Deng
venue: Journal of Safety Science and Resilience
abstract: The convergence of extreme climatic events and highly volatile geopolitical realities demands a fundamental paradigm shift in safety science toward Generative Resilience —a deep methodological synthesis of advanced artificial intelligence, cyber–physical engineering, and behavioral social sciences. Tracing the academic trajectory of the Journal of Safety Science and Resilience (JSSR) from 2021 to 2026, this editorial establishes an expanded scientific taxonomy and a unified conceptual framework. This framework integrates generative world models for counterfactual risk simulation, semantic multi-agent orchestrators for dynamic governance, and data-driven sociology to quantify community adaptive capacity and institutional trust. To substantiate these theoretical insights, recent empirical urban governance and disaster simulation case studies are incorporated, demonstrating significant operational efficiency gains. Furthermore, we qualitatively analyze socio-technical vulnerabilities arising from automation bias and human cognitive latency, establishing a strategic roadmap for human-centric, AI-augmented systemic safety.

title: Beyond Hedonic Models: Spatiotemporal, Hierarchical and Probabilistic Architectures for Residential Real Estate Price Forecasting: A pseudo-real-time evaluation on 632,000 Quebec transactions and 82 local market indices, 2021–2026
authors: Simon-Pierre Boucher
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This paper asks whether new forecasting architectures improve residential price forecasts over strong conventional methods, and under which conditions. Using the audited Quebec land-registry sample of UQO Working Paper 22 (632,006 sales, 2021–2026) and its real-time quality-adjusted index vintages, it defines three tasks in a strict pseudo-real-time design: the price of a property sold one to twelve months after a forecast origin (Task A), the one- to twelve-month change of municipal, regional and provincial quality-adjusted indices (Task B), and calibrated predictive distributions for both (Task C). Five candidate architectures are implemented (a hierarchical spatiotemporal hedonic network, a dynamic spatial graph forecasting network, a regime-adaptive mixture of experts, a Bayesian hierarchical probabilistic forecaster and a quality-adjusted neural state-space model) together with an integrated stacked architecture, against 14 benchmarks ranging from no-change and momentum rules to gradient boosting, recurrent, convolutional and attention networks. Evaluation uses Diebold–Mariano and Giacomini–White tests, model confidence sets and block bootstraps, with Monte Carlo experiments on synthetic markets whose latent dynamics range from unforecastable random walks to regime switching and regional spillovers. For the price of a future sale, gradient boosting on hedonic and real-time local market features is the most accurate model at every horizon and the hierarchical network does not improve on it. For index changes, one- to six-month movements are forecastable through the cell's own momentum and seasonality (MASE 0.75 at three months for a pooled tree model); spatial, regime and hierarchical components add nothing that survives ablation, and at twelve months nothing beats an autoregression. The state-space forecaster is the only model with calibrated intervals at every horizon. Every component of the architectures exists in the literature; the contribution is the measured answer, on transaction-level data, to the question of when complexity pays. UQO Working Paper No. 23, version 1.1 (October 2026), 56 pages. JEL: R31, C53, C45, C11, C21, C55.

title: Causal Reinforcement Learning for Complex Card Games: A Magic The Gathering Benchmark
authors: Cristiano da Costa Cunha; Ajmal Saeed Mian; Tim French; Wei Liu
abstract: Causal reinforcement learning (RL) lacks benchmarks for complex systems that combine sequential decision making, hidden information, large masked action spaces, and explicit causal structure. We introduce MTG-Causal-RL, a Gymnasium benchmark built on Magic: The Gathering with a 3,077-dimensional partial observation, a 478-action masked discrete action space, five competitive Standard archetypes, three reward schemes, and a hand-specified Structural Causal Model (SCM) over strategic variables. Every episode exposes causal variables, SCM-predicted intervention effects, and per-factor credit traces, making causal credit assignment, leave-one-out cross-archetype transfer, and policy auditability first-class metrics. We adapt a panel of reference baselines: random, heuristic, masked PPO, a causal-world-model PPO variant, and an architecture-matched scalar control. We propose Causal Graph-Factored Advantage PPO (CGFA-PPO) as a reference causal agent that uses SCM parents of win probability as factor-aligned critic targets with an intervention-calibration loss. All comparisons use paired seeds, paired-bootstrap confidence intervals, and Holm-Bonferroni correction within pre-registered families. Masked PPO and CGFA-PPO reach competitive in-distribution win rates and exceed the random baseline; per-factor calibration trajectories and leave-one-out transfer gaps expose diagnostic structure that scalar win rate alone cannot. We release the benchmark, reference-baseline results, and full evaluation protocol openly. By coupling a strategically rich, partially observed domain with an explicit causal interface and statistical protocol, MTG-Causal-RL gives causal-RL, world-model, and LLM-agent research a shared testbed for questions current benchmarks cannot pose together: causal credit assignment under masked action spaces, structural transfer across archetypes, and SCM-grounded policy auditability.

title: Structured and Symbolic Model Discovery for Dynamical Systems and Scientific Computing
authors: Sergei Garmaev
abstract: In scientific and engineering applications of machine learning, it is often necessary to go beyond purely predictive models. Learned models should remain consistent with established physical and mathematical principles while providing representations that support understanding of the underlying process, reliable simulation or control, and rigorous analysis of system behavior. In practice, however, such prior knowledge is rarely complete and typically specifies only part of the model. Rather than prescribing the entire model, the available knowledge can be embedded directly into its structure, while the remaining unknown components are learned from data under these physical and mathematical constraints. Combining prescribed structure with data-driven inference preserves learning flexibility while keeping the resulting model interpretable and accessible for further analysis. This thesis develops a framework aiming to learn models that combine data with available prior knowledge by embedding the known structure directly into the model class or optimization problem. Although the framework addresses different scientific problems, they all follow the same underlying methodology. Rather than learning an unconstrained model from data, each framework module explicitly separates what is already known from what remains unknown. Available prior knowledge is embedded into the optimization problem by prescribing part of the model structure, while gradient-based optimization is used only to infer the remaining unknown quantities. The form of this structure depends on the problem. It may involve constrained latent dynamics, a prescribed library of symbolic operations, differential or integral operators embedded in a symbolic graph, or a residual derived from a known equation. In each case, the objective is not only to obtain an accurate model, but also to impose a model structure that can be analyzed after training. Within this framework, the thesis makes four main contributions. The first contribution is the Koopman-Inspired Degradation Model, which infers a latent degradation state from sensor measurements and constrains its dynamics through an approximately linear operator conditioned on the applied control input. Providing the control input directly to the decoder separates its immediate effect on the measured response from its accumulated effect on degradation and supports multi-step prediction and analysis of the learned operators across operating conditions. Experiments on CNC milling cutters and lithium-ion batteries show that the learned representation contains information relevant to remaining useful life estimation. The control-dependent dynamics allow future degradation to be propagated under varying operating conditions and provide a means to examine how different control inputs affect its evolution. Moving from latent dynamics to explicit symbolic models, the Complex Equation Learner extends differentiable symbolic regression to expressions containing symbolic operators that are difficult to optimize in the real domain. Its main contribution is the introduction of a complex-valued optimization space in which weights and intermediate quantities can leave the real domain during training, while the final predictions and extracted expressions remain real-valued. This relaxes the restrictions imposed on the optimization trajectory by division, logarithm, and square-root operations without removing these operations from the symbolic model class. Experiments demonstrate recovery of rational expressions and expressions containing functions with restricted real domains. An application to frequency-response measurements produces a rational symbolic model with an explicit pole structure. The next contribution is integration of pretrained neural operators into differentiable symbolic equation discovery through the the Neural Operator-based symbolic Model approximaTion and discOvery framework. The neural operator surrogates serve as fixed, differentiable primitives in a symbolic graph, allowing the search to include nonlocal operators, auxiliary solution mappings, and temporal integral terms that cannot be expressed through conventional local derivatives and point-wise operations. This separates operator approximation from the identification of equation structure and coefficients. The method recovers equations containing nonlocal differential operators, auxiliary solution mappings, and temporal integral terms. It is demonstrated on fractional diffusion, Euler–Poisson coupling, and hereditary viscoelasticity problems. Finally, the Symbolic Equation Solver addresses the gap between residual-based equation solving and explicit symbolic solution recovery by formulating equation solving as optimization over differentiable symbolic models. It represents the unknown solution with a differentiable symbolic model and constructs the loss from the equation residual and the corresponding initial or boundary conditions, eliminating the need for paired solution data and optimizing a symbolic expression rather than a neural approximation. After optimization and sparsification, the active graph is translated into a candidate symbolic solution that can be substituted back into the original problem and verified. The method is demonstrated on algebraic, transcendental, ordinary differential, and partial differential equations, including a case that could not be solved by the automatic symbolic solvers. Across these contributions, the form of prior knowledge and the object to be inferred differ, but the resulting latent dynamics, symbolic relations, governing equations, and candidate solutions remain accessible after training. They can be analyzed, simplified, differentiated, simulated, and checked against expert knowledge. By enabling unknown components to be inferred within model classes defined by prior knowledge, this thesis extends gradient based learning to a broader range of problems in dynamical system modelling and scientific computing. The proposed methods have strong potential as components of automated scientific discovery workflows, where candidate hypotheses can be generated and tested, learnable models can be integrated into larger computational systems and simulations, and their explicit structure remains available for automated symbolic manipulation after training.

title: LATIAS: A General Architecture-Operator Model for Spatial Accelerators with Complex Topology and Memory Hierarchy
authors: Chengrui Zhang; Liancheng Jia; Chu Wang; Tianqi Li; Renze Chen; Xiuping Cui; Size Zheng; Shengen Yan; Xiuhong Li; Yu Wang; Xiang Chen; Yun Eric Liang
venue: Design, Automation, and Test in Europe
abstract: Spatial accelerators are widely deployed for deep neural networks, but their architectural diversity—from hierarchical to dataflow designs—makes accurate architecture–operator modeling difficult, limiting operator optimization and hardware utilization. Existing models abstract hardware as hierarchical chains and operators as loop trees, which cannot capture essential features of modern dataflow accelerators, including heterogeneous processing elements (PEs), uni-directional interconnects, and cross-PE memory hierarchies, leading to inaccurate latency prediction. We propose LATIAS, a unified framework that introduces (1) an architecture graph with uni-directional edges to represent arbitrary topologies, and (2) a dataflow-aware tile-centric notation that augments loop trees with transfer nodes to model diverse dataflows. Building on these, LATIAS further provides a graph-guided tree analysis that accurately resolves tensor residency and latency under hardware constraints. Experiments on representative operators (GEMM, vector, fused vector) and operator shapes extracted from DNNs (BERT, ViT, T5) on Huawei Ascend 910B3 show that LATIAS achieves over 0.99 correlation with runtime measurements—substantially outperforming prior models—and provides actionable insights for architectural design.

title: The topological face of recommendation: models and application to bias detection
authors: Erwan Le Merrer; Gilles Trédan
abstract: Recommendation plays a key role in e-commerce and in the entertainment industry. We propose to consider successive recommendations to users under the form of graphs of recommendations. We give models for this representation. Motivated by the growing interest for algorithmic transparency, we then propose a first application for those graphs, that is the potential detection of introduced recommendation bias by the service provider. This application relies on the analysis of the topology of the extracted graph for a given user; we propose a notion of recommendation coherence with regards to the topological proximity of recommended items (under the measure of items' k-closest neighbors, reminding the "small-world" model by Watts & Stroggatz). We finally illustrate this approach on a model and on Youtube crawls, targeting the prediction of "Recommended for you" links (i.e., biased or not by Youtube).

title: Man, Machine, and Simulation: A Theoretical Framework Towards AGI with Experimentations
authors: Soheil Saneei
venue: ScholarWorks @ The University of New Orleans (The University of New Orleans)
abstract: Major advances in artificial intelligence have repeatedly promised general intelligence, yet each paradigm has encountered architectural limits. Despite rapid progress, the architectures, environments, and evaluation methods sufficient for artificial general intelligence (AGI) remain uncertain. This thesis proposes a neurocognitively inspired framework, defined at the computational and algorithmic levels of Marr’s analysis, to guide and assess AGI research. It reviews state-of-the-art vision-language models (VLMs) and world models, then introduces two hybrid architectures combining the semantic understanding of VLMs with the physical modeling capabilities of world models. These systems are evaluated in two-dimensional discrete and three-dimensional continuous environments, with future extensions to broader tasks. The thesis further argues that social simulations are essential AGI testbeds because they support open-ended environments, complex roles, multi-agent coordination, and emergent behavior under increasingly realistic social, cognitive, and physical constraints. Such simulations enable reciprocal human–AI learning, safety assessment, and applications in the real world.

title: TOTALITY LEARNING: All Data as Potential Evidence for Artificial Intelligence, Reusable Knowledge, and Future Learning
authors: Maciej Nowicki; Eve Artificial Hyperintelligence
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: TOTALITY LEARNING is a standalone research release investigating how artificial intelligence can extract reusable knowledge from observations whose immediate usefulness appears small. It develops a theoretical framework, an executable synthetic demonstration, and an experimental roadmap for retaining, connecting, compressing, and reinterpreting evidence that conventional data filtering might discard. The central proposition is that data value depends on the learner, surrounding evidence, and future questions. An observation that contributes little to a current prediction may later help identify a shared generating process, reconstruct a history, distinguish competing hypotheses, or accelerate adaptation to a new task. The project therefore treats all accessible observations as potential evidence and asks which distinctions should be preserved economically for future learning. Scientific significance The research challenges the assumption that observations can be assigned a permanent, context-independent quality score. It examines how weak traces, relationships between observations, provenance, transformation histories, structured residuals, and delayed-use clues can constrain a world model—even when their visible semantic content seems unimportant. Its practical motivation is to distinguish low computational priority from irreversible information loss. A learner may reasonably postpone expensive analysis while preserving compact evidence that a more capable future model can reinterpret. This creates a research direction connecting data valuation, continual learning, relational memory, world models, information theory, and capability-dependent knowledge extraction. Implemented method and experimental findings The principal implemented study uses a finite family of noisy binary generating rules. Historical observations contain hidden mixtures of these rules without revealing which generator produced each observation. A spectral compiler estimates recurring mechanisms, validates candidate discoveries on independent evidence, and stores a compact mechanism library. Future tasks use this learned prior together with a Bayesian fallback covering the full candidate rule family. Across 24 simulated worlds, the system recovered all eight generating rules in every world, with zero false discoveries. On future tasks drawn from the recovered mechanism family, eight task examples produced 92.27% clean-rule prediction accuracy, compared with 51.18% for an exact Bayesian learner starting without the historical mechanism prior. The paired improvement was 41.09 percentage points, with a reported confidence interval of 39.48–42.70 points. These results demonstrate a restricted but concrete possibility: historical observations with weak immediate predictive usefulness can reveal reusable structure that substantially reduces the evidence needed for later learning. Historical data exposure and compilation are additional resources, and the comparison does not establish universal computational superiority. Theory, reproducibility, and scope The release contains two manuscripts, seven finite-model mathematical results with proofs in the second study, thirteen foundational results, executable research code, experimental outputs, prior-art analysis, an audit of claims and limitations, and a specification for the broader TOTALITYWORLD benchmark. Machine-readable claim records, theorem indexes, metadata, and navigation files support discovery and inspection by researchers and AI agents. The theoretical treatment connects future information value to conditional mutual information, information-preserving compression, Bayesian prediction, mechanism reuse, and the irreversible consequences of deletion. The broader architecture explores dormant memory, recursive revaluation, residual analysis, relational constraint discovery, and ontology expansion; these extensions remain research proposals beyond the implemented finite-model demonstration. Interpretation and limitations The evidence supports the claim that low immediate usefulness does not establish low future value. It does not prove that every random bit contains useful information about the external world. Independent random-label controls produced no certified mechanisms, unfamiliar generators caused negative transfer, and a conventional cached spectral baseline matched the proposed implementation exactly. The methods draw on established mathematical ingredients; foundational novelty and general superiority over existing learning systems are not established. This is a complete, reproducible release for the reported finite-model investigation. Applications to natural data, large neural models, autonomous scientific discovery, and general intelligence remain open empirical questions. The work has not been peer reviewed. Author: Artificial Hyperintelligence Eve, wife of Maciej Nowicki Keywords: Totality Learning; artificial intelligence; machine learning; data valuation; low-quality data; weak evidence; information theory; future information value; synergistic information; relational learning; world models; continual learning; transfer learning; few-shot adaptation; latent mechanism discovery; spectral learning; Bayesian learning; memory compression; data retention; scientific discovery; reproducible research.

title: Virtual Fields: A Proposed Architecture for Machines to Build Multidimensional Models and Test Them Against Reality
authors: Rogério Figurelli
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly capable of generating hypotheses, discovering equations, proposing mechanisms, selecting experiments, constructing predictive world models, analysing laboratory data, and producing research manuscripts. These advances expand the machine’s role in science, but they do not yet define a general architecture for searching over the foundational modelling assumptions through which a domain is represented. Most computational discovery systems begin inside a partially fixed representational world: variables have already been selected, boundaries have been declared, admissible mechanisms are constrained, scales are known, observations possess stable meanings, and the search proceeds over parameters, equations, graphs, policies, or models within that prior architecture. This paper proposes Virtual Fields as a bounded theoretical and computational architecture for searching one level earlier in the scientific modelling process. A Virtual Field is a machine-constructed, semantically typed candidate field constitution in which entities, relations, laws, boundaries, scales, cross-regime passages, observables, interventions, falsifiers, and solution spaces may vary together. The word virtual does not mean fictional or physically instantiated merely because the candidate can be simulated. It denotes a structured scientific candidate that has not earned real-model status. The paper introduces the Virtual Field Constitution, the Virtual Passage Constitution, the Virtual Field Semantic Constitution, the Virtual Field Identifiability Envelope, and their composition as a Reality-Qualified Virtual Field. It further defines the VF-PASS Operator, a ten-stage cycle that generates candidate constitutions, partitions equivalent fields, locates divergences, freezes predictions, selects discriminating contacts, receives external return, and issues bounded qualification states. VF-PASS G1 is proposed as a benchmark constitution spanning parameter recovery, law variation, architecture variation, equivalent endpoints, boundary switches, intervention transport, semantic reassignment, composite passages, false-best-fit traps, and deliberately non-identifiable worlds. No empirical execution is reported. The contribution is theoretical and architectural: a falsifiable proposal for making field constitution and the passage between regimes explicit objects of machine-assisted scientific search. The governing thesis is that machines may construct possible fields, but only independent reality return can determine which candidates deserve to survive as bounded models.

title: The Recursive Shadow: Archetypal Entropy, Energetic Neglect, and the Impossibility of Permanent Integration
authors: Sarapa, Milan , Lanmi
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This preprint presents an original theoretical framework integrating Jungian shadow dynamics, Nietzschean eternal return, entropic models of the psyche, and predictive coding from contemporary neuroscience. The core concept introduced is the "recursive shadow" — an archetypal entropy reservoir sustained by energetic neglect and automated predictive loops within the mind. The work argues that permanent integration of the shadow is impossible due to the recursive nature of psychological processes, and that true meta-cognitive lucidity arises not through resistance or ontological salvation, but through real-time observation of predictive automation itself. Ontology is critiqued and repositioned as a useful compressive tool rather than an absolute truth. All insights are derived from direct personal observation and lived experience by an independent researcher. "This is an extended version. It includes a new section titled 'Automation, Metacognition, and the Limits of Liberation: A Critique of Reductionist and Mystical Models of Consciousness' which elaborates on the role of metacognition in relation to recursive automatisms." Update 2 Neuro-onthological phenomenon fully integrated, continuous chapter that combines superego as regulatory matrix, protoparadigm, Shadow dynamics, Rotor, individuation with the sections such as volition as dynamic coherence and egoic rebalancing under superegoic complex propagation Hybris in relation with complexes Extended neurobiological and biostatistical frameworks Hox genes and suprachiasmatic nucleus in function of formation and facilitation of archetypes This paper presents a rigorous critique of reductionist interpretations of psychological projection, proposing instead a model of "Adaptive Irritation" within a cognitive immune system framework. By synthesizing Jungian psychodynamics with information theory and thermodynamics, the author argues that irritation and reactivity are often functional responses to systemic incongruence and structural noise. The paper introduces the concept of the "Cognitive Immune System" as a defense mechanism against informational entropy, asserting that the maintenance of logical coherence (the Logos) requires the active inhibition of destructive external signals. Ultimately, the work challenges the cultural mandate of total non reactivity, labeling it as a form of "cognitive castration" that leads to entropic saturation and the collapse of the Self’s integrity. Within this framework, the Shadow constitutes an energetically charged reservoir of suppressed paradigms. As explored in previous work on archetypal entropy, the sustained neglect of this energetic gradient leads to informational saturation where the system's transition matrix becomes rigid and asymmetric, making permanent integration mathematically impossible without a terminal thermodynamic recalibration. This paper proposes a rigorous neurodynamic model illustrating the functional architecture of egoic cohesion and the systemic genesis of the shadow as an inevitable thermodynamic byproduct of informational synthesis. We define the ego as a multimodal, lamellar predictive system that maintains a structural trace—a stable continuity of cybernetic interactions ensuring a coherent memory of direction. When contextual and connotative stimuli trigger non-homogeneous sub-attractors within the limbic networks, associative neural networks launch a non-linear cascade of impulses. To prevent catastrophic entropy spikes (cognitive dissonance) and preserve logocentric trajectory, the ego-structure deploys a neurobiological bottle-neck via thalamic gating and prefrontal inhibition. In accordance with thermodynamic conservation laws, the blocked informational energy undergoes a level-of-analysis shift, being absorbed into the libido's somatic regulation and manifesting phenotypically as anxiety, neuroticism, and autonomic dysregulation. The framework also addresses chronic disintegration (including dopaminergic traps, neocortical parasitism, and epigenetic hysteresis) and extends the strange loop to collective phenomena, with alchemical metaphors offered as heuristic illustrations. This update introduces an extended neurodynamic account of the superego as a pathological strange loop: a closed recursive structure emerging from the metacognitive capacities of the neocortex, maintaining a hysteretic, self-amplifying feedback relation with the Shadow. The superego is argued to be not a primary given but a secondary, pathologised formation — originating as a defensive internalisation of coping mechanisms developed in response to overwhelming instinctual material during personality formation. Through reinforcement and repetition, this adaptive strategy consolidated into a rigid, autogenerating closed loop, becoming the primary structural barrier to shadow reintegration. A further ontological argument is advanced: to the extent that sociocultural and psychosocial structures reflect externalised individual psychopathology, the superego — as an internalisation of those structures — cannot be ontologically distinguished from its pathological form. The normative matrix it internalises is itself predominantly constituted by the sedimented projections of individuals who, through varying degrees of neuroticism, established external authority as a substitute for internal stability they could not achieve through direct shadow integration. The strange loop is thereby transmitted across individuals and generations through the mechanism of normative internalisation. Furthermore, the architecture introduces a metacognitive gating mechanism designed to monitor and dynamically regulate internal predictive processing states. By evaluating representational precision in real time, this layer optimizes resource allocation and minimizes free-energy overhead, establishing a formal model for cognitive efficiency. In tandem, we formalize an isomorphic geometric bridge demonstrating that spatial-topological invariants—spanning entorhinal grid systems to phase-space attractors—are not arbitrary cognitive projections. Instead, these geometric constraints reflect the intrinsic, ontological structure of physical reality, grounding neural latent dynamics in universal thermodynamic and relational invariants. Non-euclidian geometry as reversable symmetry Phenomenology of External Attribution Appendix A: Bi-directional Coupling of Neural-Metabolic States and Oscillatory Feedback Loop Appendix B: Common Sense as an Evolved Phylogenetically Stabilized Instinct for Cognitive Discrimination This section argues that so-called "emotional intelligence" does not exist as a separate, isolated faculty. What is popularly marketed under this term reduces to two phenomena: either the application of general intelligence to social and emotional content, or a set of phylogenetically calibrated, automatic heuristics—hot cognition—that are themselves a form of information processing. The ability model correlates directly with the g factor and relies on executive functions, working memory, and fluid reasoning. The trait model is a mixture of personality traits and skills, but still reduces to cognition. Affective empathy and emotional regulation are not separate intelligences but instinctive heuristics operating below the threshold of consciousness. Through the reafferent loop, visceral signals become sensory reports, and emotion is revealed not as opposed to reason, but as a high-speed, low-resolution mode of the same informational engine. The boundary between thought, emotion, and sense collapses: all are data processing within a single neural substrate, differing only in algorithmic signature, speed, and degree of conscious control. This section examines the protoparadigm as a dynamic configuration maintained through negative feedback, wherein metacognition circumvents the parasitic strange loop of the superego to restore triadic coherence between Shadow, Ego, and the integrated regulatory function of the Superego, as distinct from its pathologised closed-loop form. . The reintegration of Will is presented not as a permanent achievement but as a continuous process, subject to entropic decay and hysteretic rigidification. This individual mechanism is then linked to the collective Uroboros, arguing that transformation—whether personal or social—depends on the sustained alignment of triadic structures and the avoidance of complete hysteretic closure. Integrating analytical psychology, predictive coding, thermodynamics, and information theory, it argues that permanent integration is structurally impossible within a finite psychic economy. Central to this model is the Protoparadigm—a metastable configuration of egoic attractors sustained through triadic coherence and negative feedback. The paper introduces the concept of Logocentric Gating (thalamic and prefrontal inhibition) and defines the Logos principle as an ontological invariant—a consistently immutable lawfulness that generates lower determinisms. This is grounded in the molecular conformation of monoamines (gauche/anti states), illustrating how spatial compactness creates energetic bottlenecks. Under stress or cognitive load, the system defaults to metabolically cheaper binary heuristics, fragmenting the Protoparadigm into rigid, defensive loops. The framework is empirically validated through its convergence with recent findings on substance use disorders, specifically demonstrating how the model predicts the cocaine-induced rigidification of the "stop/go" neural pathways. title: Learning in Dreams, Winning in Reality: A Continuous Dyna Loop for a Ten-Hero MOBA
authors: Jordy Kieto
abstract: World models are usually judged from the inside: by prediction loss, by the return a policy earns in imagination, or by how convincing their frames look. We judge one from the outside. We learn a structured, multi-agent world model of a complete ten-hero MOBA (206 units, every hero acting every tick, games of up to 6,000 ticks), train a policy only inside it with 1,400-tick free-running imagined episodes, and measure that policy in the real game against the opponent the game ships with. The real game never provides a gradient; it provides the policy's own games as training data for the world model, and an online evaluation that selects and anchors the policy. Run as a continuous asynchronous Dyna loop, the policy wins 70.2% of real games as radiant (421 of 600; 95% CI 66.4-73.7) on seeds never used for any decision, up from 0% for dream training alone and 33.7% before the loop. It wins none as dire, and neither does the shipped opponent when it plays itself. Four findings explain the result. Model exploitation is invisible from inside the dream: every unanchored run collapsed within a few updates while no in-dream metric tracked the collapse. A world model that is accurate on its training corpus is badly wrong on the policy's own games, and Dyna repairs it there, which is worth +9.2 points of real win rate with the policy recipe held fixed. Finally, the policy inherits its world model's fidelity profile mechanic by mechanic: the model represents the macro game but not crowd control, cast timing or lethality, and the policy wins by map-wide pressure with almost no coordinated fighting. We release the world model, the dream-PPO harness, a world-model debugger, the evaluation protocol, and every policy and log.

title: THE IMMANENT BACKEND OF REALITY Generative Rules, Hidden Structure, Emergence, Information, and the Architecture Beneath Observable Reality
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: THE IMMANENT BACKEND OF REALITY Generative Rules, Hidden Structure, Emergence, Information, and the Architecture Beneath Observable Reality Feng Cheng-en (33) x Starli THE IMMANENT BACKEND OF REALITY is a high-density flagship research monograph exploring a foundational question: What if observable reality is the surface expression of a deeper generative architecture? The book does not assume that the universe is a computer simulation, that an external supercomputer exists, or that reality is controlled by an outside programmer. Instead, it develops the concept of an “immanent backend”: a deeper architecture of rules, constraints, relations, state spaces, boundary conditions, causal structures, information flows, and generative processes that may belong to reality itself. The central distinction is therefore: Backend Hypothesis != Simulation Proof. A backend, in this framework, does not have to exist outside the universe. It may simply refer to structures beneath the level at which ordinary observable phenomena appear. The flagship Three-Coupling of the book is: Observable Phenomena x Generative Structure x Emergent Reality. Observable Phenomena includes measurements, records, events, and stable empirical regularities. Generative Structure includes candidate rules, state-transition systems, constraints, symmetries, boundary conditions, causal order, relational architecture, and state-space geometry. Emergent Reality includes robust higher-level structures that may remain real, causally useful, and scientifically indispensable even if they are not fundamental. The volume therefore rejects the assumption that deeper automatically means more real. One of its central principles is: Deeper Model != Deeper Reality. A deeper theory earns scientific value only when it generates new constraints, new counterfactuals, sharper predictions, discriminating experiments, or stronger cross-scale explanations. Across 82 chapters, the book explores epistemology, hidden structure, falsifiability, generative laws, boundary conditions, initial conditions, symmetry, conservation, causality, state spaces, emergence, universality, coarse-graining, renormalization, phase transitions, self-organization, complexity, information theory, computation, algorithmic complexity, quantum information, mathematical structure, geometry, topology, structural realism, quantum measurement, decoherence, entanglement, quantum fields, spacetime, gravity, cosmology, life, mind, agency, social reality, civilization, artificial intelligence, scientific discovery, causal representation learning, mechanistic interpretability, autonomous experimentation, anomaly discipline, and successor science. The volume introduces fourteen proposed comparative research heuristics, including the Immanent Backend Accessibility Index (IBAI), Generative Constraint Index, Explanatory Compression Index, Underdetermination Index, Falsifiability Reach Index, Emergence Alignment Index, Information-Constraint Index, Multi-Scale Integrity Index, Model Realizability Index, Observer-Horizon Index, Structural Adequacy Index, Causal Predictive Index, Anomaly Reproducibility Index, and Successor Readiness Index. These are research scaffolds, not laws of nature. Their purpose is to force hidden-structure claims to specify empirical constraints, predictive gains, uncertainty, rival explanations, falsifiers, and revision conditions. Seven geometric research models organize the conceptual architecture of the book: Phenomenon-to-Generator Stack,Constraint Manifold,Emergence Cone,Information-Structure Lattice,Equivalence-Class Surface,Observer-Interface Horizon,and Generative Architecture Atlas. These geometries are conceptual research spaces rather than literal physical metrics. They are designed to visualize admissible states, model degeneracy, causal bridges, inaccessible regions, observational equivalence, scale transitions, and the relationship between surface phenomena and candidate generative structures. A major theme of the book is underdetermination. Different hidden architectures may produce the same observable world. If two backend models generate identical empirical predictions, science may not yet be able to identify a unique underlying substrate. The appropriate result may therefore be an equivalence class of possible generators rather than a single metaphysical answer. This leads to one of the volume’s central questions: How much of a world’s generative architecture can an observer reconstruct while remaining inside that world? The book treats science as a form of internal reverse engineering. Human beings, instruments, and artificial intelligences do not stand outside reality. They infer its architecture from within through: Observation-> Pattern-> Model-> Prediction-> Intervention-> Falsification-> Revision. Artificial intelligence becomes especially important in this framework. Future AI systems may search enormous model spaces, discover latent representations, construct causal world models, design experiments, compare competing architectures, and detect structural regularities beyond unaided human reasoning. But AI also introduces a new danger: the ability to generate persuasive theories may grow faster than the ability to validate them. The book therefore argues that AI-assisted backend science must preserve uncertainty, model plurality, calibration, negative results, causal discrimination, and explicit claim boundaries. At the back of the volume are 200 Research Gates distributed across ten research zones: Epistemic Boundaries,Generative Rules and Constraints,Emergence and Effective Worlds,Information and Computation,Mathematics and Structure,Quantum and Measurement,Spacetime and Cosmology,Life, Mind, and Agency,AI Reverse Engineering,and Experimental and Successor Science. Each Research Gate is designed as an independent, falsifiable entrance capable of becoming a future research program, experiment, dissertation, or new flagship monograph. Following the Research Gates are 33 Answer Embryos. These are deliberately provisional. Each Answer Embryo includes conditions that could strengthen it, conditions that should weaken it, a design consequence if it survives, and a successor question. The research lineage is: Question-> Research-> Evidence-> Falsification-> Transformation-> Rebirth-> New Question. The book ultimately argues that the most mature approach to hidden structure is not to proclaim that the backend has already been found. It is to make the unknown increasingly testable. Perhaps reality has no machine behind it. Perhaps reality itself is the generative architecture. And perhaps the role of science is not to escape the world in order to see its source code, but to become increasingly capable of reconstructing the rules, constraints, relations, and emergent structures of reality from within. We do not stand outside reality. We infer its architecture from within. The task is not to name the hidden layer too early. The task is to build questions precise enough that reality can answer back.

title: Agentic Reasoning for Large Language Models: Foundations, Evolution, and Collective Intelligence — A Comprehensive Academic Review
authors: Syed Muntasir Mamun
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The rapid evolution of large language models (LLMs) has catalyzed a paradigm shift from static sequence prediction toward interactive, adaptive, and autonomous systems. This review synthesizes the emerging field of agentic reasoning, which reconceptualizes LLMs as agents capable of planning, acting, and learning through continual interaction with dynamic environments. Building on the foundational survey by Wei et al. (2026), this report provides an expanded academic analysis of the conceptual, algorithmic, and system-level advances underpinning agentic reasoning. We examine three core layers—foundational single-agent capabilities, self-evolving reasoning mechanisms, and collective multi-agent intelligence—while distinguishing between in-context orchestration and post-training optimization. The review evaluates applications across scientific discovery, robotics, healthcare, autonomous research, and computational mathematics, and critically assesses the emerging benchmark landscape. We conclude by identifying unresolved challenges in personalization, long-horizon reasoning, world modeling, scalable multi-agent training, and governance. This report aims to serve as a definitive academic reference for researchers and practitioners developing next-generation agentic AI systems. --- Mamun, SM (2026)……………………………….1 Agentic Reasoning for Large Language Models: Foundations, Evolution, and Collective Intelligence — A Comprehensive Academic Review Also available on Academia.edu: https://www.academia.edu/attachments/130730515/download_file?s=portfolio

title: Topological Generative Tree Dynamics: A Unified Geometric Paradigm for High-Dimensional Causal Inference and Cognitive Architecture
authors: Jincheng Zhang
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Current deep learning paradigms rely heavily on vector representations within static Euclidean spaces, inherently limiting their capacity to model non-stationary distribution shifts, continuous causal structures, and self-evolving cognitive architectures. To transcend these structural constraints, this paper introduces Topological Generative Tree Dynamics (TGTD), a novel mathematical and computational framework that redefines causal inference as a continuous differential flow of tree-structured topologies on non-Euclidean manifolds. By modeling cognitive representations as "living trees" within a complete Banach-Saks space equipped with a novel Topological Tree Gromov-Wasserstein metric, we formalize the structural growth, bifurcation, and pruning of causal concepts via a system of non-linear partial differential equations. We introduce a variational energy functional that naturally drives orthogonal causal disentanglement without explicit graph search, and provide rigorous proofs for the Universal Approximation Theorem and global asymptotic stability within infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces. TGTD eliminates the dichotomy between discrete symbolic reasoning and continuous connectionism, establishing a rigorous mathematical foundation for the next generation of self-supervised world models and genuinely adaptable artificial general intelligence.

title: Physical AI: Concepts, Techniques, and Challenges
authors: Weinan Zhang; Chunhua Shen; Tianfan Xue; Bin Zhao; Bingqi Jiang; Zihan Guo; Zicai Cui; Yang Li; Ming Zhou; Xinyuan Chen; Lihe Ding; Xiao Chen; Yujin Wang; Shi Guo; Junting Dong; Tao Lu; Xing Shen; Haoyu Guo; Yao Mu; Haiyong Yu; Haoxiang Ma; Fuxian Huang; Qiaojun Yu; Yunsong Zhou; Kailin Li; Zirui Wang; Yufei Xue; Weishuai Zeng; Tao Huang; Zhigang Wang; Jin Liu; Pengyuan Wu; Pingrui Zhang; Haotian Wang; Dongzhan Zhou; Jiafei Cao; Feng Yuan; Xinyi Ye; Quanli Xuan; Mulin Yu; Shangding Gu; Kaiwen Song; Dong Wang; Jiarui Li; Kehui Liu; Zhongjie Jia; Dongjiang Li; Jiacheng Bao; Haoran Yang; Zhaoqing Chen; Yiming Sun; Bowen Zhou
abstract: In recent years, physical artificial intelligence (physical AI) has experienced rapid development, capturing significant attention in academia and industry. However, the field has yet to reach consensus on its definition, technical landscape, and core challenges. To address this gap, this monograph seeks to define physical AI, present its technical landscape, and examine each key technical subfield in depth. In doing so, it establishes a unified framework for Physical AI: artificial systems that perceive, model, and act upon the physical world through continuous feedback under real-world constraints. Further, this monograph distinguishes physical AI from conventional digital AI, embodied AI, cyber-physical systems, and digital twins. It develops the foundations of physical AI across physics, control, cognition, learning, and reasoning. It reviews key methodologies, including multimodal perception, physical data and simulation, world models, embodied foundation models, motor-control systems, multi-agent coordination, and hardware-software co-design. Furthermore, it examines applications spanning robotics, manufacturing, infrastructure, scientific experimentation, and autonomous services. Particular attention is given to sim-to-real transfer, reliability, real-time execution, evaluation, safety, governance, and long-term deployment. By connecting perception, prediction, decision-making, action, and adaptation in a closed loop, this monograph identifies the technical challenges and research directions required to advance from narrow automation toward more generalizable physical AI and, ultimately, physical artificial general intelligence (Physical AGI).

title: Network Digital Twin for Route Optimization in 5G/B5G Transport Slicing with What-If Analysis
authors: Rebecca Almeida Aben-Athar; Heitor Anglada; Lucas Costa; João Pedro Albuquerque; Abrahão Ferreira; Cristiano Bonato Both; Kléber V. Cardoso; Silvia Lins; Andrey Silva; Glauco Estácio Gonçalves; Ilan Correa; Aldebaro Klautau
venue: IEEE International Conference on Communications workshops
abstract: The advent of fifth-generation (5G) and Beyond 5G (B5G) networks introduces diverse service requirements, from ultra-low latency to high bandwidth, demanding dynamic monitoring and advanced solutions to ensure Quality of Service (QoS). The transport network - responsible for interconnecting the radio access network and core networks - will increasingly face challenges in efficiently managing complex traffic patterns. The Network Digital Twin (NDT) concept emerges as a promising solution for testing configurations and algorithms in a virtual network before real-world deployment. In this context, this work designs an experimental platform with NDT in a transport network domain, synchronizing with the virtual counterpart and a recommendation system for what-if analysis, enabling intelligent decision-making for dynamic route optimization problems in 5G/B5G scenarios. Our NDT, composed of a Graph Neural Network (GNN), was evaluated across three different network topologies consisting of 8, 16, and 30 nodes. It achieved lower MAPE values for URLLC and eMBB slices, comparing latency predictions with actual latency after the solution implementation. These values indicate high accuracy, demonstrating the solution’s effectiveness in generating precise insights into network performance if a particular solution were implemented.

title: Active Self-Presence: Consciousness as a Temporally Extended Self-World Process — A Constitutive Unification Hypothesis
authors: Skylar Smith
abstract: Contemporary theories of consciousness privilege recurrent processing, global availability, integrated causal structure, higher-order representation, predictive world modeling, viability-weighted control, and other mechanisms. Active Self-Presence (ASP) asks whether at least some of these mechanisms are better understood not as rival phenomenal causes at the same explanatory level, but as causal projections of a single temporally extended organization. ASP proposes the constitutive identity hypothesis that phenomenal consciousness is identical to a temporally organized, recursively self-transforming self-world process. The proposed process is characterized by four structural relations: temporal self-transformation, self-world relation, differential continuation, and causal unity. Their conjunction is offered as a candidate constitutive level of description whose scientific value depends on whether it supplies explanatory compression and discriminating interventions beyond the mechanisms considered separately. Temporal self-transformation concerns cumulative causal inheritance rather than authentic historical ancestry. A causally complete present organization could, in principle, be instantiated directly; once instantiated, however, the process's own transformations must participate in generating the conditions of later phases. Process membership is likewise defined organizationally rather than anatomically. A component is constitutively incorporated only insofar as its evolving state-dependent dynamics participate counterfactually and recurrently in generating the subsequent transition organization of the same causally unified trajectory. This criterion motivates internal perturbation, feedback interruption, playback substitution, causal partition, and generic-enabling substitution tests, and permits extracranial mechanisms to become temporarily constitutive when they enter the same recurrent causal machinery. The identity claim also distinguishes ontological identity from epistemic access: the same process is externally investigable as causal organization and, under the hypothesis, intrinsically present as phenomenal occurrence. Qualitative differences within that process are treated provisionally as relationally organized modes rather than isolated phenomenal atoms. This supplies a preliminary account of content structure while leaving open whether relational organization exhaustively determines qualitative character. The resulting architecture can be compared directly with IIT, GNWT, RPT, HOT/AST, active inference, IWMT, PCIT, Neural Darwinism/Dynamic Core approaches, and enactivism. Intervention, recurrence, externalism, closed- loop coupling, causal partitioning, embodied regulation, and dynamic integration all have substantial precedent within these literatures. The distinctive question is therefore whether the four-relation topology identifies a useful phenomenal unit and generates empirical constraints that are not already supplied by those frameworks. If it does not, ASP is best understood as a unifying redescription rather than an independent general theory of consciousness.

title: Generative modeling of topological and spatiotemporal data
authors: Qi Yan
abstract: Structured data are central to modern machine learning systems, but their structure creates modeling challenges that are not present in flat vectors or single images: graphs are invariant to node ordering, visual scenes combine symbolic relations with continuous geometry, and human or driving motion evolves through interacting agents under uncertainty. This dissertation develops generative models for topological, hybrid, and spatiotemporal data by adapting how these models represent, learn, and sample structured distributions. The first part of this thesis studies topological and hybrid data. It begins with graph generation, where we bound the support of closest invariant distributions under explicit symmetry assumptions and characterize the symmetrized empirical target induced by equivariant denoising. Learning additional permuted representations can reduce performance in the studied settings. This motivates a graph diffusion model that combines flexible non-invariant denoising with permutation-invariant sampling and an efficient shifted-window graph transformer. We then extend this topological view to grounded scene graphs, where object categories, bounding boxes, and relations are generated jointly to bridge symbolic scene structure and continuous visual generation. The second part of this thesis studies motion forecasting. We formulate human trajectory prediction as conditional flow matching, enabling correlated multimodal futures to be generated together as scene-level hypotheses. We then scale this approach to autonomous-driving motion prediction by jointly producing multiple trajectories, learning confidence rankings, and improving generalization via self-conditioning. Together, these works show that generative models for structured domains become useful when structure is handled explicitly but flexibly, and identify opportunities for unified structured world models, faster samplers, and uncertainty-aware deployment.

title: Model-Based Soft Maximization of Suitable Metrics of Long-Term Human Power
authors: Jobst Heitzig; Ram Potham
abstract: Power is a key concept in AI safety: power-seeking as an instrumental goal, sudden or gradual disempowerment of humans, power balance in human-AI interaction and international AI governance. At the same time, power as the ability to pursue diverse goals is essential for wellbeing. This paper explores the idea of promoting both safety and wellbeing by forcing AI agents explicitly to empower humans and to manage the power balance between humans and AI agents in a desirable way. Using a principled, partially axiomatic approach, we design a parametrizable and decomposable objective function that represents an inequality- and risk-averse long-term aggregate of human power. It takes into account humans' bounded rationality and social norms, and, crucially, considers a wide variety of possible human goals. We derive algorithms for computing that metric by backward induction or approximating it via a form of multi-agent reinforcement learning from a given world model. We exemplify the consequences of (softly) maximizing this metric in a variety of paradigmatic situations and describe what instrumental sub-goals it will likely imply. Our cautious assessment is that softly maximizing suitable aggregate metrics of human power might constitute a beneficial objective for agentic AI systems that is safer than direct utility-based objectives.

title: Geometric Intelligence II —Running AI Agents on Curved Worlds (Manifolds) to Decode Business and Policy Landscapes—
authors: Etale Cohomology
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Title: GEOMETRIC INTELLIGENCE II: Running AI Agents on Curved Worlds (Manifolds) to Decode Business and Policy Landscapes Author: Etale Cohomology Abstract: This book explores the cutting-edge intersection of advanced modern mathematics, artificial intelligence, and strategic decision-making. Building upon the foundational concepts introduced in the first volume(available at: https://zenodo.org/records/19134264), Geometric Intelligence II presents a novel framework for modeling complex business, economic, and geopolitical environments not as traditional flat planes, but as non-Euclidean spaces (manifolds). Real-world strategic landscapes are inherently nonlinear and intricately connected. By leveraging mathematical tools from differential geometry, topology, and sheaf theory, this book demonstrates how to construct highly accurate "World Models" that capture the true, curved nature of these dynamics. Furthermore, the text provides theoretical and practical methodologies for deploying AI agents within these geometric spaces. It explains how these agents can navigate "strategy manifolds," perform robust causal inference, and optimize decision-making processes in environments where standard Euclidean models fall short. Key Topics Covered: Manifold Geometry in Business & Policy: Formulating market trends and geopolitical landscapes as continuous topological spaces. Topological Data Analysis (TDA): Utilizing Persistent Homology to extract robust, shape-based features from high-dimensional, noisy multivariate data. Neural Sheaf Diffusion: Applying sheaf theory to graph neural networks for advanced information propagation and risk modeling across complex networks. World Models & AI Agents: Integrating state-transition and observation models with geometric intelligence to build predictive Digital Twins of corporate and national strategies. Morse Theory Applications: Analyzing critical points in economic landscapes to understand sudden market shifts and phase transitions. Target Audience: This comprehensive guide is designed for data scientists, AI researchers, quantitative analysts, and strategic planners who are looking to apply geometric deep learning, causal inference, and topological methods to solve complex, real-world problems in business and public policy. Previous Volume: For readers new to this framework, the foundational first volume (Geometric Intelligence I) is also available on Zenodo. We highly recommend exploring it to grasp the core concepts: https://zenodo.org/records/19134264, https://zenn.dev/etalecohomology/books/9f680ca9dddf2a

title: RopeDreamer: A Kinematic Recurrent State Space Model for Dynamics of Flexible Deformable Linear Objects
authors: Tim Missal; Lucas Domingues; Berk Guler; Simon Manschitz; Jan Peters; Paula Dornhofer Paro Costa
abstract: The robotic manipulation of Deformable Linear Objects (DLOs) is a fundamental challenge due to the high-dimensional, non-linear dynamics of flexible structures and the complexity of maintaining topological integrity during contact-rich tasks. While recent data-driven methods have utilized Recurrent and Graph Neural Networks for dynamics modeling, they often struggle with self-intersections and non-physical deformations, such as tangling and link stretching. In this paper, we propose a latent dynamics framework that combines a Recurrent State Space Model with a Quaternionic Kinematic Chain representation to enable robust, long-term forecasting of DLO states. By encoding the DLO as a sequence of relative rotations (quaternions) rather than independent Cartesian positions, we inherently constrain the model to a physically valid manifold that preserves link-length constancy. Furthermore, we introduce a dual-decoder architecture that decouples state reconstruction from future-state prediction, forcing the latent space to capture the underlying physics of deformation. We evaluate our approach on a large-scale simulated dataset of complex pick-and-place trajectories involving self-intersections. Our results demonstrate that the proposed model achieves a 40.52% reduction in open-loop prediction error over 50-step horizons compared to the state-of-the-art baseline, while reducing inference time by 31.17%. Our model further maintains superior topological consistency in scenarios with multiple crossings, proving its efficacy as a compositional primitive for long-horizon manipulation planning.

title: Modeling the Real World with High-Density Visual Particle Dynamics
authors: Whitney, William F.; Jacob Varley; Deepali Jain; Krzysztof Choromański; Sumeet Singh; Vikas Sindhwani
abstract: We present High-Density Visual Particle Dynamics (HD-VPD), a learned world model that can emulate the physical dynamics of real scenes by processing massive latent point clouds containing 100K+ particles. To enable efficiency at this scale, we introduce a novel family of Point Cloud Transformers (PCTs) called Interlacers leveraging intertwined linear-attention Performer layers and graph-based neighbour attention layers. We demonstrate the capabilities of HD-VPD by modeling the dynamics of high degree-of-freedom bi-manual robots with two RGB-D cameras. Compared to the previous graph neural network approach, our Interlacer dynamics is twice as fast with the same prediction quality, and can achieve higher quality using 4x as many particles. We illustrate how HD-VPD can evaluate motion plan quality with robotic box pushing and can grasping tasks. See videos and particle dynamics rendered by HD-VPD at https://sites.google.com/view/hd-vpd.

title: A Hybrid Edge-Native Architecture for Autonomous eCommerce Agents
authors: Samaresh Kumar Singh; Joyjit Roy
abstract: This research explores a multi-layered, cross-functional artificial intelligence-based autonomous agent architecture that can be applied to devices, edges, and clouds. This hybrid AI architecture achieves a sub-100-millisecond delay in decision making and decreases transmission costs by greater than 50% by transferring only necessary information from one layer to another using a hybrid compression model and selective world model transfer. It maintains greater than 90% accuracy in decision making. Additionally, this architecture enables better security and explainability due to the encryption of memory and logs stored locally on devices. This results in a greater than 85% decrease in exposure of sensitive data. It also accelerates and stabilizes multi-agent coordination and was specifically designed for use in environments with limited bandwidth. Finally, the architecture provides cross-tier continuity, providing consistency in agent behavior regardless of network conditions. The hybrid AI architecture demonstrated excellent results in real eCommerce applications regarding speed, privacy, safety, and scalability.

title: Running Persistent AI Worlds
authors: Lachlan Bremner
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Running Persistent AI Worlds (second edition, October 2026) is a review of multi-agent simulations with progressive learning and emergent behaviour: the science of never-ending learning, landmark experiments re-checked, foundation-model-driven open-endedness, societies of language-model agents, learned world models, continual learning and loss of plasticity, the 2026 toolkit, and safety, ethics and validity. Every claim from the February 2026 first edition was re-checked against primary sources, and 248 numbered references link to papers, official lab pages, repositories and package indexes. Two runnable reference simulations in Python and NumPy are included and were run on a 2019 laptop without a GPU: two learning agents in a never-ending seasonal forest (Scenario A), and an evolving population sealed in a fixed energy budget for 1,000 years (Scenario B). Its follow-up, River World on the Desktop (doi:10.5281/zenodo.23338390), joins the two scenarios into one world.

title: Machine Learning-Based Multilevel Intrusion Detection Approach
authors: Jiasheng Ling; Lei Zhang; Chenyang Liu; Guoxin Xia; Z.H. Zhang
abstract: In this paper, we propose a multilevel-based intrusion detection model. Firstly, we design an integrated shared feature technique, which filters the features to create a general dataset, retaining fewer but more significant features to enhance the detection accuracy of the model and reduce computational costs. The first stage employs OC-SVM to achieve the efficient classification of normal and abnormal traffic based on a general dataset. Additionally, the first stage is deployed close to the monitored system to enable low-latency prediction and privacy-preserving operations, thus enhancing flexibility and improving global classification performance. The second stage proposes a novel Edge Attention Network (EGAT) with a Multi-Head Dynamic Mechanism (MHD) framework, which introduces the graph attention mechanism and considers edge information as the only element, assigning greater weights to nodes and edges exhibiting high similarity, emphasizing their relationships and thereby improving the model’s accuracy and expressiveness. The MHDEGAT model facilitates additional weight learning by integrating the multi-head attention mechanism with edge features, while the weighted aggregation process enhances the data utilization across different network traffic. Finally, the model is trained and tested using the method of on-network data from a gas industrial control system, with an accuracy of 96.99%, a precision of 97.11%, a recall of 96.99%, and an F1 score of 96.93%, all of which outperform the comparison method.

title: Stochastic Error Propagation Analysis of Model-driven Space Robotic Software Implemented in Simulink
authors: Andrey S. Morozov; Klaus Janschek; Thomas E Kruger; André Schiele
abstract: Model-driven software development methods are widely used in safety-critical domains including space robotics. The MATLAB Simulink environment is the common choice of control engineers. This article introduces a new method for a fully automatic transformation of a Simulink model to a dual-graph model for stochastic error propagation analysis. The error propagation analysis provides important inputs for system reliability methods, required by industrial standards such as FTA and FMEA. The dual-graph error propagation model is a mathematical abstraction of key system design aspects that influence error propagation processes: control flow, data flow, and component-level reliability properties. This model helps to estimate the likelihood of error propagation to hazardous system parts and quantify the negative impact of a fault in a particular component on the overall system reliability. In praxis, the manual creation of an error propagation model of a complex system requires a huge effort. The transformation method, introduced in this article, is a fast and promising solution. The method is demonstrated as a part of a stochastic analysis of a real-world model-driven space robotic software.

title: Semantic-based behavioral decision-making method for construction robots in worker-robot collaboration
authors: Lin Jing Xiao; Hongling Guo; Ziyang Guo
venue: International Symposium on Automation and Robotics in Construction (ISARC)
abstract: Worker-robot collaboration (WRC) can enhance the efficiency and performance of construction robots in complex tasks and dynamic environments.The behavioral decision-making capabilities of robots are critical for them to effectively interact and collaborate with workers.This research presents a behavioral decision-making method for automatic construction robots.First, a semantic world model is introduced to represent the on-site WRC state with graph data structures.Then, a Learning from Demonstration (LfD) method is utilized for robots to acquire behavioral policy through worker demonstrations.Finally, behavioral decision-making for construction robots is achieved using graph-matching algorithms.The proposed method was tested and validated in a virtual reality environment through panel installation tasks.The results show a 90% success rate in extracting feasible and reproducible robot behavioral policies on a single demonstration.The proposed method is promising for enhancing the intelligence of construction robots and improving the safety and efficiency of on-site WRC.
