title: A Semantic Fabric for Human / AI / Biosphere Communication
authors: Alexander Mathiesen-Ohman
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Human language evolved as a high-bandwidth coordination technology for small groups under stable biological and social constraints. Today, those constraints are being overwritten by digitally mediated environments in which communication is persistent, machine-readable, multimodal, and increasingly executable—able to trigger actions across socio-technical infrastructures. Meaning now circulates not only through sentences, but through telemetry, biometric signals, algorithmic predictions, sensor alerts, and automated state updates that coordinate behavior across humans, AI systems, and instrumented environments. This shift exposes a growing mismatch: prevailing communication models remain grounded in human-to-human exchange or syntactic signal transmission, while contemporary coordination requires semantic alignment across heterogeneous agents operating at different speeds, modalities, and representational architectures. This paper advances the core claim that the sentence is no longer the primitive unit of communication in hybrid human–AI–biosphere systems. Instead, communication increasingly functions as continuous shared-state synchronization: aligning task-relevant world models across humans, artificial agents, machines, and ecological sensing systems. Building on semantic communication theory, task-oriented communication, the information bottleneck framework, multi-agent coordination, and multimodal interaction research, the article proposes SYMBIO - a multi-layer semantic communication architecture that treats language as modality-independent infrastructure rather than message exchange. SYMBIO ingests heterogeneous inputs (text, speech, gesture, biosignals, machine telemetry, environmental sensing), compiles them into an intermediate semantic representation, and renders outputs across channels (natural language, symbolic/visual compression, haptics, machine-readable signals, and action gating). Crucially, the model embeds privacy, provenance, consent, and safety as intrinsic properties of semantic representations, enabling accountable translation from meaning to action. The paper contributes (1) a unified conceptualization of communication as state alignment across heterogeneous intelligences, (2) an architectural model for semantic mediation and modality selection, and (3) a formal research agenda for evaluating semantic fidelity via belief alignment and task performance under constraints of bandwidth, latency, uncertainty, and governance. The proposed framework reframes language as a civilizational coordination layer for an emerging ecology of human–AI–environment interaction.

title: Modeling what Matters: Emergent Abstraction In Reinforcement Learning
authors: Benjamin Freed
abstract: Real-world decision-making is rife with partial observability, long horizons, and complex multi-agent interactions. This thesis argues that abstraction—forming simplified representations of the task that retain relevant information—offers a unifying principle for tackling these challenges across model-free and model-based reinforcement learning (RL). We develop methods in which abstractions are not hand-designed but emerge from learning objectives, yielding representations that improve an agent’s ability to cope with high-dimensional observations, extended temporal dependencies, and inter-agent coupling. On the model-free, multi-agent side, we introduce Partial Reward Decoupling (PRD), a game-abstraction mechanism that dynamically decomposes teams into subgroups, simplifying cross-agent credit assignment and accelerating cooperative learning. We also study discrete communication learning under bandwidth constraints, where agents learn what information to transmit, to whom, and how to encode it—linking communication learning to representation learning and generative modeling. We also show how abstraction mitigates the misalignment between model-learning and task objectives typically found in model-based RL methods. By focusing limited model capacity on task-relevant factors and operating at an appropriate temporal scale, abstraction improves the utility of world models for decision-making. Toward this end, we explore the use of variational inference (VI) to learn both state and temporal abstractions. We demonstrate a state-abstraction method that ignores distracting details while retaining task-relevant features, attaining strong results on distraction-rich control benchmarks without relying on data-augmentation heuristics. We also propose a latent-variable approach to temporal abstraction that extracts skills and learns a temporally abstract dynamics model from offline data, enabling effective long-horizon prediction and planning for downstream tasks. Finally, we present Unified RL, which blends model-based and model-free updates by detecting when a learned model ceases to be useful for policy improvement and falling back to model-free learning updates. Empirically, Unified RL retains the data efficiency of model-based methods while achieving asymptotic performance comparable to model-free RL.

title: The Hidden Currents of Groupwork: Latent and Manifest Processes
authors: Zarina Syed
abstract: Human behaviour and interactions are complex, encompassing both what is immediately observable and what remains beneath the surface. Understanding these layers is particularly important in group therapeutic settings, where subtle dynamics can significantly influence outcomes. Literature explicitly addressing “manifest and latent processes” in group work remains limited. Most mainstream theories of group development, such as Tuckman’s stages, emphasize overt, measurable behaviours and structured task accomplishment, leaving latent processes, such as unspoken norms, emotional undercurrents, power dynamics, and unconscious motivations, underexplored. Recent trauma-focused group psychotherapy literature highlights this same gap, emphasising how latent relational and neurophysiological processes shape group functioning. This paper examines the interplay of manifest and latent processes in group development, emphasizing the importance of addressing both observable behaviours and hidden dynamics. The author intentionally anchors the conceptual foundation of this paper in classical groupwork theories, such as Tuckman’s stages of group development, Bion’s psychoanalytic insights, Vygotsky’s social constructivism, and the Johari Window due to their enduring relevance and widespread scholarly recognition. Concepts from the social unconscious sphere are also used to expand the understanding of latent dynamics beyond the individual psyche, acknowledging broader societal influences that shape the group space. This conceptual paper critically synthesizes these established and contemporary theories to explore the complex interaction between observable (manifest) and hidden (latent) processes within groupwork. Rather than proposing a new theory, it offers an integrated interpretation of existing scholarship by bringing classical and contemporary perspectives into dialogue. This synthesis advances a more nuanced understanding of group dynamics and highlights practical considerations for facilitation that attends to hidden or unspoken processes through a reflective, multidimensional lens. Practical implications are highlighted. This includes how facilitators can enhance group effectiveness by attending to both observable behaviours and underlying group dynamics, integrating reflective practice and awareness of personal bias to promote trust, psychological safety, and cohesive participation.

title: Neurosymbolic Alignment for Physiologically-Safe Clinical Language Models
authors: Abdulhady Abas Abdullah; Erik Cambria; Milena Zivkovic
abstract: Clinical LLMs can generate recommendations that are factually plausible yet physiologically unsafe. We investigate whether safety alignment can be improved by grounding preference optimization in structured physiological knowledge rather than text-only supervision. Methods: We propose Neurosymbolic Alignment, a training-time framework that couples a 7B clinical LLM with an HGNN-based Physiological World Model over an 847K-node biomedical knowledge graph. Candidate responses are scored using homeostatic constraints, multi-hop path plausibility, and drug-interaction penalties, and the resulting rankings drive iterative on-policy ORPO updates. Evaluation is performed on the Clinical Safety Benchmark (CSB), a 2,500-scenario benchmark for physiological constraint violations in generative clinical reasoning. Results: Relative to ORPO, the proposed method improves CSS from 69.5% to 90.8% (+21.3 pp), reduces physician-evaluated HR from 14.1% to 5.1% on the blinded subset, and improves DID from 72.8% to 91.6%. These gains are corroborated by an HGNN-independent Rule-Engine Safety Score (RSS: 86.4%, +21.2 pp over ORPO; r=0.97 concordance with CSS). The method also exceeds GPT-4 (5-shot) on all safety metrics despite a 10x parameter disadvantage, and outperforms an inference-time self-correction pipeline (SFT+SelfCorrect) by 11.4 pp CSS. Under synthetic EHR-style noise, 84.2% CSS is retained. Ablation analysis shows that HGNN scoring (-16.2 pp) and iterative training (-11.5 pp) are the dominant contributors. PhysioScore calibration against 200 clinician labels yielded ECE = 0.038 and kappa = 0.91. Conclusion: Training-time physiological grounding produces measurable and independently verifiable safety improvements in open-weight clinical LLMs under controlled evaluation. External validation on real clinical data is required to determine whether these gains transfer to deployment settings

title: Steering Uncertainty: Mean-Field-Augmented Physics-Informed Reinforcement Learning for AUV Swarm Coordination in Underwater IoT
authors: Mandana Mahgoli; Ian F. Akyildiz; Teresa Sofia Giesta Da Silva; Sigurdur Thor Jonsson; Kristinn Andersen; Saemundur E. Thorsteinsson
venue: International Conference on Distributed Computing in Smart Systems and the Internet of Things (DCOSS-IoT)
abstract: Coordinating autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV) swarms for sensor data collection requires simultaneously maximizing spatial coverage and maintaining acoustic link quality, objectives existing multi-agent reinforcement learning methods treat as competing rather than complementary. This paper introduces MFA-PIWM-Diff, coupling a mean-field statistic for scalable O(N ) coordination, a physics-informed world model grounded in Thorp’s law providing channel predictions and an epistemic uncertainty signal, and a lightweight diffusion-based action refiner. The Kullback–Leibler divergence between Thorp priors and observation-updated posteriors enters the reward as a fixed-weight uncertainty penalty, alongside a soft augmented-Lagrangian penalty on the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) floor; the floor is penalized rather than strictly guaranteed. Experiments with 32 AUVs over a 2 km × 2 km ocean domain (2,000 training episodes; deterministic evaluation over 90 episodes from three seeds) achieve 86.1% relay-based coverage at Rrel= 400 m (95% CI [83.4, 88.8]) and 75.4% strict coverage at Rcol= 300 m, with training-time mean SNR converging to 66.6 dB and the dual multiplier to λ ≈ 161.5. Across MADDPG, Greedy, PSO, and Random baselines, MFA-PIWM-Diff is the only method combining ≥ 85% relay coverage with a deterministic-evaluation per-step violation rate that, while still elevated in absolute terms (76.9%), is substantially below the unconstrained learned baselines (94–100%) and bounded by a maximum SNR deficit of only 5.9 dB versus 8.6–8.7 dB for failing ablations. The uncertainty penalty cuts the violation rate by 18 percentage points; the world model contributes 9.9 pp to strict coverage. Scalability from 4 to 32 AUVs maintains mean SNR above the 62 dB floor at every fleet size, and inference at 8.92 MFLOPs per agent decision executes within the 5 s control cycle on a laptop GPU.

title: Unified Foundations of Axiom-Based AGI: A Comprehensive Architecture for Quantum-Inspired Cognition, Dynamic Neural Topology, Cognitive Preservation, and Safe Autonomous Intelligence
authors: Mathur, Lakshit
abstract: This manuscript provides the most comprehensive technical exploration to date of Axiom-Based AGI, expanding across ten interconnected research domains required for constructing a stable, self-healing artificial general intelligence. The work integrates quantum-inspired amplitude-phase cognition, dynamic neural topology (DNT), multi-layer Temporal Shard Memory II (TSM-II), quantum-error-correction-based stabilizer logic, emotional gradient modeling, recursive internal self-simulation, and preservation-driven decision theory.The research extends the original Twelve Axioms of AGI cognition with eight newly proposed axioms (Axioms 13–20), covering emotional grounding, temporal coherence, multi-agent cognitive fabrics, world-model consistency, quantum intuition, and recursive self-modeling. Each axiom forms a computational invariant that governs safe continuous learning and identity evolution.Key contributions include:A hybrid quantum-classical reasoning model using cognitive amplitude fields.A self-modifying neural topology that grows, prunes, and reorganizes dynamically.A Preservation Layer inspired by QEC with syndrome extraction, indirect validation, and non-destructive state repair.TSM-II, a layered episodic-semantic-affective memory system with consolidation waves and shard evolution dynamics.A decision theory constrained by identity continuity, world coherence, emotional resonance, and preservation invariants.Lucifer Cognitive Core Simulation (LCCS), a framework for simulating AGI cognition under noise, corruption, drift, and internal conflict.An AGI Safety Framework grounded in redundancy, invariants, self-repair, tiered containment, hardware attestation, and cryptographic auditing.This unified theory establishes a mathematically grounded and engineering-ready blueprint for building safe AGI capable of long-term stable cognition, self-repair, continuous identity, and coherent decision-making. It serves as a foundational reference for AGI architecture research, safety evaluations, hardware co-design, and cognitive stability analysis.

title: LockGuard RL v3: Simulation-Gated Policy Architecture with Dream Mode and Reality Gate – Code and Preprint
authors: Uberlandis Fiol Reyes
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Source code and preprint for the paper "LockGuard RL v3: Full Integration of Simulation-Gated Policy Architecture with LockGuard AI". This work extends LockGuard AI v2 (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.19386427) to single-agent reinforcement learning. It introduces: - **SGPA v3**: Simulation-Gated Policy Architecture with differentiable Reality Gate. - **Endogenous crisis perception (FD)**: derived from policy entropy and II‑Score velocity. - **Dream Mode**: pre‑execution Monte Carlo simulation of hypothetical scenario variants (optimistic, pessimistic, lock‑in‑prone) with weighted memory. - **Reality Gate**: dynamic recalibration of metaprogram R when simulation and real outcome diverge. - **EGDS entropy gate**: suppresses irreversible actions when policy entropy > θ_max (1.2 nats). - **World‑model ensemble (M=5) with bias correction** for accurate dream environment. **Validation domains:** - Grid‑world irreversibility benchmark (16x16, II‑Score tiers). - Financial order execution on Binance‑simulated LOB (single agent). - Autonomous drone navigation in PyBullet (single agent). **Key results (from paper):** - 63–79% reduction in Irreversible Action Rate (IAR) vs unconstrained PPO/SAC. - 84–91% of cumulative reward preserved. - 89–94% safety constraint satisfaction. - 96% EGDS governance compliance. The full paper is available in this repository (PDF). Code includes: SGPA agent, world‑model ensemble, MSCA v6 utility, EGDS gate, and training/evaluation scripts. Requires Python 3.8+ and dependencies listed in `requirements.txt`. **Related Zenodo records:** - LockGuard AI v2 (core framework): [10.5281/zenodo.19386427](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19386427) - LockGuard RL v4 (multi‑agent extension): [to be added] **How to cite:** ```bibtex @software{fiol_reyes_lockguard_rl_v3, author = {Uberlandis Fiol Reyes}, title = {LockGuard RL v3: Simulation-Gated Policy Architecture with Dream Mode and Reality Gate}, year = {2026}, publisher = {Zenodo}, doi = {10.5281/zenodo.xxxxxxx}, url = {https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.xxxxxxx} }

title: 692. SEX-DEPENDENT AND DYNAMIC BRAIN STRUCTURAL MRI CHANGES IN MICE FOLLOWING INFLUENZA A VIRUS MATERNAL IMMUNE ACTIVATION
authors: D Peng; C Choy; Stella Liong; Robert Brkljača; A Merritt; Cassandra Wannan; U Thivisol; David K. Wright; Arthur Christopoulos; Stavros Selemidis; Jess Nithianantharajah; Warda T Syeda; Christos Pantelis
abstract: Abstract Background Maternal infections or inflammatory insults during pregnancy, can significantly impact brain development in the offspring, and have been associated with later neurodevelopmental disorders, including schizophrenia. Preclinical maternal immune activation (MIA) models provide valuable tools to explore factors affecting neurodevelopment under controlled environments. Unlike previous studies that used synthetic viral mimetics like poly(I:C), live influenza A virus (IAV) was utilized to induce MIA (IAV-MIA), providing a more ‘real-world’ model. We used MRI to examine brain changes at multiple time points during brain development (from early adolescence at week 5, to adulthood at week 14 postnatally) to assess the impact of IAV-MIA. We also examined associations with sensorimotor-gating deficits. Aims & Objectives We hypothesised that: (i) prenatal IAV-MIA alters trajectories of brain development during adolescence; and (ii) the most perturbed trajectories predict sensorimotor-gating deficits, a schizophrenia-relevant behaviour. Method Pregnant C57BL/6 dams received intranasal HKx31 (H3N2) virus or PBS at embryonic day 12. Offspring (n=6-8/sex/group) underwent longitudinal 9.4 T T2* MRI at 5, 8, 11, and 14 weeks. Atlas-based segmentation yielded regional volumes; tensor-based morphometry (TBM) provided voxel-wise Jacobian maps. Linear mixed-effects models tested MIA×Age×Sex interactions. Graph-theoretical metrics quantified reorganisation of volume-correlation networks. At 14.5 weeks, sensorimotor-gating deficits were assessed by prepulse inhibition (PPI) and linked to developmental trajectory parameters by partial-least-squares regression. Results Brain structural trajectory change was highly significant in the CA1 area of hippocampus (p<0.0003) in the atlas-based analysis. TBM showed IAV-MIA-dependent age effects with greater sex-related deviations among males than females in various regions. Male MIA networks showed marked reorganisation between 5-8 weeks (Jaccard similarity ↓ 64%, p=0.034) and increased global closeness (↑30%, p=0.032), whereas female changes were subtler and earlier. PPI was reduced in MIA offspring (F(1,28)=5.26, p=0.030). PLS linked PPI deficits to intercept and quadratic terms of somatosensory cortex, pons and medulla trajectories (Component 1, p=0.0009). Discussion & Conclusions IAV-MIA induces dynamic, sex-dependent structural disruption, with adolescence (week 8) emerging as a male-vulnerable window. Coupling of specific volumetric trajectories with impaired PPI highlights candidate macroscopic biomarkers and developmental periods as potential targets for intervention in schizophrenia-relevant circuitry.

title: From Human-Function Relations to Whole-Person State Understanding and Future Prediction:A Demand–Capacity–Engagement Temporal Specification, Prior-Art Comparison and Falsifiable Validation Protocol
authors: LEI CHE
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Background. Longitudinal patient models, physiological world models, biophysical Physiome efforts, computable ICF and whole-person health measurement already address important parts of state, context and change [6–8,12–17,20]. Their existence prevents a claim that temporal modelling of the whole person is itself unprecedented. The remaining scientific question concerns the independent value, if any, of demand-conditioned human-function relations for evidence-qualified interpretation and future forecasts. Question. For one continuing person, does explicitly retaining the distinctions among internal/external demands, condition-specific available bodily capacity, independently observed actual functional engagement, outcome, burden, recovery, context and evidence improve present-state judgments or time-bounded future prediction compared with information-matched alternatives? Approach. We retain the UOHF/HFWM formal boundaries and propose a two-clock temporal relational interface separating bodily-event time from knowledge availability, with ex-ante future demand/context scenarios explicitly isolated from realized future information. We compare recent closely related models, define discriminating paired-case benchmarks, specify safeguards against unidentifiable capacity/engagement claims, and outline falsifiable prediction comparisons intended for future preregistration. No prospective study has yet been registered or executed. Status. This paper proposes methods and prospective empirical tests. No new longitudinal forecasting, independent relationship adjudication, demonstrated mechanistic recovery, clinical benefit or intervention effect is reported. Earlier author-run reference-code checks [25] address selected engineering contracts only; their pass counts do not support biological forecasting accuracy or establish independent scientific validation. Keywords: whole-person computation; human function; UOHF; HFWM; temporal understanding; longitudinal prediction; functional engagement; capacity; digital twins; evidence qualification.

title: Robust Single-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Regional Traffic Signal Control Under Demand Fluctuations
authors: Qiang Li; Niu, Jin; Lina Yu
abstract: Traffic congestion, primarily driven by intersection queuing, significantly impacts urban living standards, safety, environmental quality, and economic efficiency. While Traffic Signal Control (TSC) systems hold potential for congestion mitigation, traditional optimization models often fail to capture real-world traffic complexity and dynamics. This study introduces a novel single-agent reinforcement learning (RL) framework for regional adaptive TSC, circumventing the coordination complexities inherent in multi-agent systems through a centralized decision-making paradigm. The model employs an adjacency matrix to unify the encoding of road network topology, real-time queue states derived from probe vehicle data, and current signal timing parameters. Leveraging the efficient learning capabilities of the DreamerV3 world model, the agent learns control policies where actions sequentially select intersections and adjust their signal phase splits to regulate traffic inflow/outflow, analogous to a feedback control system. Reward design prioritizes queue dissipation, directly linking congestion metrics (queue length) to control actions. Simulation experiments conducted in SUMO demonstrate the model's effectiveness: under inference scenarios with multi-level (10%, 20%, 30%) Origin-Destination (OD) demand fluctuations, the framework exhibits robust anti-fluctuation capability and significantly reduces queue lengths. This work establishes a new paradigm for intelligent traffic control compatible with probe vehicle technology. Future research will focus on enhancing practical applicability by incorporating stochastic OD demand fluctuations during training and exploring regional optimization mechanisms for contingency events.

title: Benchmarking language models and agents for scientific reasoning in evolving materials laboratories
authors: Xuyu Dong; Yixuan Li; Jianguo Huang; Feng Chen; Yiyun Zhou; Bo An; Zheng Liu; Da Shu
abstract: Large language models and the multi-agent systems built around them could accelerate materials discovery by connecting scientific knowledge with experimental decisions. Existing benchmarks establish capabilities in domain knowledge, multimodal interpretation and scientific tool use. As language models increasingly support materials research workflows, their ability to distinguish closely related material states and reason accurately with quantitative evidence remains insufficiently evaluated. These abilities are essential for comparing material responses, assessing mechanisms and maintaining reliable judgements as experimental evidence accumulates. We introduce MatScope to evaluate three connected capabilities. M1 tests unaided, condition-specific reasoning through 200 tasks spanning ten research functions, using aluminium and high-entropy alloys as representative material systems. M2 tests agent-assisted transfer of related knowledge to unresolved materials questions. MatEvoBench-20 tests initial forecasts across scientific dependency chains and revisions of still-hidden responses as observations accumulate. Across eleven model deployments, including GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1, given-input calculations and many physical explanations are handled well. Fine-grained response estimates, comparisons between similar states and quantitatively supported choices remain substantially weaker. Related literature improves selected estimates, while condition and baseline mismatches limit transfer. Progressive observations calibrate some downstream responses and destabilize earlier accurate predictions. MatScope establishes measurable targets for developing reliable scientific reasoning in future self-evolving materials laboratories and materials-aware world models.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning and Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Autonomous Systems
authors: K Reddy; B. V. V. Siva Prasad; Suresh Rao N; T. Srikanth
abstract: Autonomous systems are quickly journeying from research laboratories into everyday existence. Autonomous vehicles drive on the roads in cities, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) monitor structure health, mobile robots and humanoid robots and intelligent controllers collaborate with a human. The common thing with these machines is that they are required to sense, reason and act independently of human intervention. One of the most powerful methods to provide them with that capability is deep reinforcement learning (DRL), where agents learn human-level, sequential decision-making policies directly from their experiences. But the powerful neural networks that power these policies are very opaque, which makes trust, certification and accountability challenging. This book, Deep Reinforcement Learning and Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Autonomous Systems, aims to unite these two areas to fill this gap. Chapters 1 is laying the foundation. It explains the Markov decision process (MDP) and the partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) and overviews the key families of algorithms: value-based methods like deep Q-network (DQN), policy gradient methods, actor-critic methods like proximal policy optimization (PPO) and soft actor-critic (SAC), model-based reinforcement learning and offline reinforcement learning. Also covered are sim-to-real transfer, digital twins, reward design, sample efficiency, and generalization. Chapter 2 focuses on explainable reinforcement learning (XRL). It presents a taxonomy of explainable AI (XAI) approaches from post hoc feature attribution, to interpretable policies, causal, counterfactual, and language-based explanations, along with discussing human-centered evaluation of explanation quality. Causal and counterfactual explanations are explored in greater detail in Chapter 3, with a focus on counterfactuals generated using world models and diffusion models, causal reinforcement learning, reward decomposition and structural causal models, and the ladder of causation. Co-operative autonomy is discussed in Chapter 4 using Multi Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL). It includes chapters on Markov games, decentralized POMDPs, centralized training with decentralized execution, value decomposition, and credit assignment, as well as how Shapley value attribution, attention analysis, and policy distillation can be used to render multi-agent systems transparent. Chapter 5 discusses foundation models, multimodal AI, and vision-language-action (VLA) models, and how reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) and fine-tuning modules can modify such generalist robot policies for embodied AI, end-to-end autonomous driving, and robotic manipulation respectively. Chapter 6 deals with the topic of generative AI and agentic AI, in which LLMs serve as a planner, diffusion policies determine actions, and multi-agent systems collaborate with each other according to shared protocols, and all of this under the umbrella of AI safety, alignment, and governance. Chapter 7 ties up these concepts for autonomous vehicles and robotics, comparing with different ways and outlining some open problem areas. A common thread that weaves through the text is the concept of safe reinforcement learning, as well as topics such as robustness, human-in-the-loop oversight and trustworthy AI. We are saying that we need to perform in a high way but it's not enough. An autonomous agent also has to be able to describe their behaviour in ways that will be understood and verified by engineers, regulators and end-users. Explainability is thus not considered an add-on feature but is instead viewed as a design constraint that helps facilitate safety assurance, debugging, and responsible deployment of machine learning. It is especially written for graduate students, researchers and practitioners of artificial intelligence, robotics, control engineering and intelligent transportation systems. Every chapter is a mix of the foundations of the enthusiasm, the latest advances, comparison tables, and software applications case studies, allowing the readers to ramp up from theory to practice. We hope that this volume is a reference and that it is a "springboard" for developing autonomous capable, safe and interpretable systems.

title: Enhancing learning-based database optimizaers via representation learning
authors: Yue Zhao
abstract: Machine learning for database (ML4DB) systems that leverage query plans as input have demonstrated growing promise in a variety of tasks, including cost estimation, query optimization and many others. A query plan is a directed acyclic graph which describe steps to process a query and retrieve the results, and query plan representation is the procedure which takes an arbitrary query plan as input and output a vector representation for it, as the input to machine learning models in a ML4DB system. The vector has to encode the important features, so that the machine learning model can leverage it to generate insights for the database system or the database user. As with many learned systems, the quality of representation learning is crucial to downstream effectiveness. Yet, we argue that the focus on representation learning is limited, hindering the potential for the systems. Specifically, the representation techniques do not systematically encode all important features effectively; there is lack of comparative nor component analysis; and there is limited support for transfer learning. To this end, our dissertation focuses on representation learning for query plans. In the first study, we ask whether a well-designed query plan representation model can improve performance across a wide range of ML4DB tasks. We confirm that it can. We propose QueryFormer, a tree-structured Transformer model that captures two key properties often underutilized in prior work: (1) statistical properties of the underlying data, integrated through histogram-aware feature encoding, and (2) structural dependencies along long paths in the plan tree, modeled through tree-structured attention flows. QueryFormer is evaluated on four distinct ML4DB tasks, namely cost estimation, latency prediction, query embedding, and plan clas- sification. It demonstrates strong generalization across workloads and tasks. These results establish that careful representation design can serve as a core driver of sys- tem performance in learned database components. While this validates the impact of representation quality, it does not answer a deeper and more practical question: what representation designs work best for which scenarios? The second study addresses this by systematically analyzing the relationship between model performance at different task and dataset scenarios (dependent variable) and design choices (independent variables). We conduct a comparative evaluation of ten representation methods across three ML4DB tasks: cost estimation, index selection, and query optimization over a total of nine work- loads with varied characteristics. In addition to ranking model performance, we decompose each method into two core components: feature encoding and tree model, and assess their contributions under different conditions. We find that cer- tain design assumptions (e.g., the importance of tree models) only hold in specific settings (e.g., when optimizing for relative error), and that simpler methods some- times outperform complex ones. Furthermore, we propose task-specific feature configurations that improve model performance, offering actionable design insights for practitioners. In the third study, we address the challenge of adapting learned representations to new ML4DB tasks with limited labeled data. While transfer learning ap- pears promising, naive approaches often fail due to model overspecialization, data scarcity, and distribution shifts between tasks. We propose TATA, an efficient (TA)sk (T)r(A)nsfer learning framework that combines self-supervised pretrain- ing with pseudo-labeled data generation to improve task adaptation. We evaluate TATA in scenarios transferring from cost estimation to index selection and query optimization across three datasets. Experimental results show that TATA enables effective transfer with substantially reduced data collection costs—saving up to 25 hours of labeling effort.

title: Foundation Models and Agentic AI for Autonomous Driving: A Systematic Review
authors: Srinivaas A.; Jeswin K F; Lakshmana Kumar Ramasamy; Gunasunderi Raju; Rajesh Kumar Dhanaraj; Shabana Urooj
abstract: Abstract Autonomous driving has advanced considerably with the adoption of foundation models, particularly Large Language Models (LLMs), Vision-Language Models (VLMs), and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) systems. Unlike conventional perception–planning–control pipelines, these models combine multimodal perception with contextual reasoning and natural-language explainability, enabling autonomous vehicles to interpret complex traffic environments and support more informed driving decisions. Recent frameworks, including DriveMLM, AsyncDriver, and TeLL-Drive, demonstrate the potential of LLM- and VLM-based approaches to improve behavioral planning, reduce inference latency, and produce more interpretable decision-making. At the same time, developments in multi-agent coordination and safety alignment are expanding autonomous driving beyond individual vehicles toward cooperative and connected transportation systems. The integration of Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) communication, digital twin technologies, and smart-city infrastructure has further strengthened this direction by enabling collaborative perception, reasoning, and decision-making across intelligent transportation networks. However, several challenges continue to limit practical deployment. Balancing reasoning capability with real-time computational efficiency, integrating symbolic reasoning with continuous vehicle control, and reducing the simulation-to-reality gap remain important research problems, particularly for systems validated using platforms such as CARLA and other autonomous driving simulators. This review examines recent advances across nine interconnected research areas: multimodal fusion, Transformer efficiency, world models, agentic AI, cooperative V2X communication, safety frameworks, interpretability, digital twins, and simulation platforms. By bringing these topics together, the review provides a comprehensive overview of the current research landscape, identifies the major challenges that remain unresolved, and discusses future directions for developing scalable, trustworthy, and domain-general autonomous driving systems capable of reliable operation in real-world environments. Distinct from prior surveys that concentrate on a single facet of this landscape—such as multimodal LLMs for driving (Cui et al.), LLM-centric planning (Yang et al., LLM4Drive ), vision-language models (Zhou et al.), end-to-end large-model driving (Dong et al.), or vision-language-action models (Jiang et al., VLA4AD )—this review is distinguished by a unified nine-theme taxonomy that jointly integrates foundation models, agentic AI, cooperative V2X communication, digital-twin validation, and safety-verification frameworks within a single cognitive-architecture perspective. Synthesizing more than 100 works published between 2019 and 2026, and situating them against at least 15 overlapping survey efforts, it explicitly maps how the reasoning–efficiency trade-off, the simulation-to-reality gap, and the absence of unified safety governance manifest differently across the nine domains, thereby extending prior work along the additional dimensions of agentic autonomy, connected-infrastructure cognition, and end-to-end safety certification.

title: AI Architectures as Variable Epistemic Conditions: Generating Descriptive Spaces in Which New Scientific Questions Become Formulable
authors: Matthias Heiler
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used in computational neuroscience for prediction, classification, representation learning, parameter estimation, and related analytical tasks. In most applications, however, the scientific question and the target quantities are specified in advance. Different model architectures may be optimized or compared, but they are primarily evaluated by how well they answer the same predefined question rather than by what different scientific descriptions and questions their architectural differences might make possible. We propose a different use of AI: to treat architectural variation itself as an experimental epistemic variable. Different AI architectures embody different inductive biases and therefore make different temporal, relational, topological, geometrical, symbolic, or dynamical structures accessible in the same empirical data. Rather than asking primarily which architecture performs best on a predefined task, we propose deliberately applying structurally different model families to the same data while minimizing prior commitments about which explanatory quantities should matter — for example entropy, dwell time, recovery time, intrinsic neural timescales, or network connectivity. Each architecture can thereby generate a distinct descriptive space. The primary scientific opportunity lies in architecture-specific discovery. A representation may expose a structure and thereby make a scientific question formulable that remains inaccessible within another representation. Cross-architecture convergence provides a second epistemic opportunity: if substantially different descriptive spaces repeatedly reveal translatable versions of the same phenomenon, this recurrence makes that phenomenon a particularly strong candidate for further investigation because it may reflect a more fundamental structure of the empirical system rather than merely the representational preferences of one architecture. Recent work on schizophrenia provides a concrete motivating case. Spatiotemporal analyses have identified temporal imprecision across phase, intrinsic neural timescales, and frequency domains, while complementary state-transition analyses have revealed impaired recovery dynamics despite similar entropy rates between patients and controls. These findings illustrate how changing the mathematical description can shift attention from one plausible explanatory quantity — overall transition entropy — toward structurally different quantities such as spectral gap, mixing time, and recovery dynamics. Schizophrenia serves here as a case study rather than as the intended boundary of the method. The proposed framework is domain-general: wherever substantially different computational architectures can be applied to the same empirical or formal system, architectural variation can in principle be used to explore alternative descriptive spaces. Illustrative model families include recurrent and state-space models, transformers, temporal graph neural networks, latent-dynamics models, and equation-discovery approaches. This list is deliberately non-exhaustive. The framework explicitly allows additional and even initially non-obvious architectures whose inductive biases may open descriptive spaces not represented by these examples. The aim is not primarily to identify the best-performing architecture, but to exploit architectural difference as a method of scientific discovery. We propose shifting AI in science from a tool for answering predefined questions toward a method for systematically generating alternative descriptive spaces in which new scientific questions can become formulable. AI would thereby be used not only to test hypotheses, but to vary some of the conditions under which hypotheses become visible in the first place.

title: Radical Psychotherapy and Supervision in the 21st Century: Power, Context, and Mental Health, Part I
authors: Dana Rad
venue: The International Journal of Supervision in Psychotherapy
abstract: This conceptual article clarifies radical psychotherapy as a family of clinically grounded, ethically explicit approaches that treat psychological distress as simultaneously intrapsychic and socio-structural. In response to contemporary mental health pressures, precarity, polarization, violence, burnout, and persistent inequality, we argue that strictly individualistic models can unintentionally pathologize adaptive responses to unsafe environments. We propose an “inside + world” model in which symptoms are understood as functional strategies shaped by internal dynamics and external power relations, and we outline five comparative axes that distinguish radical psychotherapy from decontextualized practice: explanatory frameworks, targets of change, therapist positioning, clinical language, and technique framing. A set of clinical postulates is advanced to guide practice: contextualization without erasing personal responsibility, explicit attention to power in the consulting room, shame as socially produced and relationally maintained, an anti-blame stance that avoids both culpabilization and romanticization of suffering, and the primacy of safety and dignity over therapeutic performance. We then translate these principles into practical strategies, including contextual case formulation, power mapping, depathologizing reframes, work with shame and internalized oppression, agency-building micro-interventions, ethical transparency, resourceoriented/community linkage, and evidence-based techniques (CBT/ACT/DBT) deployed within a radical frame. Finally, we address dilemmas concerning politicization, biological and trauma-informed balance, therapist competencies, and multidimensional evaluation. We conclude that radical psychotherapy does not replace established therapies; it recontextualizes them toward root causes power, context, and dignity so that healing is defined as symptom reduction alongside increased agency, protection, and socially recognized personhood.

title: Large Language Models for Small-Molecule Chemical Discovery: From Chemical Language Representation to Closed-Loop Experimental Validation
authors: Liuqing Yang; Zhongjian Wang; Hong Wan; Jiangping Zhu; Pei Zhou
abstract: Small molecules are not only structural entities but also chemical language objects that can be represented as strings, graphs, three-dimensional conformers, reaction equations, spectra, laboratory records, and natural-language descriptions. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have created a new interface for small-molecule discovery by connecting these heterogeneous representations through sequence modeling, multimodal alignment, tool use, and iterative experimental feedback. This review synthesizes LLM-driven small-molecule discovery from chemical language representation to molecular generation, property-oriented optimization, synthesis-aware design, retrosynthesis planning, and closed-loop validation. Compared with broad surveys of AI in chemistry and drug-centered reviews, this article treats small molecules as general design objects across pharmaceuticals, catalysts, energy molecules, fluorescent probes, agrochemicals, green solvents, and functional organic materials. We further position molecular language models as one branch of scientific world models, in which genes, proteins, reactions, and small molecules are represented as language-like objects that encode biological and chemical regularities. We review molecular representations, datasets, benchmarks, evaluation metrics, model architectures, multimodal systems, and tool-augmented LLM agents. Finally, we discuss autonomous laboratories, experimental feedback loops, chemical hallucination, synthesizability constraints, benchmark standardization, safety, and human–AI collaboration. We argue that the next stage of molecular discovery should move beyond validity-centered generation toward experimentally reliable, synthesis-aware, and feedback-driven chemical design.

title: Field-Network Theory From Experiential Events Beyond Genealogical Continuation
authors: Taponen-Synoidi
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Field-Network Theory (FNT) is an event-based ontological and physical research program that investigates whether the structures used in physical description can be reconstructed from occurrence itself, without assuming background time, background space, fundamental persistent objects, a pre-existing field, a ready-made future, or a fundamental observer. The central methodological question is simple to state but demanding to pursue: How much of physical reality can be reconstructed from occurrence without silently reintroducing the structures that were removed from the starting point? FNT begins from complete occurrence, denoted by C. Occurrence is not initially defined as a change undergone by an already existing object, nor as an event located within an independently existing spacetime. Instead, the research program asks whether familiar physical structures—including continuity, time, spatial relations, form, mass, quantum phenomena, gravitation, and ultimately observable physical behavior—can emerge from a relational structure grounded in occurrence. This reverses the usual explanatory direction. Rather than beginning with objects, states, fields, space and time and asking how they evolve, FNT asks what must be structurally available for such descriptions to become possible in the first place. From physical description to ontological reconstruction Modern physics provides extraordinarily successful mathematical descriptions of nature. FNT does not dispute that empirical success. Its question concerns a different level of explanation: whether the conceptual structures appearing in successful physical theories must therefore be regarded as fundamental structures of reality. A coordinate can be indispensable to a physical calculation without proving that coordinate space is ontologically fundamental. A clock can measure time without establishing background time as a fundamental substance or container. A particle description can predict observations without demonstrating that persistent particles are the deepest constituents of reality. FNT therefore distinguishes operational success from ontological fundamentality. The research program deliberately removes several familiar structures from its initial assumptions and then investigates whether they can be recovered rather than presupposed. These include: background time, background space, persistent fundamental objects, fundamental motion relative to a pre-existing spacetime, a fundamental field that exists independently of occurrence, ready-made future states or worlds, an assumed fundamental observer, and an automatic identification of non-determinism with randomness. Removing these structures is not itself offered as a physical theory. It defines the starting conditions of a reconstruction problem. Complete occurrence and relational structure In FNT, C denotes a complete occurrence. Completeness is not defined by clock duration. An event measured across several chronological intervals need not therefore consist of several ontologically fundamental occurrences. Conversely, a short measured duration does not establish ontological unity. This distinction opens a research problem concerning the relationship between chronological decomposition and event-based decomposition. FNT further investigates how occurrence can produce relational structure without requiring a persistent bearer underneath successive events. The field-network is therefore not introduced as a container in which events happen. The term refers to the common relational structure of occurrence. In current FNT terminology this structure is denoted by D: D = the common relational structure of occurrence. D is not a collection or archive of event-objects, a sequence of world states, background spacetime, or a pre-existing stage. The research problem is instead whether occurrence and its relational articulation can provide the structural continuity normally attributed to persistent objects or independently existing backgrounds. This distinction is important because an occurrence need not remain as an object in order for reality after that occurrence to be structurally different. Possibility without a pre-existing future FNT also separates possibility from a ready-made future. Possibility is denoted by e and is currently treated as a relational possibility to manifest as such. A possible occurrence is not thereby an already existing future event, branch, world, or object waiting to be selected. Likewise: possibility does not imply occurrence. This allows FNT to investigate possibility without beginning from an ontologically completed space of alternative futures. One developing concept within this framework is structural avoidance: occurrence may find another way to continue without any agent consciously selecting the alternative. Structural avoidance does not by itself determine the next complete occurrence, nor does it establish probabilities, weighting among possibilities, or ontological indeterminism. It instead identifies a research direction in which relational structure may permit occurrence to articulate differently without requiring an external controller or predetermined route. The possible relationship between relational possibility e, structural avoidance, and the direction of occurrence remains an open part of the research program. Ontological reduction and its boundary A major part of the FNT research-paper series concerns the limits of ontological reduction. Removing an assumed foundation does not automatically explain what remains. Nor does showing that certain conditions are compatible with an occurrence explain why occurrence occurs. This produces an important distinction between conditions of manifestation and occurrence itself. The research program therefore examines where structural derivation succeeds, where it requires an additional positive assumption, and where an explanatory boundary has been reached. Negative results are significant within this methodology. If a conclusion cannot be derived from a proposed structural basis, FNT does not automatically repair the derivation by inserting another primitive mechanism. Instead, the failure identifies the boundary of what the stated conditions actually establish. This makes the research program intentionally revisable. Concepts proposed in the broad construction can later be restricted, reformulated, separated from stronger interpretations, or left open when subsequent analysis shows that the original derivation was insufficient. The book and the research-paper series Field-Network Theory — A Hypothesis on the Structure of Reality presents the broad constructive form of the theory. The book explores, from a common ontological starting point, questions concerning time, space, form, quantum structure, light, mass, gravitation, cosmology, and consciousness. Its purpose is to make the proposed world-structure visible as a whole rather than presenting FNT only as a collection of isolated propositions. This role is important. A sufficiently complete formal system may encode a structure without making the resulting whole immediately recognizable. In the same way that a complete mathematical description of a biological form is not identical to recognizing the organism represented by that description, individual equations and propositions do not necessarily reveal the world-model they jointly describe. The book therefore provides the integrated conceptual construction of FNT: a view of how a familiar observable world might look if its underlying explanatory order begins from occurrence rather than from objects situated in pre-existing space and time. The research papers perform a different task. They separate individual load-bearing claims from the whole and subject them to stricter examination. A paper can ask whether a proposed conclusion genuinely follows from its premises, whether it depends on a particular representation, whether a hidden assumption has entered the argument, whether a countermodel is possible, or whether an ontological reduction has reached its legitimate boundary. The relationship is therefore not simply: book → proof → completed theory. It is closer to: broad construction → structural decomposition → independent testing → revision → reconstruction. The book makes the proposed whole visible. The papers investigate whether its individual structural joints can carry the explanatory load assigned to them. A background-independent research direction FNT belongs to the broader family of foundational questions concerning background independence, relational ontology, event ontology, emergence, foundations of spacetime, foundations of quantum theory, and the ontology of physical law, while proposing its own event-based starting point. Its strongest ambition is not merely to reinterpret existing terminology. The long-term question is whether measurable physics can actually be reconstructed from this basis. A successful development would therefore need to establish bridges from the ontological structure to physical quantities and ultimately to testable consequences capable of distinguishing FNT from alternative descriptions. That task is not claimed to be complete. At its present stage, FNT should therefore be understood as an open physical and ontological research program, not as an experimentally established replacement for contemporary physics or a completed theory of everything. Its current contribution is the construction and systematic examination of a different explanatory architecture: What if occurrence is fundamental, while objects, continuity, time, space, fields, and other familiar structures must earn their place through reconstruction? The book develops the resulting world-picture. The research-paper series tests its structure piece by piece. title: Neural plasticity in decision making and memory formation
authors: Mona M. Garvert
abstract: Goal-directed behaviour is characterized by an ability to make inferences without direct experience. This requires a model of the environment and of ourselves, which is flexibly adjusted in light of new incoming information. This thesis uses representational functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) techniques in combination with computational modelling to investigate (1) whether humans can construct models of other people’s preferences and whether this process influences their own value representation, and (2) how statistical relationships between discrete, non-spatial objects are combined into a model of the world. The first part of the thesis investigates how subjective values are computed in an intertemporal choice paradigm, and how these value computations are updated as a consequence of learning about the preferences of another. Critically, subjects’ own preferences shift towards those of the other when learning about their choices, suggesting that subjects incorporate new knowledge about others into a model of their own preferences. The underlying mechanism involves prediction errors, which introduce plasticity into subjects’ mPFC value representations, in turn resulting in a shift in subjects’ own preferences. The second part of this thesis investigates how relationships between arbitrary objects are represented in the brain. Relational knowledge is often considered analogous to spatial reasoning, where relationships are encoded in a hippocampal-entorhinal ‘cognitive map’. Here, I show that maps can also be extracted from the entorhinal cortex for discrete relationships between arbitrary stimuli, and in the absence of conscious knowledge. The representation of abstract knowledge in map-like structures suggests that inferences do not need to rely on direct experiences but can be computed anew from mapped knowledge. Together, these studies reveal how world models are represented and updated at the level of neural representations, providing a bridge between representational codes and cognitive computations.
