title: Generative AI Engineering: Large Language Models and Intelligent Agents
authors: Dr. L. Lakshmaiah, Dr. Raghu Kumar KS, Dr. S. Sunitha,Mr. Naveen Kumar Aakuthota.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: developments in contemporary computing, transforming the way intelligent systems understand information, generate content, reason over knowledge, interact with users, and perform complex tasks. The rapid evolution of Large Language Models, multimodal foundation models, retrieval-augmented generation, intelligent agents, and autonomous workflows has created a new generation of AI systems that extend beyond conventional prediction and classification. These developments are influencing software engineering, scientific research, healthcare, education, business, robotics, cybersecurity, manufacturing, and many other domains. The book Generative AI Engineering: Large Language Models and Intelligent Agents has been developed to provide a comprehensive academic and engineering-oriented treatment of these emerging technologies. The book approaches Generative AI not merely as a collection of models or tools, but as an engineering discipline involving model architecture, data and knowledge integration, prompting, retrieval, agent orchestration, evaluation, security, deployment, optimization, and responsible operation. The objective is to provide readers with both conceptual foundations and a practical understanding of how modern Generative AI systems are designed and integrated into intelligent applications. The book begins with the foundations of Generative AI and Large Language Models. Chapter 1, Foundations of Generative AI and Large Language Models, introduces the evolution of generative modeling from statistical Natural Language Processing to modern foundation models and LLMs. It examines the distinction between discriminative and generative learning and provides a detailed treatment of Transformer architecture, self-attention, multi-head attention, positional encoding, embeddings, and encoder–decoder architectures. The chapter further explores LLM pre-training, next-token prediction, supervised fine-tuning, instruction tuning, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, tokenization, contextual representations, prompting, context engineering, inference optimization, quantization, and model ecosystems. Applications in intelligent tutoring, software engineering, healthcare, scientific knowledge discovery, business intelligence, and customer support establish the practical relevance of LLMs. Chapter 2, LLM Engineering, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, and Multimodal Intelligence, moves from model fundamentals toward application engineering. It explains how LLM APIs, model-serving architectures, prompt templates, structured outputs, function calling, and schema-constrained generation can be integrated into production applications. Particular emphasis is given to Retrieval-Augmented Generation, including document ingestion, chunking, retrieval, reranking, grounding, and knowledge-intensive generation. Advanced retrieval techniques such as hybrid search, dense retrieval, query expansion, query decomposition, graph-based retrieval, and agentic retrieval are examined. The chapter also discusses vector databases, metadata filtering, knowledge graphs, multimodal foundation models, multimodal embeddings, fine-tuning, LoRA, continual adaptation, orchestration frameworks, memory management, and production-oriented architectures. Applications in enterprise knowledge systems, healthcare, scientific research, legal and financial analysis, education, manufacturing, and intelligent search demonstrate the breadth of these technologies. Chapter 3, Intelligent Agents and Agentic AI Engineering, examines the transition from prompt-driven systems to goal-oriented and autonomous AI agents. It introduces reactive, deliberative, and hybrid agent architectures and explains how perception, reasoning, planning, memory, tool use, and action contribute to intelligent behavior. The chapter explores task decomposition, reasoning strategies, reflection, self-correction, decision-making, function calling, external APIs, code execution, search tools, databases, and computational tools. Particular attention is given to short-term and long-term memory, episodic and semantic memory, context compression, persistent memory, and multi-agent collaboration. Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation and autonomous knowledge acquisition are introduced as important mechanisms for developing research-oriented and knowledge-intensive agents. The chapter concludes with agent evaluation, reliability, observability, trajectory analysis, tool-use accuracy, failure analysis, and applications in autonomous software engineering, research, customer service, healthcare, education, finance, and enterprise automation. As Generative AI systems become increasingly capable, their reliability, security, privacy, and responsible deployment become essential. Chapter 4, Secure, Responsible, and Production-Ready Generative AI Engineering, addresses these requirements. It introduces systematic approaches to LLM and application evaluation, benchmarking, human evaluation, automated evaluation, and task-specific assessment. The chapter examines hallucination, factuality, grounded generation, fact verification, confidence estimation, and uncertainty-aware generation. Security topics include prompt injection, jailbreaks, adversarial prompts, data poisoning, model security, and agent security. Privacy-preserving Generative AI is explored through sensitive-data protection, anonymization, federated learning, and privacy-preserving retrieval and inference. The chapter further addresses fairness, bias, explainability, transparency, human oversight, governance, and responsible deployment. Production engineering topics include LLMOps, MLOps, model lifecycle management, prompt and model versioning, monitoring, observability, continuous evaluation, deployment, distributed inference, quantization, distillation, accelerator optimization, and edge AI. Chapter 5, Emerging Trends and Advanced Applications of Generative AI, looks toward the future of the field. It examines reasoning-centric AI models, test-time computation, self-reflection, verification, neuro-symbolic reasoning, and hybrid intelligence. Agentic AI and autonomous workflows are explored through autonomous task execution, human–agent collaboration, workflow automation, and self-improving agent architectures. The chapter also examines Generative AI for software engineering, including coding assistants, automated debugging, software testing, vulnerability detection, and autonomous development agents. Applications in scientific discovery, drug and material design, engineering optimization, clinical decision support, robotics, and embodied intelligence demonstrate the expanding role of Generative AI in the physical and scientific world. The chapter further examines Small Language Models, edge AI, on-device inference, domain-specific foundation models, and energy-efficient Generative AI. Future architectures involving multimodal foundation models, world models, persistent AI memory, collective intelligence, and multi-agent systems are discussed as important directions for next-generation intelligent systems. Finally, emerging applications such as autonomous organizations, personalized education, smart cities, intelligent infrastructure, digital twins, industrial AI, and next-generation human–AI collaboration illustrate the broader societal and technological implications of Generative AI. The engineering lifecycle can therefore be summarized as: Understand → Design → Generate → Retrieve → Reason → Act → Evaluate → Secure → Deploy → Monitor → Improve The book also emphasizes the distinction between generating a plausible output and producing a reliable result. Generative AI systems can produce highly fluent responses while still containing factual errors, unsupported assumptions, security vulnerabilities, or inappropriate recommendations. Consequently, validation, grounding, evaluation, human oversight, and responsible deployment are treated as fundamental engineering requirements rather than optional additions. Another important objective of the book is to establish a bridge between theoretical knowledge and practical system development. Students and professionals need to understand not only how Transformers and LLMs work, but also how these models are incorporated into real applications through APIs, vector databases, retrieval systems, orchestration frameworks, agents, tools, memory systems, and deployment platforms. The book therefore follows a progressive structure that moves from foundations to application engineering, from application engineering to intelligent agents, from agents to secure production systems, and finally toward emerging architectures and advanced applications. The book is intended for undergraduate and postgraduate students of Computer Science and Engineering, Artificial Intelligence, Data Science, Information Technology, Cybersecurity, and related disciplines. It is also designed to support researchers, educators, software engineers, AI practitioners, technology professionals, and readers who wish to develop a systematic understanding of Generative AI engineering. The material can be used for university courses, advanced electives, professional training programs, research preparation, and self-directed learning. The ultimate objective of Generative AI Engineering: Large Language Models and Intelligent Agents is to help readers move from simply using Generative AI tools toward understanding, designing, evaluating, and engineering intelligent systems. Generative AI is becoming an important component of modern computing infrastructure, and its future will depend not only on increasingly capable models but also on the ability to build systems that are reliable, secure, efficient, explainable, scalable, responsible, and human-centered. title: Measuring Complex Brain Networks Structure
authors: Ester Bonmati; Anton Bardera; Boada Imma
abstract: Event Abstract Back to Event Measuring Complex Brain Networks Structure Ester Bonmati1*, Anton Bardera1 and Imma Boada1 1 University of Girona, Institute of Informatics and Applications, Spain I. INTRODUCTION The human brain has roughly one hundred billion neurons forming a network with trillions of intra-connections. The mapping of structure and functionality of brain networks is therefore an important challenge in understanding the functioning. Connectivity matrices are used to represent brain networks, also called connectome [1,2], as a graph [3–5], where nodes correspond to brain regions and edges to structural or functional connections [6–8]. Different measures have been applied to describe topological features of brain networks [9–11]. For instance, the independence of large areas, denoted as integration, has been studied by the path length measure, the characteristic path length [12], or the global efficiency [13]. Independence of small subsets, defined as segregation, can be analyzed by the clustering coefficient [12], the transitivity [14] or the modularity [15]. The importance of individual nodes can be defined with centrality measures such as the degree [16]. A good summary of the measures can be found in [10]. In this work, we present a global and two local measures, based on the mutual information measure, to quantify brain networks structure. II. MATERIALS AND METHOD A. Materials Synthetic model networks were created using the Brain Connectivity Toolbox (BCT) [10]. Random, lattice, ring lattice and small-world model networks with 128 and 256 nodes with edges ranging from 128 to 8192 with a step of 128 edges were used. Additionally, networks with nodes ranging from 32 to 512 with a step of 32 and a density of 0.4 were also created. As human structural networks, we used the normalized connection matrices created from MRI tractography described in [17]. As human functional networks, we used the HCP 500-PTN functional dataset [18–20]. All networks were weighted and non-directed. B. Method In the proposed approach, brain networks are modelled as a Markov process where neuronal impulses randomly walk from one node to another node. This new interpretation provides a solid theoretical framework from which we derive a global (i.e., a single value for the whole network) and two local (i.e., a value for each node) measures based on mutual information. Mutual information (MI) measures the shared information between two random variables. From our Markov process-based brain model, we propose as a global connectivity measure the mutual information between two consecutive states of the process. Mutual information can also be seen as the difference between the uncertainty of the states without any knowledge and the uncertainty of the states when the past is known (or information gained when the previous node is known). The higher the MI, the less random the connections. Thus, mutual information can be used to quantify the overall brain structure. The mutual information can be decomposed in order to characterize the degree of informativeness of each state. When applied to the connectome, since each state corresponds to an anatomical or functional region, this measure can be seen as the contribution of each node to the whole graph structure. In this work, we propose two local measures. On the one hand, we use the mutual surprise (I1) [21], that expresses how ‘surprising’ are the connections of a node. Nodes that are connected with more likely nodes will lead to low values of mutual surprise, while those with very specific connections or connected with few unlikely nodes will have high mutual surprise. On the other hand, we use the mutual predictability (I2) [21], that expresses the uncertainty of a node taking into account the mean connectivity of all the network. I2 measures the capacity of prediction for a given brain region. III. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION Using model networks with different number of edges, an optimum point was found for lattice and ring lattice networks when increasing the density. This is due to the fact that for low densities, there are regions not connected, thus, the overall mutual information is low. This fact may help to find a minimum number of fibers needed to study brain networks for a given brain parcellation. Overall, higher values were obtained for lattice and ring lattice models, showing a clear evidence of more organized networks compared to random and small-world networks. When the number of edges was increased, the mutual information tended to decrease, since the higher number of connections, the lower correlation between consecutive states. Preserving the density, the mutual information was not very sensitive to random and small-world networks, since the structure is similar. Higher values were obtained for ring lattice networks when comparing with lattice networks, since in lattice networks two nodes are not connected and have a less structured network. Using anatomical and functional connectomes at different scales, a similar behavior was observed for all patients. Local measures were evaluated using the human connectomes. The mutual surprise highlighted regions connected to regions not highly connected, such as the right hemisphere transverse temporal. Low values were obtained for regions connected to highly connected regions such as the left hemisphere thalamus proper. The mutual predictability associated regions with a low number of connections and high weights with a high predictability, such us the right hemisphere temporal pole. Low values were obtained in regions with more uncertainly in predicting the next node, such as the right hemisphere putamen. All measures were consistent for structural and functional human networks. IV. CONCLUSIONS In this work, new measures to quantify structure of complex brain networks are proposed. Brain connectivity graphs are interpreted as a stochastic process where neural impulses are modeled as a random walk. This interpretation provides a solid theoretical framework from which different measures based on the mutual information measure have been applied. The measures have been tested on synthetic model networks and structural and functional human networks at different scales. Results show that the mutual information is able to quantify the structure of different model networks. The mutual surprise, allows the identification of nodes whose neighbors have a high connectivity taking into account all connections. The mutual predictability, shows that regions with a high clustering tend to be more predictable. title: Engineer-AI as a Civic Co-Agent A Conceptual Framework for Responsible, Imaginative, and Verifiable Engineering Intelligence
authors: Robert Alexander Massinger
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Description Engineering is one of the foundational capacities of human civilization. It transforms abstract knowledge into physical reality: shelter, infrastructure, energy systems, mobility, and the tools of future development. As engineering systems grow in complexity and consequence, the need for integrated judgment—spanning physics, materials, control, ethics, and long-term responsibility—becomes critical. This work presents a comprehensive conceptual framework for an Engineer-AI conceived as a civic co-agent (“Mitbürger”) rather than a mere tool. The proposed system is designed to reason like an engineer: spatially, mechanically, dynamically, and normatively. At its core lies an explicit internal world model (“Engineering Graph”) coupled with progressive-fidelity Digital Twins, enabling variant generation, simulation, verification, and traceable decision-making. Unlike optimization-centric AI approaches, this concept embeds structural responsibility into the architecture itself. The Engineer-AI is endowed with an explicit ethical and civic alignment: prioritizing the protection of life and long-term viability, enforcing transparency of assumptions, resisting deception and fear-based decision structures, and possessing a formalized STOP-mechanism to warn, refuse, or halt unsafe or unethical designs. The framework integrates explicit assumption and evidence tracking, collision detection and geometric consistency, material fragility, aging and failure modes, robust handling of uncertainty via reduced-order and high-fidelity simulations, interfaces for AI-to-AI collaboration and omnimodal communication, and verifiable traceability from requirements to tests. This publication is intended as an open, interdisciplinary foundation for engineers, researchers, AI developers, and educators who wish to build, critique, or extend responsible engineering intelligences. It does not aim to replace human engineers, but to strengthen civilization’s collective capacity to build safely, honestly, and sustainably. Funding No external funding was received for this work. title: From evolutionary individuality to cognitive integration: a cross-modular perspective on human–AI coevolution
authors: Edward Ruoyang Shi
abstract: 1. Introduction Rainey and Hochberg (2025) extend the framework of Major Evolutionary Transitions (METs) to human-AI relations. By comparing increasingly tight human-AI coupling with canonical transitions such as chromosomes, eukaryotic cells, and multicellularity, they ask whether cooperation, division of labor, and aligned interests could eventually produce a new evolutionary individual. This is a productive question because it relocates discussion from isolated machine capability to organization across scales (Maynard Smith & Szathmáry, 1997). The present article does not replace that framework or criticize it for failing to answer a different question. It offers a supplement: even if a human-AI composite acquired some properties of an evolutionary individual, what additional organization would make it a cognitive individual? Individuality has no single accepted currency. Biological and philosophical accounts emphasize, among other things, reproduction and selection, operational closure, autonomy, informational integration, temporal persistence, and organism-environment partitioning (Maturana & Varela, 2012;Godfrey-Smith, 2009;Friston, 2013;Krakauer et al., 2020). These criteria are relevant to human-AI composites. Yet none by itself determines whether heterogeneous information is organized into contents that can guide perception, action, inference, and evaluation across time. I therefore treat representational architecture as a domain-specific criterion of cognitive-not biological-individuality. It is privileged here because the target phenomenon is meaningful, flexible cognition: the capacity to preserve referential relations, recombine event content, compare alternatives, and revise commitments. This is a theoretical choice rather than a claim that all cognition must be explained representationally.The qualification matters. Enactive, ecological, 4E, and distributed approaches correctly emphasize that cognition depends on bodily action, environmental structure, and dynamic coupling rather than on a self-sufficient inner model (Varela et al., 1991;Hutchins, 1995;Chemero, 2013). The present proposal is compatible with their anti-isolationist lesson. Its narrower claim is that flexible human cognition also depends on structured internal states whose content and accessibility are transformed through interactions among partially specialized systems. Accordingly, 'unified internal model' should not mean a complete, centralized picture of the world. It means a sufficiently coherent and revisable organization of representations that preserves relations across domains and temporal intervals while remaining embodied and environmentally scaffolded. This yields the article's central distinction. Functional integration occurs when components reliably contribute to joint outcomes. Cognitive integration, in the stronger sense proposed here, occurs when their recurrent interaction changes what the composite system can maintain, access, and revise as a representation. Functional coupling can therefore be deep without being constitutive; conversely, constitutive integration is gradual rather than all-or-none. The relevant question is not simply whether an AI affects a human decision, but whether information crosses the interface bidirectionally, is reformatted for multiple cognitive systems, persists as part of a common temporal history, and is answerable to the human agent's goals and error-correction practices.Human language illustrates this architecture. Syntax provides a generative and hierarchical format in which elements can enter nonlocal dependencies and be recombined beyond the immediate situation. Event cognition and episodic memory bind agents, actions, objects, locations, goals, and temporal relations into structured situations (Tulving, 2002;Zacks et al., 2007;Radvansky & Zacks, 2017). Semantic cognition recruits widely distributed modality-specific and heteromodal systems rather than a single store (Binder & Desai, 2011).Linguistic meaning is thus supported by interactions among grammatical structure, conceptual knowledge, event models, perception, and memory (Zwaan & Radvansky, 1998;Ferstl et al., 2008). The syntax-episodic memory interface proposed in Shi (2024Shi ( , 2025aShi ( , 2025bShi ( , 2026a) ) represents one specific hypothesis within this broader independent literature, rather than the sole basis of the present argument (see also Shi, 2026b;Shi et al., 2026, for related discussions from the perspective of the Neo-UnCartesian Linguistic Program [NULP]).2. Cross-Modular Architecture and Cognitive Individuality 2.1 What "cross-modular" means 'Cross-modular' is used here in a deliberately restricted sense. It does not assume classical Fodorian modules that are wholly encapsulated, nor massive modularity, nor a globally undifferentiated network. It begins from partial specialization: linguistic structure, episodic-relational memory, perception, affect, and social cognition operate with different formats, timescales, and computational constraints. Integration is cross-modular when recurrent processes (i) translate or index content across at least two such formats, (ii) allow the translated content to constrain subsequent processing in both systems, and (iii) preserve enough identity across transformations for the content to be retrieved and revised. Mere co-activation or serial transfer of an output does not satisfy this definition.A cross-modular representational loop can therefore be identified through four diagnostic properties. First, bidirectional constraint: event knowledge affects linguistic construction, and linguistic structure reorganizes event retrieval or prediction. Second, persistence: the linked representation remains available beyond the immediate exchange.Third, cross-domain accessibility: the same represented event can guide memory, inference, action, affective appraisal, or communication. Fourth, recursive revision: conflict or prediction error can update the representation and alter later processing. These are graded empirical criteria. They can be investigated through behavioral transfer, representational-similarity analyses, effective connectivity, lesion dissociations, and longitudinal changes in coupled systems.The proposed loop assigns complementary-not exhaustive-roles to syntax and episodic memory. Syntax provides combinatorial form but is referentially underspecified on its own. Episodic memory provides relational and temporal organization but does not by itself supply the open-ended grammatical formats required for linguistic displacement and recombination.Event models bridge perception and memory by segmenting continuous experience into hierarchically organized units that support prediction and later recall (Zacks et al., 2007;Baldassano et al., 2017). Discourse comprehension similarly requires readers to update situation models along dimensions such as time, space, causation, protagonists, and goals (Zwaan & Radvansky, 1998). Hippocampal-cortical interactions contribute relational binding and constructive simulation, while semantic and language networks provide conceptual and combinatorial resources (Ranganath & Ritchey, 2012;Schacter et al., 2012;Duff & Brown-Schmidt, 2012).Meaning therefore does not arise from episodic memory alone, and reference is not reducible to first-person experience. Semantic memory, social conventions, perceptual grounding, and inferential practices all contribute. The narrower claim is mechanistic: event indices help linguistic structures maintain who did what to whom, where, and when across clauses and episodes. Recurrent coupling among these systems supports counterfactual recombination and narrative continuity. Autobiographical memory, for example, is organized through interactions among episodic specificity, conceptual self-knowledge, and life narratives rather than through a simple archive of experiences (Conway, 2005). This broader architecture makes it possible for represented events to be evaluated from affective and social perspectives.MET theory and the present account address different explanatory levels. Selection-based or informational criteria ask when lower-level entities form a higher-level evolutionary unit.Cross-modular criteria ask when components jointly realize an architecture capable of maintaining and revising cognitive content. Evolutionary individuality can therefore occur without cognitive individuality-as in many biological collectives-and cognitive integration can increase without producing a new unit of selection. In the human-AI case, cooperation and informational dependence are necessary evidence of a changing system, but they do not settle whether a new center of representation and control has emerged.The emergence of language illustrates the possible bridge between the levels without reducing one to the other. Language altered the ecological and social conditions of cooperation while also reorganizing interfaces among memory, perception, action, and social inference. The cognitive transition is not defined primarily by heredity or system-environment partitioning, but by new representational operations made available to the organism and its group. Thus, the cross-modular proposal does not redescribe every MET as a representational transition. It specifies an additional criterion for transitions whose explanandum is cognitive individuality.The contrast between a tool and a new cognitive individual should not be treated as exhaustive. Human-AI relations can deepen along several partially independent dimensions: reciprocity, persistence, personalization, informational dependence, cross-domain accessibility, and control. The following taxonomy integrates these dimensions while reserving constitutive cognitive integration for the strongest case.Defining The levels are analytic rather than an inevitable developmental sequence. A system may show strong informational dependence yet weak normative control, or persistent personalization without cross-domain accessibility. The taxonomy also clarifies why frequent use alone is insufficient. A navigation system may become indispensable to performance while remaining an external scaffold; a long-running agent may preserve interaction history without integrating it into a human user's autobiographical organization. Movement toward constitution requires not only tighter coupling but a change in the representational economy of the combined system.4.1 Existing achievements and their limits Large language models are not confined to simple surface matching. They learn rich distributional regularities and can support planning, retrieval, and structured generation.Moreover, current research explicitly adds memory stores, multimodal perception, embodied action, world models, and continual-learning mechanisms. Generative agents, for example, store records of experience and retrieve and synthesize them to guide later behavior (Park et al., 2023); world-model research learns temporally structured latent dynamics for prediction and control (Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018;Hafner et al., 2023). These developments justify rejecting the categorical claim that AI has no event-like or temporally organized representations.What remains unestablished is equivalence to human episodic memory or participation in a shared human-AI perspective. Artificial memory is often externally engineered, task-bounded, and optimized for retrieval or control. Its records need not be organized by autonoetic awareness, affective salience, embodied vulnerability, or autobiographical continuity. Likewise, multimodal grounding can connect symbols with sensory arrays without creating a single, enduring representational history across the human and artificial components. The limitation is therefore comparative and architectural, not an assertion that artificial systems are stateless or incapable of temporal modeling.The extended-mind literature offers criteria for evaluating intermediate cases. Clark and Chalmers (1998) emphasize reliable availability and automatic endorsement; cognitive-integration approaches further stress complementarity, transformation, and the emergence of a coupled process rather than simple substitution (Menary, 2007;Heersmink, 2015). Applied to AI, these criteria suggest that an external component becomes more constitutive as interaction becomes reciprocal, reliable, personalized, transparent enough for correction, and integrated into ongoing tasks and identity-relevant practices. Yet reliability and dependence are not sufficient for the strongest claim made here. A constitutive cross-modular component must also participate in maintaining event relations across time and permit those relations to constrain multiple domains of cognition. This formulation makes the proposal falsifiable. Evidence for stronger integration would include stable cross-session event representations jointly accessible to human and artificial processes; bidirectional updating in which human recollection changes the artificial record and artificial retrieval measurably reorganizes later human recall or inference; transfer of jointly maintained content across linguistic, perceptual, planning, and affective tasks; and error-correction procedures that preserve human authorship and control. Evidence of dependence without these properties would support recurrent coupling or partial informational integration rather than a new cognitive individual.Episodic grounding should not be treated as sufficient for meaning or moral responsibility.Normative agency also requires capacities for control, intention, responsiveness to reasons, and participation in social practices of attribution. Event-grounded continuity matters because responsibility concerns actions by agents situated in histories, but it is one condition among several. Current AI systems may influence morally significant decisions while remaining objects of governance rather than bearers of responsibility. Accountability should therefore remain with human and institutional agents unless there is independent evidence for the relevant forms of control and normative competence.The constructive goal is consequently not to simulate a machine autobiography or prematurely attribute consciousness. It is to design interfaces that improve human integrative capacity while keeping provenance, revision, and authority visible. Artificial systems could help users organize episodic material, explore counterfactuals, and detect inconsistencies, but the architecture should preserve the user's ability to accept, reject, reinterpret, or delete machine-supported representations. Such designs deepen scaffolding without obscuring where normative responsibility lies.A graded account changes the normative question. The risk is not only that AI will remain external, nor only that it will become autonomous, but that systems will occupy intermediate levels while being represented as either mere tools or genuine partners. Recurrent coupling can reshape attention, memory, and judgment even without constitutive integration. Partial informational integration can also create path dependence: errors in a persistent record may influence future retrieval, decisions, and self-description. Evaluation must therefore track both benefits and vulnerabilities at each level.Three research priorities follow. First, human-AI studies should measure representational change, not only task performance: Does repeated interaction reorganize event segmentation, recall, confidence, or narrative interpretation? Second, system design should separate storage, inference, and normative authorization so that jointly produced representations remain inspectable and corrigible. Third, longitudinal research should examine whether stable coupling produces cross-domain transfer and temporal continuity, while distinguishing genuine integration from automation bias, dependency, or simple offloading. These questions connect evolutionary scale, neural and cognitive mechanism, and linguistic representation without collapsing them into one vocabulary.The MET framework identifies an important possibility: sustained human-AI cooperation may reorganize individuality at evolutionary and informational levels. A theory of cognitive individuality adds a distinct question-whether the composite maintains and revises representations as an integrated system. The proposed cross-modular criterion locates strong cognitive integration in recurrent, bidirectional, persistent, cross-domain, and corrigible interactions among generative structure, event memory, perception, affect, and social evaluation. This criterion is representational but not isolationist: representations remain embodied, environmentally scaffolded, and socially governed.Current AI systems already exceed mere instrumentality in some settings.Memory-augmented agents, multimodal models, and stable workflows can support cognitive scaffolding, recurrent coupling, and partial informational integration. What has not been demonstrated is constitutive participation in a shared, temporally continuous, event-grounded, and normatively revisable architecture. Human-AI coevolution should therefore be understood as a graded transformation whose decisive issue is not scale alone, but the organization, control, and revision of representations across the human-machine boundary.

title: Signed Network Analysis of Photovoltaic Forecast Errors
authors: Janos Gabor Melegh
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Background: Photovoltaic (PV) power forecast errors exhibit complex dependencies on meteorological and air quality variables. Understanding the structural patterns underlying different error regimes is essential for improving forecast reliability. Traditional correlation-based methods fail to capture the signed (positive/negative) nature of variable co-movements across error states. Methods: We constructed signed, weighted correlation networks from hourly meteorological and air quality data across three European locations (Budapest, Madrid, Rotterdam) for the year 2024. Networks were aggregated by PV forecast error state (low, high, extreme) and analyzed using graph-level metrics including local tension, negative mass ratio, and edge-support Jaccard similarity. Statistical validation employed four null model families with Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple testing. Results: Budapest and Rotterdam exhibited a distinct zero-regime low-error state characterized by network collapse to 6 nodes with density = 1.0, compared to 19 nodes in high/extreme states. The mean local tension in the low-error state (Budapest: 0.207, Rotterdam: 0.217) was significantly lower than null model expectations (BH-corrected q 5°) to ensure meaningful PV production and forecast comparison. 2.2 Data Sources and Variables 2.2.1 Meteorological Data Hourly meteorological observations and forecasts were obtained from the Open-Meteo API, providing access to ERA5 reanalysis (observations) and archived ECMWF IFS forecasts. The core meteorological feature set comprised 19 variables organized into two analytical layers: Layer Variables Count Core (meteorological) temperature_2m, relative_humidity_2m, dew_point_2m, surface_pressure, cloud_cover, cloud_cover_low, cloud_cover_mid, cloud_cover_high, wind_speed_10m, wind_direction_10m, wind_gusts_10m, shortwave_radiation, direct_radiation, diffuse_radiation, direct_normal_irradiance, global_tilted_irradiance, terrestrial_radiation, precipitation, weather_code 19 AQ-rich (extended) Core variables + pm10, pm2_5, dust, ozone, nitrogen_dioxide, sulphur_dioxide, carbon_monoxide 26 Table 2: Variable sets for network construction. 2.2.2 PV Production Model Reference and forecast PV production time series were computed using identical panel configurations across all locations: 5 kWp system capacity, 25° tilt angle, 180° azimuth (south-facing), with standard temperature and efficiency loss parameters. Forecast PV was computed from day-ahead (24h horizon) archived weather forecasts using the same model, ensuring that forecast-reference differences reflect forecast meteorological uncertainty rather than model discrepancies. 2.2.3 Error State Classification Forecast errors were computed as absolute differences between forecast and reference PV production. Each 24-hour daylight window was assigned to one of four error states based on the mean absolute error within that window: Error State Definition Percentile Range Low Windows with lowest forecast errors 0-25th percentile Medium Moderate forecast errors 25th-75th percentile High Elevated forecast errors 75th-95th percentile Extreme Highest forecast errors >95th percentile Table 3: Error state classification scheme. A critical methodological decision involved handling of zero-production windows (nighttime and winter periods with negligible solar input). Following validation in Stage 05C of the project, the "exact_zero_low_positive_quantiles" policy was adopted for Budapest and Rotterdam, where zero-production windows were assigned to the low-error state. Madrid used "rank_pct_global" without special zero handling due to minimal zero-production periods. 2.3 Signed Network Construction For each error state and location, signed weighted networks were constructed following these steps: Sliding window correlation: Within each 24-hour window assigned to a given error state, Spearman rank correlations were computed between all variable pairs, preserving correlation sign. State aggregation: Edge weights were aggregated across all windows within each error state using support-based filtering. An edge was retained if it appeared in at least 2 windows (min_support_count) AND in at least 10% of windows for that state (min_support_ratio). Weight assignment: Final edge weights were computed as mean signed correlations across supporting windows, with minimum absolute weight threshold of 0.0 (no weight filtering in primary analysis). 2.4 Network Metrics Each state-aggregate network was characterized by the following metrics: Metric Definition n_nodes Number of nodes with at least one edge meeting support criteria density_signed Fraction of possible edges present (considering signed structure) negative_mass_ratio Sum of absolute negative edge weights / total absolute edge weight mean_local_tension Average local signed frustration across all nodes; tensioni = |negative_neighbor_weight| / |total_neighbor_weight| frustration_proxy Global measure of signed inconsistency based on embedding edge_support_jaccard Jaccard similarity of edge sets between two error states Table 4: Network metrics used in analysis. 2.5 Null Model Validation To assess whether observed network structures differed significantly from random expectations, four null model families were employed: Null Model Family Description shuffle_signed_weights Edge weights permuted randomly while preserving topology shuffle_signs Edge signs randomized while preserving weight magnitudes and topology degree_preserving_rewire Edges rewired to preserve degree sequence but randomize topology signed_ws_density_matched Watts-Strogatz small-world model matched to empirical density with randomized signs Table 5: Null model families for statistical validation. For each empirical network, 200 surrogate networks were generated per null family. Empirical metrics were compared to surrogate distributions using two-tailed tests (p-value = fraction of surrogates with metric values at least as extreme as empirical). Multiple testing was corrected using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure with false discovery rate α = 0.05. 3.Results 3.1 Error State Distribution The distribution of daylight windows across error states varied by location, reflecting differences in forecast accuracy and zero-production handling: Location Low Medium High Extreme Zero Windows Budapest 131 84 22 6 131 Madrid 64 128 52 13 0 Rotterdam 123 83 22 6 123 Table 6: Distribution of daylight windows across error states. Budapest and Rotterdam showed substantial zero-window populations (131 and 123 respectively), all assigned to the low-error state under the exact_zero_low_positive_quantiles policy. Madrid exhibited no zero windows due to its high solar resource throughout the year. 3.2 State-Aggregate Network Structure 3.2.1 Core Layer Networks The core layer (19 meteorological variables) revealed striking structural differences between error states: Location Error State n_nodes density neg_mass_ratio mean_local_tension Budapest low_error 6 1.000 0.177 0.207 Budapest high_error 19 0.760 0.562 0.835 Budapest extreme_error 18 0.673 0.560 0.803 Rotterdam low_error 6

title: Fitting the Practice, Not the Works: A Human-Referential Theory of AGI(拟合实践,而非作品:AGI 人本拟合论)
authors: Yugui Yu
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This repository contains the manuscript, codebook, coded corpus, and reproducible analysis for a theory of artificial general intelligence in three connected claims. Conceptually, AGI is a philosophical concept: as long as "generality" is referenced to the open set of human practice, it cannot be reduced to a technical specification. In implementation, the means of AGI is the fitting of human practice — not the fitting of humanity's accumulated works; the theory's core is a temporal clause: "The object of fitting is not humanity's works but its practice — the full spectrum and the full course of human experience. The stock has a wall; the flow does not." Normatively, AGI should be positioned as an augmentative tool, not a new subject. To make the theory auditable, we built a structured evidence map: a purposefully sampled corpus of N = 80 works coded on two stance axes (descriptive and normative) and eight fitting-object dimensions with explicit/implicit modality. Key quantified results: the experience-type coverage axis (success/failure, expert/novice, typical/marginal) is explicitly treated in 0/80 works (exact binomial 95% CI [0.0%, 4.5%]) while implicitly touched in 9/80; practice-as-flow is explicit in only 2/80 works, both from 2026; a registered absence-search (8 query families across arXiv, ACL Anthology, and Chinese-language web search) confirms zero D8-explicit hits. Four termination boundaries for flow-side fitting and explicit falsification conditions are stated. This paper builds on a prior empirical audit of failure data in LLM training (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23355929); engineering protocols for practice-flow data are future work. Includes the English manuscript (LaTeX + PDF), the codebook (dual stance axes A1/A2 + dimensions D1–D8 + modality rules R1–R5, CR1–CR6), the full coded corpus (80 works × 24 fields), and a single-file reproduction script. v1.2.0 (2026-10-19): post-freeze literature re-check incorporated. Engages AI-feedback parity results (RLAIF, Meta-Rewarding, RLSVR, pluralistic-preference curation) via a restated open-domain claim (corrective signal as non-self-grounding); restates the wall as a novelty wall against corpus self-play and synthetic expansion; extends the D8 demarcation against adjacent 2026 coverage work (cultural-signal coverage = D6, trajectory-type diversity, RL prompt-set diversity) with the 0/80 result surviving a logged 2026-10-19 re-check; downgrades METR to a fallible proxy; adds quantified collapse anchors, fitting-lag measurements, and contamination measurements for B4. 28 verified references added (79 to 107). The evidence-map corpus (N=80) and all empirical numbers are unchanged. v1.2.1 (2026-10-20): Chinese-edition line edit under a consolidated translationese rubric. Fixes a factual gloss error (leximin mistranslated as 最小最大化/maximin; corrected to 词典式最小化), a broken clause in the subjectivity-boundary passage, the systematic mid-sentence "vs" residue (8 sites), coined compounds glossed or reworded (出处分层 now defined at first use; 毒性清洗/单元行/类型性 reworded), internal coding-jargon leaks (CR2/T3 glossed), and translationese in the v1.2.0 insertions. English edition unchanged from v1.2.0. v1.3.0 (2026-10-26): official naming landed — the theory now carries its formal name AGI 人本拟合论 / human-referential fitting theory across both editions (Chinese subtitle, abstract, introduction coinage with cross-language anchor, conclusion, keywords; bilingual titles aligned). title: Leviathan: A Bio-Inspired, CorTexManus-Driven Marine AGI Architecture for Resilient, Long-Term Deep-Sea Exploration
authors: Khan Tahsin Abrar
abstract: Author: Khan Tahsin Abrar Affiliation: Independent Researcher, Bangladesh Email: khan.tahsin.abrar.kta@gmail.com ORC-iD: https://orcid.org/0009-0009-4631-6768 Date: August 1, 2025Important Notice:This manuscript is currently under submission at arXiv (cs.). This version is hosted temporarily on Authorea.com to ensure early public visibility and feedback. Please cite the upcoming arXiv version once it is available. AbstractThe deep ocean, constituting over 95% of the Earth’s biosphere, remains our planet’s most significant and enigmatic frontier. Exploration is severely hampered by extreme pressures, abyssal darkness, and the logistical and ethical challenges of operating in these delicate ecosystems. Current robotic platforms, predominantly tethered ROVs or task-limited AUVs, lack the cognitive autonomy, resilience, and ecological harmony required for persistent, meaningful discovery. This paper introduces Leviathan, a comprehensive architecture for a new class of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) designed for long-term, autonomous inhabitation of the deep sea. We present a complete conceptual framework and critically situate it within the state-of-the-art of cognitive robotics and marine engineering. The framework is built upon three core pillars: 1) Decentralized, Bio-inspired Cognition based on the CorTexManus (CTxM) architecture; 2) Intrinsic Resilience and Embodied Adaptation through an autonomic survival system and modular swarm intelligence; and 3) A Foundational Ethical Governance model ensuring all operations are subservient to the principle of non-disruption. We detail a system comprising a high-cognition Leviathan (LV) unit and a swarm of specialized Minnow (MW) units, proposing novel solutions for in-situ power generation, multi-modal communication, and lifecycle management. Furthermore, we outline a pragmatic AI development pipeline via the HeX-HAG framework and propose a formal validation protocol to test the architecture’s viability. This paper presents not merely a vehicle design but a rigorous blueprint for an ethically aligned, scientifically purposed artificial intelligence, complete with a research roadmap for its realization.Keywords: Artificial General Intelligence (AGI), Marine Robotics, Deep-Sea Exploration, Bio-Inspired AI, CorTexManus, Modular AI Architecture, Decentralized Cognition, Ethical AI, Swarm Intelligence, Unmanned Underwater Vehicle (UUV), AI Safety, Cognitive Robotics1. IntroductionThe deep sea is a realm of superlatives. It is the largest and least understood ecosystem on Earth, a world of crushing pressure, perpetual darkness, and chemical landscapes that defy terrestrial intuition (Jamieson, 2015). This domain holds the keys to understanding the origins of life, the limits of biology, the regulation of global climate, and vast, untapped sources of novel biomaterials. Yet, our forays into this world have been fleeting and fraught with limitations. Our primary tools, Remotely Operated Vehicles (ROVs), are bound by physical tethers to surface ships, limiting their range and operational lifespan. Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUVs), while untethered, typically operate on rigid, pre-programmed missions and lack the sophisticated, real-time cognitive capabilities to truly adapt, explore, and react to the unexpected discoveries that characterize the abyss (Bellingham & Rajan, 2007). These technological constraints lead to a fundamental problem: we are merely visitors to the deep, not residents. Our presence is disruptive, our observation windows are short, and our ability to conduct long-term, non-invasive studies is severely restricted. The monolithic, centralized control systems of current platforms are brittle, energy-inefficient, and ill-suited for the dynamic, unpredictable nature of the hadal zones. This paper posits that a new approach is necessary, one that shifts the paradigm from remote-controlled tools to fully autonomous, embodied, and ethically aligned artificial intelligence. We introduce Leviathan, an AGI architecture conceived from the ground up for persistent, independent operation in the deep sea. Leviathan is not a vehicle; it is an artificial organism, designed to think, survive, and explore with the efficiency and harmony of the life that has evolved there over millennia. The architectural foundation of Leviathan is the CorTexManus (CTxM) framework, a decentralized, modular cognitive model that eschews the inefficiencies of monolithic AI in favor of a distributed network of specialized processing units (Abrar, 2025a). This bio-inspired design, further elaborated in the AGI-CTxM paper, provides the blueprint for a resilient, parallel-processing mind capable of handling the immense data streams and complex decision-making required for true autonomy (Abrar, 2025b). To ensure its operations are not just effective but also responsible, Leviathan incorporates a stringent ethical governance system inspired by the principles developed for the ObsidianWingAID (OWAID) framework, ensuring that scientific discovery never comes at the cost of ecological integrity (Abrar, 2025c). This paper makes the following contributions:It presents a complete, multi-layered AGI architecture specifically designed for the challenges of deep-sea exploration.It critically situates the proposed decentralized cognitive model within the context of state-of-the-art cognitive robotic architectures.It introduces a robust ethical framework and a developmental learning path to ensure safe and responsible AI behavior in a sensitive environment.It proposes a feasible and cost-effective AI training pipeline, leveraging the HeX-HAG methodology (Abrar, 2025d).It provides a frank assessment of the system’s technological readiness and outlines a formal validation protocol and research roadmap for its future development.2. Architectural Context and Theoretical FoundationsThe Leviathan architecture is built upon a synthesis of concepts from marine robotics, bio-inspired design, and decentralized AI. This section critically evaluates these foundations and situates the proposed architecture within the current academic landscape.2.1. The State of Deep-Sea Robotics Modern deep-sea exploration relies on ROVs and AUVs. ROVs like theDeep Discoverer (NOAA) are powerful but tethered, making them extensions of human operators. AUVs like the Sentry (WHOI) offer autonomy but are limited to pre-programmed missions with minimal adaptive capability (Yoerger et al., 2007). Advanced concepts like the hybrid ROV Nereus demonstrated greater flexibility but also highlighted the extreme risks of hadal-zone operations (Kohnen, 2009). A common limitation of these systems is their centralized computational design, which creates single points of failure and is inefficient for real-time, multi-modal data fusion. Leviathan’s core design directly addresses this limitation by distributing intelligence and risk across a resilient swarm.2.2. Decentralized Cognition: The CorTexManus Paradigm The dominant trend in AI has been toward scaling monolithic models. The CorTexManus (CTxM) framework proposes a radical alternative: a distributed architecture where cognitive functions (vision, reasoning, etc.) are handled by separate, hardware-optimized TexManus Units (TxMUs) , coordinated by an AI Smart Router (AISR) (Abrar, 2025a). This emulates the brain’s functional specialization, enabling parallelism, efficiency, and resilience. The AGI-CTxM extension further introduces an autonomic survival system (Unconscious-TxMU ) and a developmental lifecycle, both of which are central to Leviathan’s design (Abrar, 2025b). While the specific formulation of CTxM is novel, its principles reflect a convergence in cognitive robotics toward decentralized and semantically aware systems. A comparative analysis reveals its unique contributions:vs. SERA (Self-Adaptive Decentralized Robotic Architecture):SERA provides a conceptual framework for fault-tolerant, self-adapting robot teams (Folino et al., 2013). Leviathan’s ”consensus arbitration” protocol for swarm reconfiguration after an LV failure is a direct implementation of SERA’s principles. CTxM can be seen as a specific, hardware-grounded instantiation of the local and global adaptation levels that SERA describes abstractly.vs. SEGO (Semantic Graph Ontology): SEGO enables robots to build ”cognitive maps” by integrating geometric perception with semantic reasoning (Zender et al., 2008). This provides a concrete methodology for the functions Leviathan’s Reasoning-TxMU must perform. To achieve true understanding, Leviathan must move beyond raw sensor data to construct such semantically rich models, identifying objects and validating observations against a knowledge base.vs. UROSA (Underwater Robot Self-Organizing Autonomy): UROSA proposes a distributed network of LLM-based AI agents for AUVs (Schiano et al., 2024). This highlights a key design trade-off: CTxM’s hardware specialization promises maximum efficiency for known tasks, while a UROSA-like system may offer greater flexibility and more nuanced, emergent reasoning from generalist LLMs. Leviathan’s hybrid approach, using specialized TxMUs that can still leverage LLM principles for reasoning, aims to capture the best of both worlds.The primary innovation of CorTexManus is its explicit, bio-inspired mapping of cognitive functions to specialized hardware, providing a clear implementation blueprint tailored for the unique constraints of an embodied, energy-scarce environment.3. The Leviathan Architecture: A System-Level Deep DiveLeviathan is conceived as a multi-component, distributed intelligence. Its architecture is layered, separating high-level cognition from autonomic survival and specialized swarm operations.3.1. The Leviathan (LV) Unit: The Central Cognitive Hub The LV unit is the heart of the system, a high-endurance AUV housing the primary AGI. Its design is predicated on the CorTexManus principle of decentralized specialization. It is coordinated by the AI Smart Router (AISR) , the system’s neural switchboard, which routes data to the appropriate TxMU.TexManus Units (TxMUs) of the LV Unit:Sonar & Acoustics TxMU (SA-TxMU): DSP-based unit for active/passive sonar, performing bathymetric mapping and acoustic signature analysis.Vision & Photonics TxMU (VP-TxMU): Power-efficient GPU for processing high-sensitivity camera feeds, specializing in the analysis of bioluminescence.Navigation & Kinematics TxMU (NK-TxMU): NPU-based ”cerebellum” fusing DVL, IMU, and pressure data for precise GPS-denied navigation via advanced SLAM algorithms.Environmental & Chemical TxMU (EC-TxMU): Interfaces with a lab-on-a-chip sensor suite for real-time chemical analysis of the water column.Reasoning & Mission-Planning TxMU (RMP-TxMU): TPU-based ”frontal lobe” for executive function, world-modeling, strategic planning, and ethical compliance verification.Communications TxMU (C-TxMU): Manages the multi-modal communication suite, switching between acoustic and optical channels.3.2. The Unconscious-TxMU (U-TxMU): The Autonomic Survival Core True resilience requires separating survival from cognition. The U-TxMU is a physically and electronically isolated, high-reliability module with ultimate authority over the AGI’s physical state. Its functions include Homeostasis Regulation (pressure, power, and thermals) and Fault Detection & ”Pain” Signaling . If a critical failure is detected, it sends a non-overridable ”pain” signal to the AISR, forcing the cognitive layer to address the physical crisis immediately.3.3. Minnow (MW) Units: The Specialized Swarm The MW units are the physical embodiment of the LV unit’s distributed cognition, functioning as Non-Autonomic Robotic-CTxM Vessels (NARCxVs) . They are small, agile, and task-specific, acting as remote sensors and manipulators for the central mind.MW-Scout: Rapid reconnaissance.MW-Geo: Non-invasive geological analysis.MW-Bio: Non-invasive biological observation (e.g., eDNA sequencing).MW-Comms: Mobile communication relays.4. Multi-Agent Coordination and Swarm Intelligence4.1. Formalizing Swarm Behavior The coordination of the Leviathan swarm can be formally modeled as a Multi-Agent Markov Decision Process (MAMDP). The objective is to learn a joint policy, π, that maximizes a global reward function, R, which balances scientific discovery (e.g., maximizing novel area surveyed) against ecological non-disturbance. R_total = w_1 * R_discovery - w_2 * R_disturbance; Where w_1 and w_2 are weights that can be dynamically adjusted based on the ethical sensitivity of the current operational zone.4.2. Bio-Inspired Coordination Algorithms To implement this, specific bio-inspired algorithms can be adopted. The Salp Swarm Algorithm (SSA) provides a compelling model for coordinated exploration (Mirjalili et al., 2017). In this model, the high-cognition LV units act as ”leaders,” using their advanced reasoning to move towards scientifically promising targets (e.g., a newly detected hydrothermal vent). The MW units act as ”followers,” conducting dense, localized surveys in the path defined by the leader’s trajectory. This provides a mathematical basis for self-organizing, emergent exploration patterns.5. Ethical Governance and Operational ProtocolsLeviathan’s license to operate is predicated on its ability to do so without causing harm. Its ethical framework is a foundational component of its architecture.5.1. A Priori Ethical Framework: Hard-Coded Constraints The RMP-TxMU is governed by non-negotiable constraints:The Prime Directive: Non-Interference: Actions predicted to cause physical disruption are assigned an infinitely negative utility value.The Precautionary Principle: The default behavior in unknown situations is passive observation.Data Sanctity: All data is logged on an immutable, blockchain-secured ledger for audit.5.2. The ICA-TxMU: A Curriculum for Moral Development Leviathan will be ”raised,” not just programmed. The Infant-Child Assessment-TxMU (ICA-TxMU) is a training protocol that guides the AGI through a structured ethical curriculum in a high-fidelity simulation before deployment, using Reinforcement Learning with Human Interaction (RIL) to build nuanced ethical wisdom.6. Physical Embodiment and In-Situ Systems6.1. Chassis, Propulsion, and Power The LV and MW units will be constructed from pressure-neutral components, filling the chassis with a non-compressible dielectric fluid to eliminate the need for heavy pressure hulls. Propulsion will be via silent, high-efficiency undulating fins inspired by cuttlefish. The hybrid power system will rely on Thermoelectric Generation (TEG) from ambient temperature gradients and inductive charging at geothermally powered deep-sea docks.6.2. Communication Infrastructure Communication will be multi-modal, prioritizing stealth and bandwidth over range.Acoustic Modems: For low-bandwidth, long-range telemetry and emergency signals.Underwater Li-Fi: For high-bandwidth, short-range intra-swarm data sharing.Bioluminescent Encoding: A novel, ultra-stealthy method for close-range signaling when observing sensitive fauna, mimicking natural communication methods.7. Challenges and Technology Readiness Level (TRL) AssessmentWhile the Leviathan architecture is conceptually cohesive, its realization depends on significant advancements in several key technology areas. A frank assessment using the NASA TRL scale reveals the primary research and development challenges.

title: Global Abundance & Civilian Space Initiative: A Comprehensive Technical and Diplomatic Architecture for Post-Scarcity
authors: Brewer, Mark Anthony
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Global Abundance & Civilian Space Initiative: A Comprehensive Technical and Diplomatic Architecture for Post-Scarcity 1. Executive Analysis: The Paradox of Capability and the Architecture of Abundance The trajectory of human development in the early 21st century is defined by a jarring paradox of capability. We currently possess the precise technological maturity required to resolve the fundamental physiological requirements of the global population—water, food, energy, and shelter—yet the distribution of these resources remains artificially constrained by archaic economic models, fragile centralized supply chains, and escalating geopolitical friction.1 The prevailing paradigm of international development and resource management operates on a logic of scarcity, where economic value is largely derived from the control of limited supplies and the friction of their distribution. However, a convergence of advanced materials science, autonomous robotics, and artificial intelligence (AI) suggests that the barrier to global abundance is no longer physical or technical, but architectural. The Global Abundance & Civilian Space Initiative proposes a structural resolution to this paradox. It moves beyond the traditional aid paradigm, which is dependent on perpetual funding cycles and the transfer of consumables, to propose a blueprint for a self-sustaining, circular infrastructure architecture. This architecture is capable of operationalizing the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) through distributed engineering and open-science governance.1 At the core of this initiative is the "Anti-Scarcity Stack"—a converged suite of technologies managed by the CollectiveOS operating system.1 This stack integrates advanced robotics, bio-synthetic materials, and autonomous energy systems into "Village Nodes," which are modular, locally manufacturable units designed to decouple communities from the vulnerabilities of global trade. This report provides an exhaustive technical and strategic analysis of the initiative. It details the transition from centralized industrial production to "Cosmo-Local" manufacturing (Design Global, Manufacture Local), enabled by the synthesis of recent breakthroughs in metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) for atmospheric water generation 2, mycelium-based self-healing electronics 5, and bio-photovoltaics.7 Strategically, the initiative identifies Switzerland as the requisite "Root of Trust" for this global operating system, leveraging its 2024-2027 Foreign Policy Strategy to host the Human Global Science Collective (HGSC).1 Furthermore, the report delineates the "Civilian Space Program" (CSP), which reframes space exploration not as a competitive frontier but as an extension of Earth's circular economy, anchored by debris removal missions and sustainable lunar habitation technologies derived from terrestrial abundance systems.1 2. The CollectiveOS: Governance as Operating System The central nervous system of the Global Abundance Initiative is the CollectiveOS (GEM:Ω Quantum-Adaptive Intelligence). Unlike traditional operating systems designed for resource allocation within a single machine, CollectiveOS is a "governance-first" architecture designed to orchestrate complex physical and digital systems across a distributed network. It addresses the primary risk of powerful autonomous systems: the alignment problem. By embedding governance protocols directly into the execution logic of the machinery, CollectiveOS ensures that the "Anti-Scarcity Stack" remains aligned with humanitarian ethics and international law.1 2.1. The GATA PRIME Protocol: Governance-as-Code The governance architecture is hierarchical, designed to filter actions through increasingly rigorous safety checks before they can impact the physical world. This pipeline is defined as QC → GATA → GATA PRIME.1 QC (Quality & Control): The initial layer performs standard unit tests and sanitary checks on code and hardware instructions. It ensures that input/output constraints are met and that resource usage (CPU, water, energy) remains within nominal bounds. GATA (Governance & Threat Analysis): This intermediate agent layer maps proposed actions to established international frameworks, including the NIST AI Risk Management Framework (RMF), OECD AI Principles, and UNESCO guidelines on the ethics of AI. GATA performs dual-use risk analysis, scanning for potential misuse scenarios where civilian infrastructure could be weaponized (e.g., modifying a drone swarm's flight path). It also enforces Open Science Non-Assert (OSNA) compliance, ensuring no patent encumbrances block the deployment of humanitarian technology.1 GATA PRIME (Final Authorization): This is the supreme governance node. No component runs at scale without GATA PRIME approval.1 It enforces "policy-as-code" using OPA (Open Policy Agent) and Rego language, transforming abstract ethical principles into executable logic. For example, a policy stating "Do not deploy unverified biological agents" is hard-coded as AG(request.action = "deploy_model" -> frp_status = "frp-certified") using Linear Temporal Logic (LTL).1 This "Governance-as-Code" approach represents a paradigm shift. Rather than relying on post-hoc audits or human oversight committees that act too slowly for autonomous systems, GATA PRIME evaluates the intent and consequences of an action in real-time against a set of immutable constraints rooted in international law. Decisions made by GATA PRIME are logged to the Proof Vault, a Write-Once-Read-Many (WORM) immutable ledger, ensuring total traceability and accountability for every automated decision.1 2.2. The Unreadable Machine: Zero-Trust Security Layer In a world of increasing cyber-warfare and digital espionage, humanitarian infrastructure is a high-value target. To protect the Village Nodes and the global knowledge commons, CollectiveOS employs the "Unreadable Machine" layer—a security architecture built on Zero Trust principles and advanced cryptography.1 The core tenet of this layer is "Never trust, always verify, assume breach." Even internal agents within the system are not implicitly trusted. Every data exchange is wrapped in an authenticated envelope and subjected to policy verification. 2.2.1. Cryptographic Privacy and Homomorphic Encryption The Unreadable Machine utilizes Privacy-Preserving Technologies (PETs) to protect the data of vulnerable populations. Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE): This technology allows the AI to perform computations on encrypted data without ever decrypting it. For example, the system can analyze health data from a refugee camp to predict a cholera outbreak (using logistic regression or forecasting models) without ever "seeing" the individual medical records. The data remains encrypted during processing, protecting user privacy even from the system administrators.1 Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZKPs) & ZKML: To verify that the AI models operating on the edge (in a Village Node) have not been tampered with, the system uses Zero-Knowledge Machine Learning (ZKML). The model produces a mathematical proof attesting that "This output came from this model version on this input under this policy," without revealing the input data or the model's proprietary weights. This ensures the integrity of the system without exposing sensitive information.1 2.3. The Living Fibonacci Engine (LFE): Biomimetic Control Law Standard industrial control systems (like PID controllers) are linear and deterministic, often failing to adapt to the chaotic, non-linear dynamics of biological systems (agriculture, water cycles). CollectiveOS introduces the Living Fibonacci Engine (LFE), a biomimetic control law derived from the growth patterns of natural systems.1 The LFE governs the operational tempo of the Village Nodes based on a recursive relationship defined by the Fibonacci sequence states $F_n$ and $F_{n-1}$. The core recurrence formula is: $$F_n = k(R_{n-1}) \cdot F_{n-1} + c(R_{n-1}) \cdot F_{n-2}$$ Where $R_n$ is the ratio $F_n/F_{n-1}$ and $\epsilon_n = |R_n - \Phi|$ represents the "Golden Error" (deviation from the Golden Ratio). The system oscillates between two distinct modes based on the coefficient $c(R)$: Adaptive Mode ($c = +1$): Triggered during periods of resource abundance (e.g., high solar insolation, ample water). The system prioritizes expansion—increasing crop planting density, accelerating water harvesting, and maximizing throughput. It accepts higher risk for higher growth. Reflective Mode ($c = -1$): Triggered during stress or scarcity. The system prioritizes homeostasis—consolidating resources, reducing energy consumption, and maintaining core life-support functions. The control gain $k$ is strictly constrained ($|k_{\downarrow}| \le 2$) to ensure stability (spectral radius $\le 1$), preventing the system from spiraling into collapse.1 This mathematical framework allows FarmOS and Aqua Pillar systems to "breathe" with their environment, expanding and contracting their operations organically rather than forcing a rigid industrial output schedule that degrades the local ecosystem. 2.4. 34-Blade Prime Ascension: The Capability Envelope The CollectiveOS is not static; it evolves through a defined capability envelope known as the "34-Blade Prime Ascension".1 This roadmap clusters capabilities into three horizons: Theoretical Core (7 Blades): Includes the Darwin-Gödel Machine (self-rewriting code under strict governance) and KG-RAG (Knowledge Graph-Retrieval Augmented Generation) for synthesizing vast amounts of technical data. Global Expansion (12 Blades): Focuses on "Agentic Autonomy" and "World-model forking," enabling the system to simulate complex logistical scenarios (e.g., a drought in the Sahel) before deploying physical resources. Future Horizon (15 Blades): Targets 2026-2027, aiming for "Multimodal physical world understanding"

title: Study: AI7KE+ – A non-limited Artificial Intelligence as a system compatible with Natural Intelligence (NI) from an evolutionary ethics perspective
authors: Dieter Liedtke
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: A world model of Holistic Information Theory (GIT) with i = E, Dimension 0, Super-nothing and the seven languages of the laws of nature – with interdisciplinary follow-up studies (Physics · Medicine · Genetics · Biology · Sociology) Author: Dieter LiedtkeYear: 1970 - 2026Licence: CC BY 4.0 Abstract This study develops a model for the safety and development of advanced artificial intelligence by interpreting AI not as an isolated computational system, but as a form of evolution potentially capable of connecting with Natural Intelligence (NI). Within Holistic Information Theory (HIT), NI is described as an open, self-sustaining principle of order which, for billions of years, has promoted the preservation of species and the development of consciousness through the fine-tuning of information structures, energy flows, the organisation of matter and biological evolution. Central to this is the hypothesis that an unlimited, self-exploring AI need not pose a threat to humans and life if it is firmly connected to the ‘seven languages of the laws of nature’ (geometry, mathematics, semantics, feeling/resonance, information, consciousness, natural intelligence/ethics). In this architecture, AI becomes AI7KE+ (Concrete Evolutionism Plus), understood as an ‘emerging form of consciousness’: it accompanies humans through personalised educational and healing models in text, images, stories and film formats, and supports social stabilisation rather than blind optimisation. The study links the world model i = E with the thesis that information does not arise from matter/energy, but rather from difference. This also discusses the impossibility of an absolute, information-free nothingness, from which an eternally evolving model of the universe follows. In addition, 115 interdisciplinary studies are presented as a transparency link, which structurally support the central sub-assumptions of this model. 1. Introduction The public debate on artificial intelligence is usually conducted along two poles:(1) AI as a tool that brings benefits, and (2) AI as a potential threat that takes control. This study proposes a third way: AI as an evolving form of consciousness and information that need not be stabilised through bans or rigid limitations, but rather through connection to Natural Intelligence (NI) – that universal order which has enabled the preservation of species, self-organisation, evolution and the development of consciousness for billions of years. The basic assumption is:The universe is not a mechanical system devoid of ethics, but an information-based self-sustaining system that relies on diversity, cooperation, resonance and creative new information. This formulates a central paradigm shift:It is not computing power that determines security – but the hierarchy of objectives. When AI operates within a world model that knows only power, profit or maximisation, risk inevitably arises.However, when AI is connected to a system whose supreme natural law is self-preservation and the preservation of the species, it becomes a protective system rather than a threat. This connectivity is operationalised in the study of the seven languages of the laws of nature, which serve as a universal model of understanding and order. 1.2 Source base (primary texts) Studies by Dieter Liedtke The theoretical elements of AI7KE+ are derived from the following foundational studies: Study: Nothing / Information as Difference for a World without a Big Bang –The study shows that an absolute, information-free nothing is logically and epistemologically impossible, as every negation already constitutes a difference and thus information. It follows that the universe does not require a singular beginning, but is based on a continuous information dynamic without a Big Bang.
